Cunningham's anti-trans comments open WNBA to its latest hijacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
02:03:03 UTC
11:03:03 KST

analysis
Sophie Cunningham's stance on transgender athletes has opened WNBA up to its latest hijacking
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.
Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.
However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.
White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.
"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.
"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."
White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.
It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.
Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.
Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".
White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.
Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.
The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.
A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.
For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.
Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".
When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".
"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.
"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."
Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.
Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.
Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.
"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.
"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."
The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.
While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.
Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".
Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.
Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.
It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.
White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".
Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.
Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.
The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.
She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.
There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.
Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.
Republican party's bid to claim Clark
Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.
While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.
Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.
That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.
Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.
The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".
The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".
Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.
As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.
Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".
Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.
A bizarre sex toy invasion
The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.
Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.
The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.
Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.
Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.
One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.
"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens,"
Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".
"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.
"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."
Loading...
The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.
A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.
Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.
That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.
Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

She wants the public to get to know him — the son, the brother, the young man that she knew. “I find the way people talk about him incredibly painful, to be honest,” she says. “He was a good person.”
These are the subjective recollections of a mother who cannot and will not accept what her son did — and whose account is difficult to reconcile with what authorities established about him both before and after the attack.
She asks that her name not be published, nor any photograph or recording of her voice.
“I have two other children I have to think about,” she says.
* * *
On the evening of July 25, Ballout drove a rented van into a crowd on the fringes of Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade.
After coming to a stop, he got out of the car and, according to authorities, began attacking people with a machete before fleeing on foot. One person was killed, and at least 29 were injured.
Around 20 hours later, special forces tracked Ballout to a garden in suburban Spandau, where he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife when they tried to arrest him. Police opened fire, and Ballout was shot dead. Nine days later, he was buried at Gatow Cemetery in Berlin.
The person killed in Ballout’s attack was a 65-year-old woman from Poland who had traveled to Berlin with her daughter specifically for Christopher Street Day.
Not far away, a gay refugee from Iraq was celebrating at an electronic music event when panic spread through the streets. He had fled a country where being openly gay could put his life at risk. Germany was supposed to be different.
Granted anonymity to speak openly, he said: “For many people, freedom is something they never have to think about. For me, it means being able to love someone, to leave the house in the morning without wondering whether I could be attacked or killed for who I am.”
After the attack, he said, that feeling of safety cracked. “That old fear was suddenly back.”
Sitting across from me just weeks later, Ballout’s mother is dressed in all black, her headscarf framing a face that looks exhausted. There are deep shadows beneath her eyes. She speaks so quietly that at times I have to lean in to hear. The only other sound in the room is the monotonous hum of a fan.
Advertisement
On the coffee table lay empty coffee cups, an open packet of TUC crackers and a box of iron tablets. Propped between them is a framed photograph of Ballout, a faint grin on his face.
She doesn’t want to begin our conversation with the attack; she wants to start with her son. She reaches for her phone and starts showing me videos. In one, he is a little boy in swim trunks, running along a beach and laughing. In another, he is an adult, dancing exuberantly through the living room with his family. He jumps onto the couch and pulls his sisters along, making everyone laugh.
His mother talks of evenings spent together watching television or playing Monopoly, how he would sometimes cheat if he were about to lose. As she speaks, her smiles give way to tears, and her tears give way to smiles.
The contrast with the image of the terrorist could hardly be greater.
* * *
Four days before our interview, I visited the neighborhood where Ballout grew up. Children were crisscrossing a courtyard, neighbors leaning out of windows or standing outside doorways. I asked them about him.
All their answers were strikingly similar: “He always said hello;” “he was polite;” “he was helpful.”
No one disputed what Ballout did. No one tried to excuse it. And yet, no one could explain how the young man they knew was capable of such an act.
Sitting in his mother’s living room a few days later, her phone rings, and for a brief moment, Arabic singing fills the room. “That’s his voice,” she says. Her ringtone is a recording of her son reciting an Islamic prayer.
But is it just an innocuous recording?
Court records show Ballout repeatedly posted videos containing Islamic State propaganda dating back to 2024, before starting to circulate recordings of his own. In some of the audio files obtained by WELT, which is — like POLITICO — part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters network, he recited the Quran; in others, he appeared to preach. He had hundreds of followers on TikTok and Telegram, with comments praising his voice.
But Ballout’s online messages were radical, speaking of “unbelievers,” God’s “agonizing punishment,” and his rejection of democracy and the German legal system.
Advertisement
Online, he went by the name Abu Muawiyah — a reference to the first caliph of the Umayyad dynasty who emerged victorious over the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali and his followers, from which Shiite Islam later emerged. It is also a signal of his shifting faith, as Ballout converted from Shiite to Sunni Islam in 2021.
Was this also a break with his family? His mother gives no indication it was.
She speaks calmly about religion, and without hesitation. She says she was born in Beirut and grew up in Germany. She can neither read nor write Arabic and has therefore never read the Quran in its original language.
“I’m not particularly strict about religion,” she says. But her son was different.
For the last several years, he had increasingly been trying to push her toward stricter observance, urging her to pray regularly, to take her religious obligations more seriously and to engage more deeply with Islam.
“He told me every single day how important it was to pray and that it was my duty.”
* * *
Speaking about the days leading up to the attack, one word keeps coming up in our conversation: fear.
Her son had changed, she says. He seemed more nervous, more tense, more restless. He had started changing his phone number constantly — at least five times in 10 days.
“Why are you changing your number again?” she had asked him. But his answer was always roughly the same. Some people kept calling him; he felt followed, harassed and no longer safe.
Advertisement
To this day, it makes no sense to his mother. But to investigators, this is the behavior of someone who had realized he was on their radar — and was planning something big.
In late May 2026, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office classified Ballout as a high-risk individual capable of committing a serious act of politically motivated violence. And the reasons for this are documented across dozens of pages of case files.
In 2021, Ballout took part in street dawah events organized by a Salafist group in Berlin, where Islamists seek new followers and often distribute copies of the Quran. This is where Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office first took an interest in him.
From 2023 onward, he increasingly frequented mosques influenced by Salafist ideology — which espouses an ultraconservative, fundamentalist view of Sunni Islam — while investigators noted he began openly expressing his rejection of Germany’s free democratic order.
In the summer of 2024, he repeatedly posted propaganda from the Islamic State organization, and in May 2025, attempted to join the terrorist group in Africa but was refused entry into Mauritania. Shortly after, he tried to travel to Syria via Lebanon to receive weapons training, communicating with IS members through Telegram.
Lebanese authorities arrested Ballout in July 2025, and a military court sentenced him to three months in prison for incitement to religious conflict. In court, he spoke of two cousins on his father’s side who had died fighting in Syria.
Returning to Germany in November 2025, Ballout was then arrested at Berlin airport and taken into custody on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. According to the case files, he presented himself as a preacher in prison. His religious fervor intensified, and his appearance changed. Ballout’s father later told Der Spiegel that he had argued with his son over his long hair and beard, which he regarded as a sign of religious extremism.
Advertisement
Finally, in May of this year, Ballout was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison but was initially released under the supervision of a probation officer while the court deferred its verdict on whether to suspend the sentence. This judicial decision is now at the center of a heated debate in Germany over how the country handles high-risk Islamist offenders.
From then on, police kept him under surveillance.
Did his mother know any of this? She shakes her head.
* * *
There is only one incident Ballout’s mother is willing to discuss: July 2 this year, his birthday. That day, she says, showed just how closely her son was being monitored.
Ballout had been playing outside with his sister, spraying her with a water gun, she says. Shortly afterward, officers from the State Criminal Police Office appeared. They had assessed the situation as a possible threat.
But investigators describe the scene differently.
It was already dark, and Ballout had stepped outside for just a few seconds, holding what appeared to be a handgun but was difficult to identify, they said. He tucked it into his waistband and went back inside. When officers eventually searched the apartment, they found only a toy gun.
Investigators believe the 21-year-old was testing whether he was under surveillance — and how much time he had before police would intervene.
And while his mother insists she noticed nothing that would suggest Ballout was preparing an attack, she does not rule out the possibility that others knew of her son’s plans. However, she gives no names.
He spent most of his time with family, she says. He had few friends, at least no one she knew particularly well.
* * *
The day of the attack began, in her memory, just like any other. Both mother and son slept in late, then ran errands. Ballout was unemployed and had no particular obligations, she says. In the late afternoon, he left the apartment before a family gathering that evening.
Then, suddenly, the calls started piling up.
At 5:10 p.m., Ballout called his mother. An hour later, he called again. Then again. Each time, she says, the conversation revolved around the same question: “Are you okay?” He had never done that before.
Advertisement
Then, after one of the calls, she received a short message: “Take care of yourself.”
The words still haunt her today.
At 7:05 p.m., Ballout called again. He asked that his mother inform her partner of over two years that he had a new phone number again. Ballout’s parents have been divorced for three years, but Ballout continued to see and speak with his father regularly, she says. And as the family prepared for the evening, the phone kept ringing.
They were supposed to have dinner at his sister’s place. Schnitzel, his favorite meal, was on the menu. Ballout loved these family gatherings, his mother says. “They always made him happy.” That is precisely why so much of what happened next is incomprehensible to her.
“He wanted to live,” she says, her voice rough.
He had spoken of the future, about having a family of his own, about all the things that still lay ahead of him. Nothing had suggested this might be a farewell.
Shortly before 10 p.m., her partner received one more call. They were the last words Ballout deliberately addressed to his family: “Get my mother to safety.”
Minutes later, the van drove into the crowd.
* * *
By the time Ballout’s mother was driven home by her partner that night, the first reports of the attack had started to circulate. At that point, she still didn’t know exactly what had taken place. But when she entered the apartment, she says, something immediately caught her attention.
A key was still in the door.
And right beside it, on the hallway shoe cabinet, were documents that seemed to be deliberately placed where they could not be overlooked. It was the rental agreement for a small van. It listed Ballout as the renter.
Advertisement
“That was when I knew immediately that it couldn’t mean anything good,” she says.
That same night, she took the documents to the police. And as she was questioned, a picture slowly started to emerge — one she initially refused to accept.
At the same time, she kept trying to reach her son, sending message after message. But there was no reply. She only learned the truth the next day, when her daughters called and told her about the reports on the news.
Her son was dead.
Since then, she has spent hour after hour in her Berlin apartment searching for explanations, her thoughts circling endlessly around her son’s last words, his fear and whether there may have been something in those calls that she failed to recognize. She cannot let go of the distorted image she has of her son, of the good boy who wanted to start a family.
Advertisement
Asked what she would say to the victims of the terrorist attack, she thinks for a long time. She is sorry, she eventually says.
“I would also tell them that wasn’t my son.”
Additional reporting by Lennart Pfahler.

BUDAPEST, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Russia swept all three gold medals and China claimed two silvers on the opening day of the 2026 World Aquatics Junior Artistic Swimming Championships in Budapest on Wednesday.
Performing to the theme "In the Mist," China's He Zhien scored 241.5683 points to take silver in women's solo technical. Aleksandra Zavialova of Russia won with 251.9833, while Spain's Daniela Suarez Fernandez took bronze.
Russia's Zakhar Trofimov won the men's solo technical title, with Spain's Eneko Sanchez Aguilar and Kazakhstan's Viktor Druzin taking silver and bronze respectively.
China's 16-year-old Chen Keyu finished ninth with 205.7751 points. He made a minor error in a leg combination, which resulted in the element being downgraded to its base difficulty.
"Today was my first competition and I was a little nervous," Chen said. "I will learn from it and keep working hard in the upcoming three team events and mixed duet technical event."
In team technical, Chen and seven female teammates delivered a steady performance and finished second with 283.0642 points. Russia claimed the title with 290.1267, while Spain took bronze.
The World Aquatics Junior Artistic Swimming Championships is held from August 12 to 16, featuring 11 events. Nearly 300 athletes from more than 35 countries and regions take part in the competition, with China sending a 14-member squad to compete in all events. ■

THE HAGUE, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Former Barcelona player and coach Xavi Hernandez has been appointed head coach of the Netherlands national team, the Royal Dutch Football Association (KNVB) announced on Wednesday.
The 46-year-old Spaniard signed a contract through the 2030 FIFA World Cup, replacing Ronald Koeman.
Xavi called the appointment "a great honor," saying his football education at Barcelona, shaped by Dutch icons including Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels, had given him a lifelong connection to Dutch football.
"You could say that I am a bit of a son of Dutch football," Xavi said, also crediting Louis van Gaal and Frank Rijkaard as major influences on his development as both a player and coach.

KNVB technical director Nigel de Jong said Xavi's philosophy aligned with the federation's vision for the national team, citing his commitment to proactive, possession-based football while retaining the tactical flexibility needed at the highest level.
The appointment marks Xavi's first role in international management. He began his coaching career with Qatar's Al Sadd in 2019 before returning to Barcelona in November 2021. During his two-and-a-half seasons in charge, he led the Catalan club to the 2022-23 La Liga title, its first league championship since 2019, and the Spanish Super Cup before departing at the end of the 2023-24 campaign.
Widely regarded as one of the greatest midfielders of his generation, Xavi made 767 competitive appearances for Barcelona, winning eight La Liga titles and four UEFA Champions League crowns.
At international level, he earned 133 caps for Spain and played a central role in the country's most successful era, helping La Roja win the 2010 FIFA World Cup and back-to-back UEFA European Championship titles in 2008 and 2012. ■

Feature: How two grassroots leagues are reshaping northeast China's sports economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:00:35 CST
11:00:35 KST

by sportswriter Wang Junbao
HARBIN, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Wang Yong still remembers the excitement when he watched a snow football match on the frozen Songhua River in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province last winter.
As a tourist from the tropical island province of Hainan in southern China, he rarely sees snow, let alone football matches played on a snow field with temperatures plunging to minus 20 degrees Celsius.
"The atmosphere is amazing. Snow football is so much fun. This trip is absolutely worth it," Wang said, adding that he extended his two-day trip to five days to watch more matches.
Months later, the frozen river thawed, the playing fields turned green and thousands of fans were filling stadiums to support their hometown teams.
The contrasting scenes reflect a growing sports economy in northeastern China, driven by two homegrown competitions: the "Ice Super League" in winter and the "Northeast Super League" in summer. Together, the competitions have extended the region's sports calendar, attracting visitors and supporting local businesses.
WINTER: ICE SUPER LEAGUE
Heilongjiang, a two-time host of the Asian Winter Games and the birthplace of many Winter Olympic champions, has long been a center for ice and snow sports in China.
Last winter, the province launched the inaugural Ice Super League and organized thousands of related events as part of a broader push to expand participation in winter sports.
Guan Na, a visitor from south China's Guangdong Province, experienced winter sports for the first time in Qitaihe, a city known for producing multiple Olympic and world champions in short track speed skating.
"I've never been to China's cold northeast before, and it was my first time trying an ice slide. It's quite addictive," Guan said after taking part in activities on a frozen lake in January.
Launched in December 2025, the Ice Super League was designed to combine sports, tourism and local commerce while encouraging broader public participation.
"We want people of all ages to take part, so we've included plenty of recreational activities," said Wang Xianyu, director of the Heilongjiang Provincial Sports Bureau.
Official figures showed that the province built 3,000 public ice and snow sports facilities last winter.
The events have also been used to promote tourism. In Mudanjiang, known for its heavy snowfall, a hiking race through snow-covered forests introduced participants to local scenery and cuisine.
"It reminded me of a movie filmed here. After the race, I decided to stay longer and explore the city," said Wang Pei, a participant from Zhejiang Province.
Mudanjiang also organized food festivals and distributed spending vouchers to participants alongside sporting events to encourage tourism and local consumption, Vice Mayor Sun Li said.
Official data showed that winter sports events in Heilongjiang generated 775 million yuan (107 million U.S. dollars) in direct consumer spending during the 2025-26 winter season.
SUMMER: NORTHEAST SUPER LEAGUE
The inaugural Northeast Super League kicked off on May 23 with matches in Shenyang, Changchun, Harbin and Hohhot, becoming China's first cross-regional amateur football league. Eight teams from Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang and Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region are competing in a season that runs through early October.
Opening-day attendance topped 100,000 across the four host cities, with tickets priced at 19.9 yuan.
The league has also boosted business around match venues.
Li Qiang, who runs a barbecue restaurant near Harbin's home stadium, said business has surged since the season began.
"On match days, the place is packed with fans from out of town," Li said. "Normally I stay open until 2 a.m., but everything is sold out by 9 p.m. Around match days, customer traffic increases by about 40 percent."
Like similar regional leagues in Jiangsu and Guizhou, the Northeast Super League is intended to promote tourism and local spending alongside football.
The four host regions have jointly launched a "Super Northeast Tour" campaign featuring seven travel routes. Fans can use match tickets to receive discounts at participating hotels, restaurants, shopping malls and bathhouses.
"We've organized more than 20 restaurants. Any customer with a Northeast Super League ticket receives a complimentary specialty dish per table," said Lou Baozhong, president of the catering chamber of commerce in Harbin's Acheng District.
The league has also encouraged travel between host cities. According to Tongcheng Travel, one of China's leading online travel agencies, searches for trips from Jixi, Yanbian, Harbin and Tongliao to Shenyang have risen by more than 70 percent since the league began.
Commercial interest has also grown. Sponsorship revenue has exceeded 100 million yuan, with more than 30 companies signing partnerships, ranging from national brands such as Geely Auto and CATL to local restaurants and retailers. In Liaoning, six key competition days of the Northeast Super League generated a total of 7.6 billion yuan in consumption across related industries.
TWO EVENTS, ONE MODEL
The Ice Super League runs from December through March, while the Northeast Super League is held from May through October, creating a nearly year-round calendar of sporting events.
"From the Ice Super League to the Northeast Super League, the transition is not coincidental, it is by design," Wang Xianyu said.
Despite taking place in different seasons, the two competitions follow a similar model by combining sports with tourism, culture and commerce.
"Both leverage low ticket prices to maximize accessibility and participation. Both recognize that the real economic value lies not in ticket sales alone, but in tourism, dining, accommodation and retail spending that fans generate before and after the games," said Zhang Qiang, director of the Acheng District Bureau of Culture, Sports, Radio, Television and Tourism.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) identifies the sports event economy as a development priority, with the country's sports industry expected to generate more than 7 trillion yuan in output by 2030.
"Winning or losing doesn't matter," said Liu Wei, a factory worker from Jilin. "What matters is that a 19.9-yuan ticket stub can unlock a city, and that a football match on a summer night can remind an entire region of what it means to come together." ■

Why India is eyeing France’s next-generation combat aircraft tech amid jet shortage
The move could boost strategic cooperation with France and ensure India has a credible sixth-generation fighter jet option, analysts say
3-MIN READ3-MIN
5
 Listen
India is looking to join France’s sixth-generation fighter programme in a long-term bid to secure a role in the next era of air warfare, from advanced aircraft technology to the industrial work of designing and building future combat systems.
But analysts said the move, while potentially a major step in India’s defence partnership with France, would do little to ease the country’s immediate shortage of combat jets.
The defence ministry told Indian lawmakers last week that it had “initiated efforts” to join the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), a French-led programme aimed at developing the next generation of combat aircraft and connected air warfare systems.
Sixth-generation systems are expected to pair piloted fighter jets with drones, sensors and data networks, allowing aircraft to share information and coordinate strikes across the battlefield.
Antoine Levesques, senior fellow for South and Central Asian defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said FCAS was a logical “next step and step-change” for France-India strategic cooperation, but not a fix for the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) current shortage.

Nearly 200-country study shows China’s Belt and Road Initiative cuts debt and corruption
Data analysis spanning more than 20 years across 197 countries and regions challenges ‘debt trap diplomacy’ narrative
They found the trade and investment scheme – which spans Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond – was also associated with improved corruption control and that it reduced debt risks.
The team – from the university’s Centre for Asia-Pacific Development Studies and led by Mao Weizhun – said their findings challenged characterisations of the trade and infrastructure initiative as a “failure”, “vulnerability trap”, “road of corruption” or a “debt trap”.
They published their research in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Quarterly Journal of International Politics in late July.
The study involved analysis of data from 197 countries and regions between 2000 and 2023. That included 146 countries that signed belt and road cooperation agreements with China and 135 countries where belt and road infrastructure projects had been launched or completed.
Critics have said the initiative – launched in 2013 – lacks transparency, that the projects fuel unsustainable debt, exploit workers, cause environmental damage and are used by Beijing to wield influence.

Los Angeles Lakers to be sold again in record 12.5-billion-dollar deal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:00:10 CST
11:00:10 KST

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Los Angeles Lakers are set to change hands again in less than a year, with the iconic NBA franchise being sold to a group led by former Disney CEO Bob Iger and venture capitalist Joshua Kushner for a record-breaking 12.5 billion U.S. dollars, U.S. media reported Wednesday.
If approved by the NBA, the transaction would establish a new record for the most expensive sale of a professional sports franchise, surpassing Dodgers owner Mark Walter's purchase of the Lakers from the Buss family in 2025 for a then-record valuation of approximately 10 billion dollars.
Kushner and Iger had recently been exploring the possibility of becoming involved in a future NBA expansion franchise as the league considered potential teams in Las Vegas and Seattle. Instead, the pair made an aggressive offer for one of the most valuable and recognizable franchises in professional sports.
"As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world," Kushner and Iger said in a statement. "Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."
The transaction still requires approval from the NBA's board of governors, a process that could take several weeks.
Walter's ownership group also has interests in the Los Angeles Sparks, Chelsea FC, the Professional Women's Hockey League and several motorsport organizations.
Walter is reportedly selling only his interest in the Lakers. The Dodgers and Sparks are not part of the transaction. According to multiple reports, Walter is under federal scrutiny by prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission over potential financial improprieties involving his insurance companies and related businesses.
Kushner, 41, founded venture-capital firm Thrive Capital and is co-founder and vice chairman of Oscar Health. He is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law.
Kushner has previous experience as a sports investor. He owns a minority stake in the Miami Heat, which he will have to sell to complete the Lakers transaction, and previously held a minority interest in the Memphis Grizzlies. His investment firm also recently expanded into sports through long-term ownership ventures.
Iger, 75, stepped down as Disney's CEO in March after serving two separate terms as the company's chief executive. He remains a Disney board member and senior adviser until the end of the year.
Iger is no stranger to professional sports ownership. In 2024, he and his wife, Willow Bay, acquired a controlling interest in Angel City FC of the National Women's Soccer League. The deal valued the club at approximately 250 million dollars, at the time a record valuation for a women's professional sports franchise. ■

====================================================================================================

The one French politician who’s not on vacation this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break.
Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field.
“It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.”
But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste.
Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round.
Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France.
Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch.
“We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser.
Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls.
“A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser.
The right track
It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages.
But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters.
At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences.
He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization.
The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French.
French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land.
For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives.
But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage.
He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label.
One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine.
Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

Rubio and Bessent stayed on decoy flight from Turkey as Trump switched planes, official says
WASHINGTON (AP) — The two most senior members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, flew out of last month’s NATO summit in Turkey on what was effectively a decoy plane following an Iranian threat, while Trump was secretly moved to a smaller military jet, a senior U.S. official said Wednesday.
The official, who was briefed on the situation and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details of presidential travel, said Rubio was aware of the switch and details of the threat behind it but could or would not say why he had stayed on the plane. The official said Bessent was likely aware but did not know for sure.
The official, however, noted that security precautions for the president — especially one who has been the target of several assassination attempts — are more robust than those for even top members of the Cabinet.
Under the U.S. Constitution, the secretaries of State and Treasury follow the vice president and the highest ranking member of each chamber of Congress in the presidential line of succession.
Trump had flown to the annual gathering of NATO country leaders in Ankara, Turkey, in a new Qatari-gifted and retrofitted red, white and navy blue jet. But ahead of departing Turkey, he said he would fly partway home on an older-model baby blue Air Force One plane instead.
The president at the time said the new luxury jet was being flown out ahead of his departure from Ankara to give some U.S. troops based in eastern England a chance to check out the new Air Force One.
The Washington Post reported this week that Trump wasn’t on the old Air Force One on the return flight from Turkey and that he instead was smuggled onto another jet via a catering cart to avoid a possible Iranian assassination plot. The ruse was carried out as journalists and some White House staff members were led to believe they were on the same plane as the president as he began his journey back to Washington.
The New York Times and CBS News had reported last month that intelligence officials had raised concerns about a potential attack on the president or his jet, triggering additional precautions and the decision not to use the newly inaugurated aircraft gifted to Trump by Qatar for the first leg of Trump’s trip home from Ankara.
Trump acknowledged the transfer late Tuesday.
“It’s only up to the Secret Service. I just follow what they’d like to do, so I go by Secret Service and the military,” the president told reporters at Joint Base Andrews. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane, equal safety, but they wanted me to do it, so I do it, I do what they say.”

Zimbabwe’s land reform enters a new chapter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:48:39 UTC
10:48:39 KST

Zimbabwe’s land reform enters a new chapter
A new land policy is reopening disputes over farms seized during Zimbabwe’s land reform after 2000.
Harare, Zimbabwe – More than two decades after Zimbabwe seized thousands of mainly white-owned commercial farms, some of those properties are set to change hands again.
But President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s government insisted the move is not a reversal of the land redistribution programme that reshaped Zimbabwe’s countryside after 2000.
Instead, officials said they are resolving three separate categories of land claims involving foreign investors, Black Zimbabwean owners and white farmers who remained on acquired land.
Sixty-seven farms protected by bilateral investment promotion and protection agreements (BIPPAs) are being returned to investors from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Another 840 farms that officials said were included in the acquisition process in error during land reform are to be restored to their Black Zimbabwean owners.
And 409 white farmers who have remained on farms alongside land reform beneficiaries will be allowed to buy the farms or portions they occupy through a set-off mechanism linked to compensation for eligible improvements.
“The BIPPA process is about resolving outstanding legal obligations relating to investments protected under bilateral agreements. It should not be mistaken for a return to the pre-land reform era,” Agriculture Minister Anxious Masuka told Parliament.
The distinction matters because land remains one of Zimbabwe’s most politically charged issues, closely tied to the colonial era and the liberation struggle.
A colonial legacy
At independence in 1980, white commercial farmers controlled a disproportionate share of Zimbabwe’s most productive farmland, reflecting colonial policies that restricted Black Zimbabweans’ access to prime agricultural land.
Under the Lancaster House settlement, redistribution initially operated largely on a “willing buyer, willing seller” basis with Britain helping finance parts of the early programme.
But redistribution was slower than many Black Zimbabweans expected.
In February 2000, voters rejected a government-backed constitutional referendum that would have expanded the state’s powers to acquire land. Soon afterwards, war veterans and supporters of the ZANU-PF party, which has governed Zimbabwe since independence, began occupying white-owned farms.
The government formalised the occupations through the Fast-Track Land Reform Programme (FTLRP).
Supporters saw the seizures as the unfinished business of independence. Human Rights Watch documented violence, intimidation and political discrimination during the process while disputes over ownership and allocation continued for years.
The upheaval severely disrupted commercial agriculture and contributed to Zimbabwe’s wider economic crisis, which had multiple causes, including monetary and fiscal problems, drought and other policy failures.
More than two decades later, Zimbabwe is still grappling with the competing claims that upheaval created.
Three categories
The policy distinguishes between three categories of claimants, each with a different legal and political basis.
The 67 BIPPA-protected farms involve foreign investors whose investments were covered by bilateral agreements. Officials said the properties were designated for compulsory acquisition during land reform but remained unoccupied and are being returned to investors as Zimbabwe addresses its obligations under those agreements.
The second group is 840 farms that officials said were included in the acquisition process in error during land reform. They are to be restored to their Black Zimbabwean owners.
The third comprises 409 white farmers who have remained on farms alongside land reform beneficiaries. They will be allowed to buy the farms or portions they currently occupy rather than simply receiving them back.
Taken together, the three categories illustrate how Zimbabwe’s land question has become increasingly complex with competing claims rooted in different legal, political and historical foundations.
‘We could have done it better’
Milton Gurajena, a war veteran who participated in the farm occupations, remembered them as a national mobilisation.
“We just went into the farms, guided by the national fever. It was just arriving at the farm and giving the owner little notice. Our aim was to take our land back. Oftentimes, the big guys would take it from us and advise us to find another farm,” he said.
But he acknowledged that many participants did not understand the legal consequences.
“We did not have much knowledge except party directives and the common line that ‘we are taking our land back.’ Of course, we had some grievances, but when I look back, we could have done it better and more orderly without turning the process into a war,” he said.
His account reflects the central tension of the land reform: A programme intended to correct a historical injustice was itself marked by violence, political pressure and legal uncertainty.
Investment pressure
For Mnangagwa’s government, the land decisions are not only about resolving historical disputes; they are also part of a broader effort to rebuild relations with Western governments and international lenders.
Zimbabwe is seeking debt relief, renewed access to international financing and improved investor confidence. Analysts have linked the return of the BIPPA-protected farms to those broader efforts to improve the country’s investment climate and relations with international creditors.
The BIPPA process is separate from Zimbabwe’s $3.5bn compensation framework for eligible former commercial farmers, agreed in 2020. That programme covers improvements made to farms acquired by the state while ownership of the land remains with the state.
Zimbabwe began making payments under that framework in 2025, but the government has faced financial constraints in meeting the wider commitment.
At the same time, the government said it is issuing title deeds to farmers who benefitted from land reform, seeking to give them greater security of tenure and encourage investment. Officials insisted that land reform itself remains irreversible.
A return to the farm
For some former owners, the latest moves have revived hopes of regaining access to properties they lost more than two decades ago.
Michael Kwaramba, a second-generation heir to his family’s estate, said his father suffered after the farm was mistakenly designated for compulsory acquisition by the state during land reform.
“He went through a lot when our farm was wrongly gazetted, which I think contributed to his untimely death. We have been waiting for years, and the announcement is encouraging,” he said.
Willem Jansen, a Dutch-born Zimbabwean farmer now based in South Africa, also hopes to regain his family’s farm.
“Hopefully, I will get my land back. It was our family land, and we had created an ecosystem that even after our forced removal, farm workers and nearby villages were affected, lost jobs and opportunities we were creating together,” he said.
But for those who fought for land reform, the prospect of former owners regaining a foothold on the land remains difficult.
Marko Dzingirai, a war veteran, said he was unsure what the changes would mean for farmers who settled on land after the reform.
“Just like in the beginning when we invaded the farms, we did not know about the existence of all these treaties and agreements on the farms. So now, I don’t know if the farm here is part of the BIPPA or not,” he said.
“We supported the party because of moves like these. Hopefully, they are not betraying our sacrifices,” he said.

5 indigenous small modular reactors targeted by 2033, Jitendra Singh tells LS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:45:29 UTC
10:45:29 KST

Union MoS Jitendra Singh speaks in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon session of Parliament
NEW DELHI: A key objective of the govt under the Nuclear Energy Mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033, minister for department of atomic energy Jitendra Singh said in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous SMR technologies, including the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200) and 55 MWe SMR-55 for power generation. BARC is also developing a high temperature gas cooled reactor (HTGCR) of up to 5 MW capacity, which can be coupled with a suitable thermochemical cycle for hydrogen production.Singh said India is steadily strengthening its indigenous nuclear energy ecosystem with a focus on advanced reactor technologies, SMRs, domestic manufacturing capabilities, private-sector participation and long-term utilisation of the country’s abundant thorium resources. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition. This includes deployment of large indigenous reactors such as 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) and advanced reactor designs at greenfield sites, alongside development and deployment of SMRs at brownfield locations, including retiring fossil-fuel-based power plants, captive plants for energy-intensive industries and off-grid applications in remote areas.
The minister also highlighted continuing work of the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in advancing the second stage of India’s nuclear power programme. IGCAR is pursuing multidisciplinary scientific research and advanced engineering development for sodium cooled fast breeder reactors and associated closed fuel-cycle facilities, technologies that remain a cornerstone of India’s long-term nuclear strategy.
On thorium, Singh said India is pursuing its three-stage nuclear power programme, based on a closed fuel cycle, to optimise utilisation of its uranium resources and progressively harness its abundant thorium reserves. Thorium, being a fertile material, needs to be converted into fissile uranium-233 in a nuclear reactor before it can be used for energy generation.India has already undertaken sustained R&D towards thorium utilisation. Thorium Oxide (Thoria) pellets have been used in the initial cores of operating PHWRs, while Thoria-based fuels have also been irradiated in BARC research reactors. The irradiated Thoria pins have been reprocessed to obtain uranium-233, which has subsequently been fabricated as fuel for the KAMINI reactor at IGCAR, Kalpakkam. Singh said the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025 has been enacted to enable wider participation of both public and private entities in the nuclear sector.

Low-income Australians should accept substandard homes, Liberal frontbencher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:43:15 UTC
10:43:15 KST

in brief
- Liberals are this week pushing for a reduced housing code, which could streamline construction at the cost of quality.
- Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg conceded that the proposal would come with "trade-offs".
The Coalition's plan to boost housing stock will involve "trade-offs", a Liberal frontbencher has said, after suggesting low-income households should accept living in substandard homes.
Opposition housing and homelessness spokesperson Andrew Bragg announced on Wednesday that the Opposition would reduce the national housing code from 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.
When asked by ABC Radio National on Thursday morning whether his policy means low-income earners should just accept living in substandard housing, he replied: "Yes, definitely."
He went on to say that building more homes under a streamlined code would come with "trade-offs".
"It's more important to have a house than to not have a house. And so, given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system, we need to just build more houses," he told the ABC.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Bragg's comments follow remarks made by his Liberal colleague and treasury spokesman Tim Wilson, who suggested in some cases people could put "a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money" on improving housing quality.
He told ABC RN on Wednesday there should not be a one-size-fits-all policy — such as mandated energy efficiency — for construction.
"There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it's not necessary," he said.
"We have a risk that Australians can't afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government's own budget design. We need housing stock that meets different needs in different environmental conditions. Queensland is not the same as Tasmania or Victoria. Western Australia is different again."
Proposal does 'nothing to fix' housing crisis, advocate says
Affordable housing advocates told SBS News that stripping back construction regulations is a way for developers to profit from "unliveable" homes.
"Too many renters are already living in homes that are freezing in winter, stifling in summer, riddled with mould and damp, and expensive to heat and cool," Everybody's Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said in a statement.
"Older people and people with disability already struggle to find homes they can safely and comfortably live in."
Azize added that the government should focus on social housing that is "built to last".
"We have a housing crisis because people cannot afford a home. Building more poor-quality homes does nothing to fix that crisis. It simply gives developers another way to profit from it," Azize said.
Australian Council of Social Services CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie agreed, adding that construction of social housing should "drastically scale up".
She described Bragg's comments as shocking.
"The changes to the building code proposed by Senator Bragg would simply remove costs from the builder and move them onto the household - locking them into higher power bills for decades, deepening inequality, risking lives, leaving future generations with homes that are expensive to run," she told SBS News.
The Housing Industry Association on Wednesday welcomed Senator Bragg's announcement, but argued it was more important to disentangle layers of complexity than target a specific size of the code.
Cutting red tape
The national housing codes set minimum requirements for the safety, health, amenity, accessibility, and sustainability of certain buildings, as detailed in over 2,000 pages.
The Coalition's new standards will focus on cost-effective structural, fire safety and health-related building standards.
Bragg said reducing the code has been a shifting policy for the Coalition.
"This was in Angus Taylor's budget reply back in May, and we have committed to getting it to 200 pages, but we actually found a way to get it to less than 100 pages. It tends to be by picking up the New Zealand building code, which is about 80," he explained.
While New Zealand's building code appears to be about 80 pages long, the country has other compulsory building requirements on durability and energy efficiency, outlined in separate documents that builders must comply with.
Labor announced it would freeze the National Construction Code following its productivity roundtable in mid-2026.
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil brushed off calls from the Coalition to cut the construction standards to 200 pages earlier in 2026.
"I've talked to builders about that, they laugh their heads off. That is absolutely ridiculous," O'Neil told the National Press Club in May.
The government is not far off presenting a final plan to the building minister later this year to streamline the code, Treasurer Jim Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Wednesday.
Bragg has also called for the creation of a federal pattern book of model homes that could receive automatic approval from the states and territories.

IN-SPACe approved country’s first fully commercial earth observation sat constellation: Jitendra Singh

The consortium named Allied Orbits Private Limited is led by Pixxel Space India and includes Dhruva Space, PierSight Space and Satsure Analytics India
NEW DELHI: Space regulator IN-SPACe has approved and signed under the PPP model an agreement with a private consortium for the country’s first indigenous, fully commercial earth observation constellation, with a view to enhancing the country’s space-based observation capabilities and building a self-reliant earth observation (EO) ecosystem in the country, minister for department of space Jitendra Singh informed Lok Sabha on Wednesday in response to a Parliament question.The consortium named Allied Orbits Private Limited is led by Pixxel Space India and includes Dhruva Space, PierSight Space and Satsure Analytics India. It will invest more than Rs 1,200 crore for setting up the constellation, which is to be developed and operationalised by 2029.
The consortium will design, build, own and operate the 12-satellite constellation, which will have panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) capabilities, supported by indigenous ground infrastructure. All satellites are to be manufactured domestically and launched on Indian launch vehicles, with mission control based in the country.The programme includes designing, fabrication, integration and the testing of EO satellites, including five ultra-high resolution optical satellites with 4 bands, 3 multispectral satellites with 8 bands, 2 hyperspectral optical satellites with 250 bands and 2 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in X-band, by the Indian industry. The EO programme will use Indian launch vehicles (either private or Isro facilities) for placing the satellites into orbit. The programme also allows collaboration with academic and research institutions for capacity building and application development, the minister said.

Colombia earthquake rescue efforts enter 'final phase' as death toll rises
Rescuers in Colombia faced a race against time Wednesday as they searched collapsed buildings for survivors after the country's strongest earthquake this century. The magnitude 7.4 quake has killed 265 people and injured more than 3,500, with nearly 500 still missing.
Colombia's earthquake rescue efforts entered what officials called the "final phase" on Wednesday, as rescuers searched for signs of life beneath collapsed buildings before the critical first 72 hours came to an end.
The magnitude 7.4 quake, the strongest to hit Colombia this century, has killed 265 people, injured more than 3,500 and left almost 500 missing, according to local authorities.
In the city of Pereira, crews focused on a collapsed bakery where they believe a street vendor trapped since Monday's earthquake may still be alive beneath the rubble.
Using equipment that detects vibrations, rescuers said they had picked up possible signs of life from Pablo Loaiza, prompting anxious relatives to gather outside the wreckage.
"They tell us it could be him," said 16-year-old Sara Loaiza, his niece. "My heart is about to burst out of my chest," she cried.
Relatives said the trapped man appeared to respond when rescuers asked him to knock twice, then three times from beneath the rubble, drawing applause from those gathered at the scene.
Read moreColombia declares three days of mourning as search for quake survivors continues
Crews are approaching 72 hours since the quake, a period when survivors are considered most likely to be found alive beneath collapsed buildings.
"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said Wednesday. "That doesn't mean there won't be survivors afterwards, but it is more difficult."
In Cali and Pereira, emergency crews prepared to work through a third night with their bare hands, cranes and sniffer dogs, stopping not to rest, but to listen for signs of life.
"Every half hour we make everyone be quiet to see if we can find people alive," volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez told AFP.
"So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead."
Colombia's newly installed president has declared the disaster an "economic emergency" and announced three days of national mourning.
"We will do what is necessary," Abelardo de la Espriella said in a statement, vowing to "emerge again as a country and as a society."

Overseeing jury trials – the demanding job of a High Court judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:10 UTC
10:30:10 KST

Overseeing jury trials – the demanding job of a High Court judge
A complex and lengthy criminal trial, often conducted under the glare of public scrutiny, is perhaps the greatest test of a judge’s mettle
Jury trials are a rarity among the world’s legal traditions, but a fundamental bedrock of the common law system.
The jury’s role as the decider of a defendant’s guilt makes them the natural centrepiece of a criminal trial, but an often overlooked part of the process is the role of the trial judge.
The judge does not sit in the back seat while waiting for the jury to deliver its verdict; rather, the judge acts as a conductor of an orchestra, ensuring that each party plays their proper role and that the case can be tried smoothly.
This is no easy task, especially when complex criminal cases can easily last for many weeks, and involve difficult points of fact and law.
That burden is made heavier by the chronic understaffing of the judiciary in Hong Kong. With too few judges for the volume and complexity of work, cases press harder and harder upon sitting judges.
Multiple long trials are often fixed together in close succession, with any free days in the court’s calendar quickly filled up with several shorter hearings, such as sentencing and bail applications, that need to be handled quickly to ensure swift access to justice for defendants.

Stop mourning Hong Kong. It’s evolving, not dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:07 UTC
10:30:07 KST

Hong Kong has changed since the turmoil of 2019-20. Few people would dispute this. The more important question is what kind of city it is becoming.
It is evolving into a more nationally integrated yet still distinctive city. The emerging model seeks to combine market dynamism and international connectivity with clearer alignment to national development. This is not decline. It is a search for a viable identity and role.
Critics such as Stephen Roach 
have argued
 that the Hong Kong of old is finished and that the city has become little more than another large Chinese city. The conclusion rests on a particular assumption: that sharp political and institutional change, especially when it compresses earlier expectations of autonomy, amounts to the end of the place itself. This assumption is selective.
Political systems everywhere have experienced sharp institutional shifts. Brexit permanently altered Britain’s relationship with Europe. In the United States, the Trump administration has 
moved to dissolve
 the United States Agency for International Development, sharply downsize the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and remove or attempt to remove leaders of other independent bodies.
The US Supreme Court has expanded presidential authority to dismiss heads of such agencies without cause. Few observers would conclude from these changes that America is therefore “over”. The same restraint should apply when assessing Hong Kong.
The claim that Beijing 
cut in half
 its promised 50-year high degree of autonomy also needs precision. Article 5 of the Basic Law protects the capitalist system and way of life for 50 years. This high degree of autonomy is an authorisation under China’s Constitution and the Basic Law.

Former US sheriff deputies arrested for using licence plate reader cameras to stalk people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Former US sheriff deputies arrested for using licence plate reader cameras to stalk people
Michael Levenson
ATLANTA, Georgia – Three former Georgia sheriff’s deputies have been arrested on charges that they used Flock cameras to stalk people, the latest cases to raise concerns about potential abuse involving the widely used network of licence-plate readers.
The Bibb County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement that an internal audit conducted with help from Flock revealed that the deputies had used the camera system’s licence plate data for “personal, non-law-enforcement purposes”.
All three were involved in separate incidents tracking people with whom they had a “personal relationship at the time”, the sheriff’s office said.
The deputies were arrested on Aug 10 on charges that included stalking, prohibited use of licence plate data and violating their oaths as public officers. They have since been released on bond.
Two of those charged, Toni Lewis and Coznavian Stubbs, resigned from their positions as patrol deputies during the investigation, and the third, Joseph Callaway, resigned as a K-9 deputy shortly after his arrest, the office said.
The Bibb County sheriff, David Davis, said that a tool that Flock introduced in April, called Audit Assistance, had uncovered the deputies’ misuse of the system. Flock says the tool continuously monitors system activity and flags search patterns that “fall outside an agency’s typical usage”, allowing police departments to identify instances of potential abuse.
“I was saddened by it,” Davis said in an interview on Aug 12.
“Each one of these deputies were good deputies who had been here for several years and were doing a good job. However, they made some poor decisions and crossed the line.”
Stubbs said on Aug 12 that he had been accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his girlfriend but that he had only used the system to look up the licence plate on his own car. The case, he said, had been “blown way out” of proportion.
Callaway declined to comment on the charges. Lewis could not be reached at phone numbers listed under her name, and it was not immediately clear if she had a lawyer.
A national debate has been brewing over Flock cameras, which can be found on roads in every state but Alaska. About 7,000 law enforcement agencies, or 40 per cent of all departments in the United States, have contracts with the company, which is based in Atlanta.
Flock’s cameras, which use artificial intelligence to automatically identify and track vehicles, are connected, creating a vast, searchable network. Investigators have praised the system as a valuable tool that helps them track down stolen cars, find missing or wanted people, and solve crimes
Critics, including local watchdog groups and civil liberties organisations, have said the cameras create an umbrella of surveillance that can be easily misused.
In Milwaukee, an officer was charged with using camera data to track someone he was dating and the person’s ex. In Texas, an officer used the cameras to track a woman across state lines who was suspected of self-administering an abortion. In Georgia, a former Polk County officer was charged with using the camera system “for non-law-enforcement purposes”. Other officers across the country have been disciplined or fired for tracking romantic partners.
In Bibb County, Georgia, which is home to about 158,000 people and includes Macon, Davis announced in June 2023 that his office had been awarded a US$1.6 million (S$2.05 million) state grant to deploy Flock cameras and to set up a Strategic Information Centre to monitor the licence-plate data they collect.
Davis said that at one point more than 220 deputies had access to the cameras, but that number had since been cut to around 160. He said he planned to work with community members to ensure the system is only used for legitimate investigations.
“We will continue to monitor and audit the use of this technology and take appropriate action whenever those standards are violated,” Davis said in a statement. “Protecting the public also means protecting the public’s trust.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Trump signed memo to allow use of cyber tools to target transnational criminal organisations, White House says

Trump signed memo to allow use of cyber tools to target transnational criminal organisations, White House says
- US President Trump signed a memo to allow federal law enforcement and private companies to use cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations targeting Americans.
- The memo creates a framework for private firms to collaborate with government agencies to gather threat information and conduct cyber operations under government control.
- The Department of Homeland Security will oversee a programme for cyber operations that disrupt foreign criminal groups, with companies required to maintain a US$1 million bond.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump signed a memo on Aug 12 that the White House said was aimed at empowering federal law enforcement to use cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations that operate in foreign jurisdictions to attack Americans.
Trump signed the national security presidential memorandum directing his administration to “leverage the capability and innovation of the private sector to help conduct these cyber operations under the direction, control, and authority of the US Government,” the White House said.
The White House, in a fact sheet about the memo, cited ransomware attacks, financial frauds and other crimes run by foreign-based criminal organisations, referred to in the memo as “transnational criminal organizations.”
The memo creates a framework that encourages private sector companies to enter into agreements with other private entities, as well as federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies to gather threat information on transnational criminal organisations and propose cyber operations to address those threats, the White House added.
The memo directs the Department of Homeland Security, through the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Centre, to create a programme “to conduct specific cyber operations that disrupt foreign TCOs” that will be overseen by DHS and the Department of Justice.
Under the supervision of the federal government, participating companies, once vetted, will conduct “cyber surveillance operations” and “cyber effects operations” against specified targets, according to the memo.
“Cyber effects includes the potential manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems, networks, physical or virtual infrastructure controlled by information systems, or information resident thereon,” according to the memo.
Participating companies will have to maintain a bond or escrow of at least US$1 million (S$1.28 million), according to the memo.
The idea of private sector firms participating in cyber operations against criminal and other targets is not new, and has been controversial in the past, for fears of escalation, inadvertent consequences, and inter-agency coordination issues.
DHS and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for additional details about the programme. REUTERS
