12 August solar eclipse brings thousands of tourists to Gormaz fortress in Soria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:08:54 UTC
04:08:54 KST

The caliphal fortress of Gormaz in Soria became a prime vantage point to view the total solar eclipse, drawing crowds of visitors from Spain and abroad to this Castilian town.
Since it was built in the 10th century, the 28 towers and 1,200 metres of walls of the caliphate fortress of Gormaz, perched on a promontory overlooking the Castilian plateau, have witnessed six total solar eclipses.
The one on 12 August 2026, the seventh, is for the first time drawing large numbers of domestic and international tourists who have travelled to Gormaz to observe this astronomical event, as the path of totality runs very close to the thousand-year-old monument.
It is estimated that the first total solar eclipse visible over the Iberian Peninsula since 1912 could prompt between 400,000 and 1.5 million additional car journeys to the areas of totality, bringing up to 164,000 visitors from abroad and 282,700 from within Spain.
The event represents a prime showcase for towns like Gormaz, in the province of Soria and far from the coastal sun-and-beach destinations that traditionally draw foreign tourists.

New York cracks down on ‘predatory’ Polymarket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
19:02:19 UTC
04:02:19 KST

New York cracks down on ‘predatory’ Polymarket
New York City Council is investigating Polymarket, Kalshi, and other predictive market platforms for “deceptive and predatory” marketing practices, accusing the industry of encouraging gambling and insider trading.
Council Speaker Julie Menin notified Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, and Gemini Titan of the investigation on Tuesday. In a letter to Polymarket seen by Bloomberg, Menin referenced “troubling” news reports suggesting that the company and its competitors “target young adults – and thus potentially minors – with false, deceptive, and unconscionable advertising.”
According to the reports, Polymarket allegedly paid influencers to promote its platform without disclosure, produced videos showing fake trades on its site, presented losing bets as winners, and encouraged insider trading.
“Prediction markets aggressively entice consumers to bet and wager on sports, politics, culture, weather, and pretty much anything. We refuse to let New Yorkers, especially our young people, become collateral damage,” Menin said in a statement on Wednesday.
Prediction markets have snowballed into a $240 billion-per-year industry, counting the annual trading volume of Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, and Gemini Titan. By allowing customers to bet on politics and world events – for instance the likelihood that a world leader will be ousted by a certain date – they have reportedly become rife with insider trading.
A White House staffer has been investigated for allegedly making bets based on her advance knowledge of US President Donald Trump’s remarks, while a US special forces soldier has been arrested for using classified Pentagon materials to pocket $400,000 by correctly predicting the removal of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power in January.
Suspicious trades surged during the US-Israeli war on Iran, with The Guardian counting more than $1 billion in “perfectly timed” wagers, including an $850,000 bet just before US strikes on Iran began on February 28, and roughly $950 million in oil futures hours before US Trump announced a ceasefire. Suspicion fell on Washington insiders, and the White House warned staff against insider trading in April.
The federal government has defended prediction markets against state-level oversight, arguing that event contracts are financial instruments and therefore different from traditional gambling. After New York Attorney General Letitia James attempted to shut down Kalshi for violating state gambling laws in July, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CTFC) stepped in this week and ordered the platform to remain operational in the state.
Responding to Menin’s letter, a spokesperson for Polymarket said that the company looks “forward to engaging with The New York City Council on this matter.”

Supp is branded as a "recruitment app that's made for the rush", and since 2017, it has been operating as a central hub for bars, pubs and cafes to advertise work.
Individuals can sign up to the platform and apply for shifts posted by businesses, with a description of the work and the hourly rate.
The Supp website refers to workers as "independent contractors" and says it is workers' responsibility to divide their payments to "meet their relevant taxation and superannuation obligations".
Rather than hospitality businesses paying workers through an ordinary payroll system, the Supp platform handles payment on their behalf.
Employment lawyer Fay Calderone told the ABC she is concerned this arrangement could be leaving workers without their correct entitlements, including to superannuation.
"One of the key legal risks in this area is assuming that contractual labels will be determinative," Ms Calderone, a partner at Hall and Wilcox, said.
"The mere fact that a worker holds an ABN or is described as an independent contractor does not determine their legal status."
The Fair Work Ombudsman spokesperson said it will make inquiries into Supp: "We are unable to comment on those further."
"We encourage any workers with concerns to contact us directly for assistance," the spokesperson said.
"The FWO also has an online anonymous report tool, including options to report in languages other than English."
Concerns about sham contracting in the gig economy, where employers say workers are independent contractors not employees, have been raised for years, with companies battling claims in court.
Supp rejects 'sham contracting'
The Supp website states that it has links to at least 15,000 venues, and more than 200,000 workers, across Melbourne, Sydney, Los Angeles and New York City.
One Melbourne-based hospitality worker has been using the Supp platform for more than three years. He requested anonymity as he still uses Supp for work.
He believes the type of work he has been hired to do reflects that of an employee, rather than a contractor.
"They'll be asking me to do whatever, [for example], you'll be behind the bar serving people," he said.
"They'll let you know if it's going to be mainly customer service or if you'll be in this area or that section."
Ms Calderone said there was a number of factors to take into account when determining if someone was a genuine contractor, rather than an employee.
"The question is not whether a worker enjoys some flexibility, but whether the arrangement as a whole reflects a genuinely independent business relationship [and] a number of factors are commonly examined," she said.
"Including the degree of control exercised over the worker, whether the worker can genuinely operate an independent business, whether they can delegate work to others and whether they bear any real commercial risk."
In a statement to the ABC, Supp's chief executive Jordan Murray said: "We reject any suggestion that Supp deliberately misrepresents working relationships or facilitates sham contracting".
"Supp was built to address two longstanding problems in hospitality: venues filling short-term gaps through informal networks like Facebook groups, often with very little transparency or protection around the transaction, and workers wanting greater visibility, choice and access to both additional income and permanent opportunities.
"Supp was designed to bring those transactions into the open with visible rates, digital payments, minimum rate protections, two-way reviews and a portable work history."
'I started to get a little more concerned'
In July 2022, the monthly minimum income threshold for compulsory superannuation was removed, meaning any employee over the age of 18 was now eligible for entitlements regardless of earnings.
Supp's chief executive told the ABC that it was not Supp's responsibility to pay superannuation.
"Supp is not the engaging business or employer in any engagement, and businesses using the platform are responsible for complying with their legal obligations to the people they engage," Mr Murray said in a statement.
Daniel McBurnie, who has been using the Supp platform since 2021, said chasing up unpaid superannuation contributions through individual businesses would not be worth his time.
"I've done a one-off shift at many venues and that one-off shift probably I've accumulated maybe just short of $20 super," he said.
"So for a one-off claim to go back and go through the process of disputing things and waiting for responses and then escalating it if you're not happy ... I go, well, why would I do this to myself?"
He is worried thousands of workers using the platform are missing out on building their retirement savings.
"As the app got more popular, and as it seems like more businesses were starting to use it, I started to get a little more concerned," he said.
While he initially used the app to pick up last minute shifts, he started to notice more regular shifts offered.
"I started seeing the same businesses every single week, every time I opened the app."
The Supp app shows some businesses have used the platform to fill thousands of shifts.
Even contractors may be entitled to super
Even workers legitimately engaged as contractors may still be entitled, in some circumstances, to superannuation contributions paid by businesses, Ms Calderone said.
"That is an area that is often misunderstood by both businesses and workers," she said.
"Even where a worker is properly characterised as an independent contractor for employment law purposes, superannuation obligations may still arise where the contract is wholly or principally for the worker's labour."

Angus Taylor plays a risky game in trying to capitalise on melon saga

analysis
Taylor is using the melon saga to mount an all-out assault on Albanese's character
Today marks six months since Sussan Ley was dumped by her colleagues.
She's been on an unusual journey of discovery since then.
After being defeated by Angus Taylor for the Liberal leadership and quitting parliament, Ley fulfilled a long-time dream of riding on Greyhound buses down the length of inland USA. She found a bleak interior and plenty of misery.
"Chains. Parking lots. Cheap builds. No trees. No spaces to gather," Ley wrote in The Australian Financial Review. "It was the underlying weariness. Everyone works hard. That part is true. But working hard is no longer enough."
Reflecting on the experience, Ley told 7:30's Sarah Ferguson of her great discovery: the extent of disconnection.
"This feeling of disconnection I found by the end of the trip really quite interesting, quite fascinating."
A problem of disillusion and disconnection
Ley wasn't deliberately sending a message to anyone in particular but it served as a powerful reminder. Political leaders need to stay focused on what really matters. The disconnected aren't interested in political games.
The dramatic shift in support away from the major parties in Australia this year points to a similar problem of disillusion and disconnection.
Much of this shift happened on Ley's watch. She carries at least part of the blame for weary voters walking away from the Liberal Party.
Ley was often criticised, including by her own colleagues, for whipping up issues that just didn't connect.
Issues like the prime minister's choice of T-shirt, Penny Wong's capacity to shed tears in public, or whether Kevin Rudd should be recalled as ambassador for upsetting Donald Trump.
Too much hyperventilating over the wrong issues. Not enough focus on the substantive concerns of disconnected voters.
Which brings us to the melons.
Taylor shifts direction
In his first speech as Liberal leader, six months ago today, Taylor vowed a "change or die" reset. Cost of living, immigration and Australian values would be his focus. In large part, he's so far stuck to those priorities.
This week, however, with the return of parliament after the five-week winter break, Taylor shifted direction.
He's gone after the prime minister's ill-fated and now infamous decision to appear on the satirical Bush Deep podcast where Anthony Albanese talked about the "melons" given to him by his Japanese counterpart.
The opposition leader has not been half-hearted in his pursuit. Repeatedly demanding Albanese apologise in Question Time, trying to move a motion in parliament to condemn the prime minister, accusing him of damaging relations with Japan.
The Coalition has even asked the Australian Federal Police to investigate who leaked a confidential note from Tokyo suggesting the Japanese government believed there was no "ill intention" behind the comments.
It's been a full court press from the opposition. And the government has been unable to shut it down, despite the efforts of various ministers from Tanya Plibersek to Katy Gallagher to defend the prime minister.
Having already issued an apology for his comments on the podcast about Kylie Minogue, Albanese has so far refused to offer another. He rejects any interpretation he was engaging in lewd jokes about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Japan, for its part, is trying not to stoke the issue further.
"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki told the ABC.
Barnaby Joyce, himself familiar with the odd embarrassment or two, reckons there's no doubt what most people will make of it all.
"Turn the volume down and watch him [on the podcast]. You have a man in a T-shirt, with an empty bottle of bourbon in front of him, gesticulating with his arms, and anybody would say, 'I think I know what you're talking about there, mate,'" said the One Nation MP. "Imagine if for instance I had done that. It would be a riot."
Loading
Bipartisanship behind closed doors
Behind the scenes, Taylor and Albanese have been engaged in a rare level of cooperation this week.
They've been holding a series of personal meetings aimed at reaching bipartisan deals on gambling ads, forcing tech giants to pay for journalism, and reining in the NDIS. Both leaders have a pragmatic interest in squaring these issues away.
But in public, Taylor is using the melon saga to mount an all-out assault on Albanese's character. "He's full of hubris. There's no humility when he makes a mistake," the opposition leader told 2GB.
Choosing to pursue this may prove to be the right strategy. It's the sort of thing that can cut through and damage the prime ministerial image. Labor was devastatingly effective in going after Scott Morrison's character whenever they had the chance.
There is a risk for the Coalition, however, that weary, disconnected voters might not feel this is really the main game. They might feel there are bigger problems affecting their lives that deserve such attention.
Either way, Taylor is marking six months in the job this week with a slight detour from the plan he laid out at the start.

====================================================================================================

Torah dictatorship: How Israel’s ultra-Orthodox parties gained their influence – and why they risk losing it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:57:37 UTC
03:57:37 KST

Amid the unresolved situation in Gaza and the continued presence of Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election campaign is already in full swing. Most polls give neither the current coalition nor the opposition the 61 seats needed for a majority, meaning various smaller parties could once again determine the fate of the government — as they have many times in Israel’s history. For Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the key players are the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties, without which he has little chance of forming a majority. But the ultra-Orthodox are frustrated by the government’s failure to pass the promised law exempting most yeshiva students from military service, and as a result, their support can no longer be taken for granted. This time, the “kingmakers,” as Israel’s ultra-Orthodox parties are known, risk finding themselves on the losing side.
Knesset arithmetic
On the night of July 17, the 25th Knesset passed a self-dissolution law that officially ended its term — one of the most contentious in the country’s history, as it encompassed both the October 7 Hamas terrorist attack of 2023 and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran that followed in the three years since. The period was also characterized by deep internal divisions in Israeli society over Benjamin Netanyahu’s attempts at judicial reform and disputes regarding ultra-Orthodox military service. The current campaign to elect a new Knesset to grapple with these problems promises to be no less contentious.
Polls so far offer neither the parties in the governing coalition nor the opposition a clear path to a majority, though as of late July some polls gave the Zionist opposition parties — excluding the two Arab lists — a projected 60–61 seats. The governing coalition’s Zionist parties were averaging 34 seats without the ultra-Orthodox and 50–52 with them. However, the picture was somewhat better for the coalition in polls published by Channel 14, which supports Netanyahu: 45 seats without the ultra-Orthodox and 62 with them.
According to some polls, the opposition could win more than 60 seats; according to others, Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox could secure that many
The distinction between Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties is important, as both are considered part of the anti-Zionist bloc. Arab parties, naturally, do not consider themselves part of the Jewish national movement. Most ultra-Orthodox Jews, meanwhile, have rejected secular Zionism (the idea that Jews should achieve national self-determination through their own state). As the election campaign heats up, the most serious question concern cooperation between the potential winners and the non-Zionist parties of various stripes — namely, who is willing to sit with them in the same government and who is not?
Another debate revolves around who considers it permissible to form a government with Likud, led by Netanyahu, and who categorically refuses to sit at the same table as the current prime minister. There is also the reverse question: how stable is the opposition bloc, given diversity that ranges from the far-left Democrats to Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu?
In any case, public opinion polls are constantly shifting, and not all parties have even entered the race yet. As usual, new alliances emerge before elections, and unexpected coalitions may form. Some parties may fail to clear the electoral threshold, leading to a redistribution of seats. And after the election, politicians’ promises never to sit in a government with a particular party may be broken yet again. For example, Naftali Bennett, one of the leaders of the current BeYachad electoral list and a former prime minister, promised in 2021 never to join a coalition with Arab parties, but he later went back on his word, citing the interests of the state and society as his justification for doing so.
A parliamentary majority consists of 61 seats. After the election, the president consults with all the parliamentary factions and asks the lawmaker he believes has the best chance of securing the Knesset’s support to form a government and become prime minister. This is not necessarily the leader of the largest party. In 2021, for example, Bennett became prime minister even though his party held just seven seats — and even then, not all of its members supported the new government.
Moreover, a formal confidence vote can pass without 61 votes in favor. For example, the government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid was approved by a vote of 60–59, with one abstention coming from a lawmaker of the Islamist Ra’am party. The party itself, meanwhile, made history by becoming the first Arab political movement in Israel to sign a coalition agreement with the Zionist camp by supporting the Bennett–Lapid government.
A party can also remain outside the coalition and receive no ministerial posts while supporting the government in confidence and budget votes. In the 1990s, for example, Arab factions helped keep Yitzhak Rabin’s minority government in power without joining it. But for a cabinet to function stably, it generally needs either its own stable coalition or guaranteed outside support. The Bennett–Lapid government, which lacked these requisites, lasted just over a year before announcing its dissolution.
Under the current political configuration, Netanyahu needs the ultra-Orthodox vote to have any hope of maintaining a majority. He may still find allies among smaller parties, but some of these categorically rule out supporting a government led by him or involving his Likud party — at least for now. However, they might agree to compromise in the event that Netanyahu agree to give up the premiership in the name of national unity.
“Kingmakers” – what the ultra-Orthodox want
The ultra-Orthodox are primarily interested in their own agenda, which involves state funding for their communities (including religious education), the sustained authority of rabbinical courts, and exemptions for yeshiva students from military service. They are willing to join forces with any party that best promises to satisfy their demands.
Attempts to reach an agreement on these issues began even before Israel declared its independence. In 1947, David Ben-Gurion, the country’s future first prime minister, promised to preserve the status quo: Saturday would be the official day of rest, state institutions would observe kosher dietary laws, marriages and divorces would remain under the jurisdiction of religious courts, and religious schools would retain their autonomy. In return, Ben-Gurion sought to secure the ultra-Orthodox’s support for the establishment of a Jewish state.
The situation changed dramatically in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1977, the left-wing camp, previously led by Mapai and later by the Labor Party, lost power for the first time. In 1981, Likud and the left-wing bloc won almost identical numbers of seats — 48 and 47, respectively. Neither the right nor the left could count on forming governments exclusively with ideologically like-minded partners, and horse-trading with smaller parties began. The ultra-Orthodox proved particularly useful because, in Israeli political terms, they did not identify with either the right or the left, particularly when it came to the Arab-Israeli conflict and, above all, the Palestinian issue.
Today, the ultra-Orthodox camp is represented by two electoral lists but in fact consists of three parties: Shas, Degel HaTorah, and Agudat Yisrael. Since 1992, the latter two parties have run together under the United Torah Judaism list, which primarily represents Ashkenazi Haredim — descendants of Jews from Central and Eastern Europe. But the list contains two separate party structures, each subordinate to a different rabbinical council.
Agudat Yisrael (“Union of Israel”) consists primarily of Hasidic communities. The party was founded in Poland in 1912 as a movement of Orthodox Jews opposed to secularization and political Zionism. In Israel, the party’s influence is divided among several Hasidic courts, the largest of which have their own rabbis, educational institutions, and political representatives. Final decisions are made by the Council of Torah Sages, which includes leaders of influential Hasidic communities.
Degel HaTorah (“Banner of the Torah”) represents the Lithuanian, or Litvak, tradition. The party was founded in 1988 by Rabbi Elazar Shach after a conflict with the Hasidic leadership of Agudat Yisrael. Its leading religious authorities today are Rabbis Dov Landau and Moshe Hillel Hirsch. Their directives determine how Degel HaTorah lawmakers vote on key issues and which coalition they can join.
The two parties run together in elections because competing separately would put both at risk of failing to clear the 3.25% electoral threshold. Still, within United Torah Judaism, disputes over the allocation of seats, positions, and budgets are constant.
Shas (Sephardim – Torah Guardians) represents another segment of ultra-Orthodox society: Jews whose families originated mainly in the Middle East and North Africa. It was founded in 1984 by Rabbi Ovadia Yosef with the support of Rabbi Shach. One of the reasons for its creation was discrimination against Sephardim within the Ashkenazi system of religious schools, yeshivas, and political organizations. The party’s highest religious body is the Council of Torah Sages.
One of the clearest examples of the rabbis’ influence over the choice of prime minister can be found in the 1990 political crisis known as the “dirty trick.” Labor leader Shimon Peres secured a no-confidence vote against Yitzhak Shamir’s national unity government and attempted to form an alternative coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties, but the deal fell apart after religious authorities intervened. Rabbi Shach opposed an alliance with the left, and two Agudat Yisrael lawmakers failed to show up for the decisive vote. Peres was unable to form a government, after which Shamir formed a new right-wing coalition.
For many years, however, the Haredim’s alliance with the right was not unconditional. In 1992, Shas joined Yitzhak Rabin’s government alongside Labor and the left-wing Meretz bloc. Labor had 44 seats, Meretz 12, and Shas six, giving the government a 62-seat majority. However, after Shas left the coalition, Rabin’s cabinet became a minority government and depended on outside support from Arab factions.
In 1999, Shas joined Ehud Barak’s center-left government, having by then won a record 17 seats. United Torah Judaism, with five lawmakers, also joined the coalition.
There have also been governments without the ultra-Orthodox. In 2003, Ariel Sharon opted for an alliance with the anti-clerical Shinui party, and in 2013, Netanyahu left Shas and United Torah Judaism in opposition, reaching an agreement with Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett instead. The most recent government without the ultra-Orthodox was the short-lived coalition that formed in 2021.
In the 25th Knesset, Shas and United Torah Judaism had a combined 18 lawmakers, and both remained key partners for the ruling coalition for most of the term. July polls projected the ultra-Orthodox to take between 15 and 17 seats in the October vote, but there is still no guarantee that they will support Netanyahu, who failed to keep too many promises over the past four years.
The ultra-Orthodox’s main grievance
The main complaint Shas and United Torah Judaism have against Netanyahu and their other coalition partners is the failure to pass a law that would guarantee exemptions from military service for yeshiva students (the bill never reached a final vote), who since 1948 have been granted deferments under the principle of “Torah is their vocation.” Initially the provision applied to only about 400 students, but since 1977 there has been no limit on their number. The provision had been enshrined in law several times, but those laws were struck down by the Supreme Court starting in July 2023, though the government subsequently issued a temporary order that yeshiva students not be drafted, hoping to pass a new law.
In June 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that the government could not grant such an exemption on its own and ordered the state to apply the general Military Service Law to the ultra-Orthodox. The army then began sending out draft notices — and later issuing arrest warrants — for conscripts who failed to report. By July 2026, some 72,000 Haredim aged 18 to 24 who were subject to the draft had not enlisted. The resulting arrests triggered mass protests within the community.
By July 2026, some 72,000 Haredim aged 18 to 24 were subject to the draft but had not enlisted
After nearly three years of war — in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, along with continued tensions in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) — the Israeli military is facing a manpower shortage that has placed an enormous burden on reservists. From October 2023 to the present, 27% of reserve soldiers have served a total of 150 to 300 days, while 20% have served more than 300 days. Against this backdrop, the idea that part of society is ignoring their obligation to service has sparked strong negative feelings.
The issue is not simply a demand to send all yeshiva students into the army immediately. Most Arab citizens of Israel are also exempt from the draft, while the IDF already has units adapted to the needs of the ultra-Orthodox, where special kosher requirements and gender segregation are observed. Supporters of the draft see this as proof that integration is possible, while most ultra-Orthodox Jews fear that mass military service would undermine their religious way of life. At the same time, there are concerns that adapting the army to accommodate ultra-Orthodox service could limit opportunities for female soldiers.
The issue, therefore, is much broader. Should the army adapt to the demands of the ultra-Orthodox community, or should the community adapt to the army’s general rules? Can military service be replaced with civilian service, and can that contribution to the nation truly be considered equivalent? And should a particular community be allowed to maintain near-total autonomy if the burden of its protection and funding falls on everyone else? Ultimately, the dispute over military service has become a debate over what the State of Israel should be and what obligations its citizens should have toward it.
In any case, as the election approaches, one element of this complex problem stands out: Netanyahu has alienated the ultra-Orthodox community. Moshe Gafni, the leader of Degel HaTorah, says the previous coalition arrangement will not be repeated after the election, promising: “Before forming any government, we will first pass a military draft law.” Technically, this is possible. The new Knesset can begin legislative work while the outgoing government remains in office, and the ultra-Orthodox parties could delay signing a coalition agreement until after the law they want has been finally passed.
Shas uses less forceful language and has not ruled out siding with the right-wing bloc, but the party’s fundamental demand is the same. Back in May, Shas leader Aryeh Deri said: “We will not join a coalition or government until we resolve the status of those who study Torah.”
The legislative blitz
Once it became clear that fulfilling the ultra-Orthodox’s main demand before the election was impossible, the Knesset entered what Israeli journalists called a “legislative blitz.” In the final days, lawmakers passed a series of laws demanded by the Haredim, who in return agreed to keep parliament working until a date that suited the prime minister by helping Netanyahu pass initiatives he and other coalition members needed. These included weakening the powers of the government’s legal adviser and reforming the media market.
The ultra-Orthodox secured a Basic Law on Torah study, albeit in a heavily watered-down version of the original proposal. Israel does not have a single written constitution — Basic Laws partly serve that role, so even a short declaration formally has constitutional status. The original version equated sustained Torah study with “meaningful service” to the state (that is, military service) and would have allowed it to be taken into account when allocating rights and benefits. This triggered a wave of criticism, including from within the coalition.
The ultra-Orthodox secured a Basic Law on Torah study, albeit in a heavily watered-down version of the original proposal
As a result, the substantive provisions were removed from the text. All that remained was a single provision: “Torah study is a fundamental value of the heritage of the Jewish people and the State of Israel.” For the Haredim, this amounted to historic recognition. Aryeh Deri called the vote “a victory for the Torah world,” while Gafni described it as the creation of “the state’s value compass.” But even within the Haredi community, questions arose as to whether the law had become a consolation prize.
A more effective measure was supposed to be a law suspending the arrest of Haredim who failed to report for military service after receiving draft notices. It barred the military police from detaining yeshiva students, initiating new criminal proceedings against them, or continuing cases already underway. The protection also covered those who reached draft age after the law took effect. Formally, the restrictions were set to remain in place until November 30, but given the election and the transition period, they could have remained in force until the end of January 2027. However, the Haredim did not have time to make use of the law. Less than 24 hours later, the Supreme Court suspended it.
Still, the Haredim did manage to secure some gains. The Knesset repealed the kosher certification reform adopted by the previous government and expanded the possibility of separate education for men and women at universities. Previously, special programs for Haredim existed primarily at the undergraduate level. Now the Council for Higher Education can authorize separate master’s and doctoral programs. At mixed-gender institutions, segregation is permitted in classrooms, and participation must be voluntary. Such programs will be available not only to Haredim but also to other students who cite religious beliefs. To secular Israelis, however, the law amounts to segregation and has further deepened the divide between the opposition and the coalition. For Netanyahu, though, this only works to his advantage, as it increases the chances that the Haredim will remain with him.
Against the backdrop of the heated public debate, the ultra-Orthodox do not have many options, as their agenda does not align with that of many other opposition parties. Asher Medina of Shas, for example, warned against an alliance with the left-wing camp, saying that its “only common denominator is hatred of the Haredim.”
But Israeli politics is known for its unexpected alliances and sudden twists. There are almost three months to go before the election, and the balance of power could change many times before then.

U.S. budget deficit surged in July to highest level since March 2021

The U.S. budget deficit soared to its highest monthly level in more than five years amid a surge in Medicare costs and as interest on the federal debt continued to weigh on the nation's fiscal picture, the Treasury Department reported Wednesday.
In addition to the big single-month jump, the collective red ink across the first 10 months of the government's fiscal year rose to nearly $1.8 trillion and surpassed the same period in 2025.
The July shortfall totaled $432.3 billion, up some 48% from the same period a year ago and the largest monthly deficit since March 2021.
Medicare expenses for the month totaled $174 billion, up from $103 billion in June and now at $955 billion for the full year. It was the single largest expenditure in July, well ahead of the $141 billion spent on Social Security and $104 billion in net interest on the national debt.
Tariff refunds also hit the budget, costing $33 billion as the administration continues to provide rebates for levies that the Supreme Court ruled illegal. Additionally, the budget took a $99 billion hit because the first of the month was a nonbusiness day, accelerating various benefits outlays as well as Supplemental Security Income and Medicare payments.
Debt financing for the full year is behind only Social Security and Medicare as a proportion of government expenses. For the fiscal year to date, the U.S. has paid out $1.17 trillion on the $39.9 trillion national debt, of which $32.1 trillion is held by the public. Debt servicing costs in the same period a year ago totaled $1.01 trillion. Net interest, or the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives, totaled $931 billion.
President Donald Trump for years had been pressing the Federal Reserve to lower benchmark interest rates as a way to reduce debt costs. He has held off on criticizing the central bank since his nominee, Kevin Warsh, took over as chairman in May.
Until recently, markets had been looking for the Fed to raise rates to control inflation that has been running above the central bank's 2% target for more than five years. However, recent benign inflation data and a soft payroll reports have tempered those expectations, though futures traders aren't pricing in any chance of a rate cut for the next five years.

Netanyahu rose through Likud democracy. Now he risks hollowing it out from within - analysis

18:55:23 UTC
03:55:23 KST

No one has ever confused Likud primaries with genteel affairs. They are loud, messy, and extremely competitive.
But even by Likud’s rough-and-tumble standards, the run-up to Monday’s primary looks like an extraordinary mess.
There are the battles over the district slots, the party court rulings, the attempts to protect veteran ministers, the eight places Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was given to fill with candidates of his choosing, and the additional guaranteed positions he demanded – and received – for Defense Minister Israel Katz, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, and Likud Central Committee chairman Haim Katz.
Taken together, Netanyahu will control 11 of the top 29 positions on the party’s next Knesset slate. That is enormous influence, especially since the Likud, which currently holds 32 seats, is polling at an average of only 23-24.
It also means that a significant number of today’s Likud MKs will not be parliamentarians tomorrow. That has left them embittered and battling for their political lives in what is essentially a zero-sum game.
And that type of bitterness tends to spill into the public arena – as it has.
Then came Netanyahu’s first personal selection: Oren Dobronsky, a hi-tech entrepreneur with years of Silicon Valley experience who was supposed to add economic and technological heft to the list.
Netanyahu apparently meant to undercut Nir Barkat, once a possible successor
He was also, if reports are to be believed, meant to undercut Economy and Industry Minister Nir Barkat, himself a former hi-tech entrepreneur.
Why would Netanyahu want to undercut Barkat, once widely viewed as a possible successor? Because according to a Channel 12 report, Barkat and Yuli Edelstein – who has since left the Likud to form a new party with Gilad Erdan – were behind an unsuccessful attempt immediately after October 7 to replace Netanyahu.
According to the report, Barkat and Edelstein tried to secure the support of the 13 Likud MKs needed to replace Netanyahu through a constructive vote of no confidence. They were unable to agree on who would take his place, and Edelstein reportedly proposed becoming interim prime minister, followed by a Likud leadership primary in which he would not run.
The report said Haim Katz learned of the effort and warned Netanyahu, who moved to thwart it. Some believe Netanyahu is now protecting Katz while reportedly using the primary to settle scores with Barkat.
The scriptwriters of a political drama could hardly have come up with a better storyline.
All of this points to a larger problem facing the Likud: How does a party that prides itself on being democratic ensure that its primary produces a list able to appeal to those beyond its base?
Unlike most Israeli parties, Likud has long taken pride in allowing its members to choose its Knesset candidates. This is a significant part of its identity. The Likud likes to contrast its broad, grassroots membership with parties led by the likes of Avigdor Liberman, Yair Lapid, and Naftali Bennett, whose lists are determined by the leader or a small committee.
There is merit to that argument. Primaries give party members a voice. They force politicians to maintain contact with the grassroots.
There is also no small irony in Netanyahu’s effort to undercut the primary system. He entered the Knesset in 1988 by prevailing in Likud’s old Central Committee-based selection process, despite opposition from parts of the party establishment. Five years later, a party-wide leadership primary enabled him to defeat David Levy, Benny Begin, and Moshe Katsav and take control of the party.
The Likud’s internal democracy did not merely help Netanyahu; it was critical to his political rise.
But that was then. In recent years, the primary system has exposed a serious downside.
To succeed, candidates need name recognition across the country. Quiet legislative work, expertise in a particular field, or a record of effective committee work doesn’t exactly provide that. Television appearances do. So do provocative statements, attacks on political opponents, and inflammatory social-media posts.
The louder the candidate, the greater the likelihood that Likud members will know their name when they reach the primary ballot box.
That system has helped propel figures such as Tally Gotliv to prominence. Gotliv is constantly in the headlines. She attacks the courts, the Attorney-General’s Office, the media, her political opponents, and occasionally members of her own party. She knows how to appeal to a significant part of the Likud base.
And she is now among the fiercest critics of Netanyahu’s reserved slots. But Netanyahu’s dilemma is understandable.
He wants a party list that can attract voters beyond the Likud faithful. Internal polling reportedly indicates that some candidates popular with Likud members are far less attractive to moderate right-wing and swing voters whom the party will need in the election.
Netanyahu therefore wants the ability to balance the list: to add people from hi-tech, economics, security, and other fields who can broaden the party’s appeal and give it greater governing credibility.
That, at least, is the argument for the reserved slots, and it is not an unreasonable one.
The problem is the scale.
Giving Netanyahu eight handpicked positions, followed by guaranteed places for three senior ministers, means that he will effectively determine a third of the party’s realistic list. At a certain point, these types of “corrections” to the primary system begin to hollow out the primary itself.
Some veteran Likud figures look back nostalgically at the days when a much smaller party forum played the decisive role in choosing the list, including through the famous shvi’iyot, in which Central Committee members selected and ranked candidates in groups of seven.
Old system wasn't perfect, but produced some high-stature Likud representatives
That system was far less democratic. It was also vulnerable to deals, pressure groups, and political horse-trading. It should not be romanticized.
Yet it did produce Likud representatives of considerable stature: Dan Meridor, Roni Milo, Benny Begin, Michael Eitan, Uzi Landau, and others who combined strong ideological views with independence, policy expertise, and respect for the institutions of the state.
Would figures of that type survive today’s Likud primary?
Meridor’s defense of the judiciary would have made him unelectable in a Likud primary today. Eitan’s years of serious parliamentary work would mean little against a candidate producing daily viral videos. And a thoughtful candidate such as Yuval Steinitz might find it difficult to generate the excitement needed to prevail in a contest driven by social media and combative television appearances.
That doesn’t mean the old system was necessarily superior. Nor does it mean Likud members are incapable of choosing serious candidates. It does mean that a large national primary creates incentives that favor confrontation, ideological purity, and name recognition over depth, experience, and independence.
Netanyahu is now trying to correct those distortions from above. But in doing so, he risks undermining the democratic character that distinguishes Likud from nearly every other Israeli party.
This is the balancing act at the center of Monday’s primary.
Leave the process entirely in the hands of the membership, and the result may be a list filled with candidates who fire up the base but repel many of the voters Likud needs to win the election.
Intervene too heavily, however, and the party’s much-vaunted internal democracy becomes largely cosmetic – a primary in which the leader has already determined more than a third of the realistic list.
There is no selection system guaranteed to produce top-tier politicians. A small committee can choose mediocrities and cronies just as easily as a primary can reward demagogues.
But Likud’s current predicament is acute: The party wants the democratic legitimacy of a mass primary and the broad electoral appeal of a carefully put-together list. The chaos surrounding the August 17 vote shows how difficult it is to have both.

U.S. Marines Purchase 10 Tempest Air Defense Systems — The Type Is Used in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:55:19 UTC
03:55:19 KST

The U.S. Marine Corps has approved the purchase of 10 Tempest mobile air defense systems of a type already used in Ukraine.
The Pentagon contract says that Vertex Modernization and Sustainment has received a $19 million contract to supply 10 combat vehicles.
The agreement also includes software, spare parts, personnel training and other technical support services required to operate the systems in the field.
The contract is to be completed by August 2027.
The Tempest air defense system is designed to counter enemy drones, helicopters and low-flying aircraft in all weather conditions.
The combat vehicle is built on a chassis similar to that of the commercial Can-Am Maverick X3 buggy and is designed for operations in which high mobility and a low signature are key.
The system is equipped with two AGM-114 Hellfire missiles for engaging targets. During the presentation, the developer did not specify the exact missile variant, but it is likely to be the AGM-114L Hellfire Longbow, which is equipped with a radar seeker.
A radar station is mounted on the buggy’s frame and likely provides target detection and tracking, as well as target designation for the missiles. Optical sighting systems and laser guidance equipment were not demonstrated at the exhibition.
This may indicate that the radar is the primary means of detecting and tracking targets, further supporting the assumption that AGM-114L missiles are being used.
The company says the radar’s modular architecture allows the platform to quickly switch between mobile and stationary configurations without losing situational awareness or tracking accuracy.
In addition to the mobile version, V2X offers the Tempest on a trailer for static or semi-fixed missions, including the defense of military bases and airfield perimeters.
The vehicle has a limited ammunition load of only two missiles per launcher, but the Hellfire missiles are equipped with a powerful warhead weighing about 9 kg.
This is sufficient to destroy strike drones in the air while minimizing collateral damage on the ground caused by falling debris.
Tempest air defense systems are already in use in Ukraine.

US embassies in Middle East brace for prolonged reduced operations amid Iran conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:55:08 UTC
03:55:08 KST

The US State Department is requesting that US embassies in the Middle East develop “reduced operations” plans, as the conflict with Iran shows no immediate signs of resolution, according to a CNN report published on Wednesday.
Sources have informed CNN that, although plans have not been finalized, the State Department has encouraged US embassy staff to reduce both their assignments and staff numbers. There is a general expectation that officials do not anticipate returning to normal staffing levels in the region anytime soon.
However, reports indicate that the State Department has yet to determine whether all affected posts will implement these changes.
Any plans for “reduced operations,” once finalized, could provide some clarity to US diplomats and their families who have been displaced, CNN reported.
A spokesperson from the State Department spoke with CNN regarding the reported changes at the embassy. They stated, “do not discuss internal deliberations or post-specific contingency planning,” but noted that the department “continually reviews the security and staffing posture at every diplomatic mission based on conditions on the ground and adjusts personnel levels as appropriate.”
“Decisions regarding the status of any post are made based on a range of security and operational factors, in close coordination between posts and Washington,” they added.
Fewer diplomats on the ground may affect the State Department's ability to provide timely consular assistance to Americans abroad and to support the administration's priorities, former diplomats told CNN.
However, a State Department spokesperson refuted the notion that US diplomatic efforts are “limited” due to a reduced number of personnel on the ground.
“We have seen sustained engagement from the highest levels of the Trump Administration with our partners in the Middle East, and our relationship with our allies in the region continues to get stronger,” they said.
Embassy evacuations begin with the US-Israel war against Iran
The State Department ordered nonemergency personnel and family members to leave almost every diplomatic post in the region shortly after the US-Israel war with Iran began in late February.
A decision that was followed by nearly six months of uncertainty about whether the posts could return to normal and whether all diplomats could return to their assignments.
The State Department did not reduce staffing at most embassies in the region prior to the start of the US-Israeli military campaign. Before the war, only Lebanon and Israel were designated under "ordered and authorized departure status," meaning non-emergency personnel and their family members had the option to leave but were not required to do so.
As the conflict intensified and US diplomatic facilities in the region became targets for Iran and its proxies, facing drone and missile attacks, the State Department ordered the departure of non-emergency personnel and their families from Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
The abrupt reduction in staff left many diplomats and their families, who had several years left on their assignments, struggling to create temporary situations for themselves back on American soil. They found themselves unable to make long-term commitments upon returning home and had to plan around the expectation that they would need to quickly return to the Middle East if the political climate shifted.
In response to growing concern among embassy staff, the State Department spokesperson told CNN the department remains “committed to supporting our workforce and their families throughout this process and will provide updates through appropriate channels as decisions are made.”

Ukraine Liberated 745 Square Kilometers, 26 Settlements in Eight-Month Offensive, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian forces liberated 745 square kilometers and retook 26 villages across three southeastern regions during a months-long offensive in the Oleksandrivka direction, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on August 12.
In the statement, posted to his official Telegram channel, Zelenskyy stated that troops from Ukraine's Air Assault Forces and other attached units had carried out the operation between January and August.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This offensive operation of ours was carried out precisely—exactly as it was planned," Zelenskyy wrote, describing the campaign as matching the objectives set for it.
Zelenskyy claimed the operation had killed at least 9,550 Russian soldiers and wounded more than 6,600, while also adding to the pool of prisoners available for future exchanges. The recaptured villages are spread across the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, according to his account.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, Chief of the General Staff Ihor Skybiuk, and Air Assault Forces commander Oleh Apostol had reported to him on the operation's results and the next steps.
The operation fits a broader Ukrainian effort to wrest back the strategic initiative in the east through active defense, aimed at grinding down Russia's offensive capacity.
That approach has already made Russian advances in the Donetsk region extraordinarily costly, with Moscow estimated to be losing more than 400 troops for every square kilometer of ground it seizes there.

Steelers’ Aaron Rodgers wishes Thursday’s preseason game with Packers could take place in Green Bay
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers has one regret about starting his final NFL season with an exhibition game against the team that drafted him.
He would have preferred Thursday’s matchup with the Packers take place in Green Bay rather than Pittsburgh. Rodgers wanted to have one final moment in the place where he spent his first 18 seasons and won four MVP awards and a Super Bowl.
“I was really hoping this one was going to be in Green Bay, not just to get back at Lambeau one more time, but to head out to Chives for a dinner and maybe head out to Green Bay Country Club for a quick nine or something,” Rodgers said Wednesday in a Zoom session with Packers reporters. “I was really hoping it was going to be in Green Bay, for a lot of reasons.”
This will be the second time Rodgers has faced his former team since leaving the Packers in 2023, though there’s no indication yet on whether he will play Thursday. Both games were in Pittsburgh, so Rodgers will head into retirement after this season having never played against the Packers at Lambeau Field.
“It would have been strange, being in that locker room and stuff,” Rodgers said. “But I would have found my way over, like many former players have over the years, found my way over to Flea’s (Packers head athletic trainer Bryan Engel’s) office and hang out back there and see some of the guys and see some of the trainers and equipment staff and all the people I really care about that still work there.
“Yeah, I was definitely bummed out that we weren’t in Lambeau for this one.”
Rodgers’ Steelers lost 35-25 to the Packers last October. Jordan Love, the quarterback Green Bay selected in the first round of the 2020 draft to become Rodgers’ eventual successor, threw for 360 yards and three touchdowns that night.
When he was asked what he missed the most about Wisconsin aside from football and the fans, Rodgers talked about the house he owned during his Packers years, the meals he enjoyed at Chives and the rounds of golf he played. Then he turned the subject back toward football.
“The falls there are just awesome, when the weather gets that cool little nip,” Rodgers said. “I loved the night games at Lambeau, especially the Sunday nights, Monday nights and occasional Thursday nights. Just so much fun. There’s nothing like that crowd. I’ve been other places, I knew that when I was in Green Bay, but there’s nothing like that fan base and the way they travel and the crowds at home.
“Players around the league, they talk about how special it is to play at Lambeau, and sometimes you might miss that or forget about that when you’re playing because it becomes so normal to have such an amazing crowd and they’re tailgating and they’re loud and they rarely sell their tickets to other teams’ fans. There’s a lot of great things about Wisconsin. I grew up there, really, and became a little more mature as an adult over the years there and had a great time and still have a lot of close friends there, a lot of fond memories.”
Rodgers did play his other former team as a visiting player last season when he made his Steelers debut and led Pittsburgh to a 34-32 victory over the New York Jets in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Rodgers was with the Jets from 2023-24 after they acquired him from Green Bay, though he missed virtually all of 2023 after tearing his Achilles tendon in the season opener.
The Steelers host the Jets on Aug. 21 in their second preseason game.

Ex-Southern Poverty Law Center official charged in broader criminal case against group, lawyer says

Ex-Southern Poverty Law Center official charged in broader criminal case against group
RIVERSIDE, Calif. (AP) — A former Southern Poverty Law Center official has been charged in the Department of Justice’s broader criminal case against the Alabama-based civil rights group, a frequent target of conservative critics who claim the nonprofit is politically biased.
Heidi Beirich, a political extremism expert who left the law center about six years ago, was named in an indictment unsealed Wednesday.
Beirich, 59, of Palm Springs, California, is charged with wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to submit false statements to a federally insured bank and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. She was charged in the government’s existing case against the SPLC in Montgomery, Alabama.
In ankle cuffs and wearing a red T-shirt, Beirich made her initial court appearance for a bond hearing in Riverside, California, Wednesday afternoon. She did not enter a plea and U.S. Magistrate Judge David T. Bristow ordered her to surrender her passport and appear in court in Alabama within two weeks.
The judge released Beirich on her own recognizance after prosecutors declined to file a request for detention. Her lawyer, Michael Proctor, said in court that Beirich is a “highly, highly responsible, pro-social and trustworthy” member of society with no criminal history.
Outside the courthouse, Proctor said his client is innocent of the charges and described the case as politically motivated.
“She has dedicated her life to fighting the KKK, neo-Nazi groups, extremists. And for all of that life’s work, we’re all safer. We’re all better as a community,” he told The Associated Press. “It is not just ironic, but terrible, that for this work she’s been indicted by the current Department of Justice.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the new charges at a news briefing in Washington, but did not name Beirich. CNN was first to report on the charges against Beirich.
“This is exactly what we said would happen in a case like this,” Blanche said. “Our investigators and the U.S. Attorneys and the agents working the case will keep on working it even after the initial indictment.”
An SPLC spokesperson said the case against it and Beirich “will not shake our resolve.”
“Taking on violent hate and extremist groups is among the most dangerous work there is, and we believe it is also among the most important work we do,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We are confident in our position and look forward to presenting the evidence and making our case in court.”
Beirich led the SPLC’s Intelligence Project, which incurred the anger of conservatives with its annual report on organizations that it classified as hate groups. Critics accused the law center of unfairly tarnishing right-wing groups with the same label that it applied to white supremacists.
Beirich co-founded the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism in 2020 after leaving the SPLC. She has testified before Congress about far-right extremism and is frequently interviewed about the subject by news outlets. Her current organization did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment Wednesday.
A superseding indictment filed in June appears to refer to Beirich as “Employee-2” and by her former title as director of the SPLC’s Intelligence Project.
The indictment alleges that between 2007 and 2023, more than $4 million in donated funds were secretly funneled to people who infiltrated or were associated with violent extremist groups. Prosecutors said some of the money was used for recruiting new members and purchasing Ku Klux Klan robes and materials for cross-burning ceremonies.
The indictment says “Employee-2” oversaw the payment of donor money to SPLC informants or “field sources,” including KKK members and white nationalists who initially approached the SPLC for help leaving the extremist organizations. The SPLC employee was in a romantic relationship with a source who infiltrated a neo-Nazi group at the direction of the law center, the indictment alleges
Proctor said Beirich “won’t be silenced or intimidated by the government’s false and politicized allegations.”

Kunzelman reported from Washington and Chandler from Montgomery, Ala. Associated Press writers Eric Tucker, Alanna Durkin Richer and Collin Binkley in Washington and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed to this report.

Montana State University launches a new Wool Lab to revive an old industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:53:01 UTC
03:53:01 KST

Montana State University launches a new Wool Lab to revive an old industry
On a hot August afternoon, wool expert Brent Roeder strode among sheep, combing his fingers through their fleece to assess color, length and uniformity. Roeder, an extension specialist at Montana State University, tends to the college-owned flock at an old off-campus cavalry barracks called the Fort Ellis Research and Teaching Farm. The flock exists to give agriculture students hands-on experience. That includes learning how to raise high-quality sheep for sales like the one in Miles City that Roeder plans to take six animals to this September.
“You’re taking your best of your best,” Roeder said.
Roeder is on a mission to revitalize the regional wool industry. He manages the university’s new Wool Lab, a facility dedicated to making wool production more efficient and more profitable for Montana’s sheep ranchers. He has spent a lifetime watching synthetic fiber undermine demand for wool. Now, Roeder hopes the new facility can show students “why the wool industry is still important and relevant.”
“I’m a little gray-haired. Finding this next generation was part of the investment in this lab, to be able to teach that next generation so they could innovate,” Roeder said.
The new building opened in July. The on-campus facility also contains the Montana Department of Livestock’s Veterinary Diagnostic Lab and the Montana Department of Agriculture’s Analytical Lab. The Wool Lab cost about $10 million, funded by a combination of legislative appropriations and donations from private industry.
The Wool Lab’s previous home, located about a mile from the new one, dates back to the 1940s. The Montana Legislature first approved funding for that lab in 1945, when the industry was mid-boom after years of substantial government subsidies for the wool industry during World War II. In the mid-twentieth century, wool labs were common at land-grant universities. But today, the only similar facility outside of Bozeman is at Texas A&M, according to Roeder.
The disappearance of wool labs tracks with the wool industry’s slow and steady decline. Over the last 80 years, the U.S. sheep herd has decreased by 90%. That’s partly driven by rising agricultural input costs, regional drought and an increase in imported lamb.
Montana has not been immune to the squeeze. Over the last 30 years, in-state wool production has dwindled by two-thirds, and sheep-ranching operations have declined by half. As of 2024, Montana was home to about 190,000 sheep and about 1,100 wool operations.
Synthetic fabric has overwhelmed the market share that wool once ruled, according to Roeder.
“It’s really only been over the last 70 or 80 years that synthetics have come in. And they’ve completely dominated the whole fabric manufacturing system,” Roeder said.
So Roeder has aligned himself with the natural-fiber industry, which includes cotton and wool-based clothes. He decries synthetic clothing’s environmental cost — it’s made from fossil fuels, releases microplastics when washed and doesn’t biodegrade — and describes natural products as more comfortable to wear.
“I’m not against plastic or the oil industry, because I have a lot of friends in that industry, but maybe we shouldn’t be making $5 plastic shirts and importing them from China,” Roeder said.
Roeder wants the Wool Lab to innovate cheaper ways to produce and process wool. Montana ranchers help steer the direction of the lab’s research. Every two years, 25 sheep producers come to campus to grade Roeder’s work.
Those assessments aren’t public. But Stefanie Leach, executive assistant with the Montana Wool Growers Association, which wrote a $100,000 check for the new lab, told Montana Free Press the facility is doing necessary work.
“Without the research there, our industry stays stagnant. Without them doing research, we have no new innovation,” Leach said.
One way the lab hopes to boost the regional market is by helping ranchers breed animals that produce wool that can be worn comfortably next to human skin. That requires that wool fibers be less than 30 microns (0.001 inches) thick. Next-to-skin wool doesn’t itch. And most of the country’s domestic supply of next-to-skin wool comes from Idaho, Utah, Wyoming and Montana, according to Leach.
Becky Weed, a sheep rancher near Belgrade who utilized Wool Lab resources during her early days in the business in the 1980s, said modern ranchers don’t just need help producing a particular grade of wool — they need help processing and selling it. She said the market was different when she got into the wool industry four decades ago.
“The mainstream wool growers at that time weren’t paying as close attention to what happened to their fiber, who was using it, who was marketing it, and how much they were getting paid for their wool,” Weed said.
But that changed as the industry shrank. Now, sheep ranchers have to be more intentional, Weed said.
She said she’s glad the Wool Lab is getting “a shot in the arm” and praised Roeder as “a real leader amongst the wool growers.”
Roeder said conditions for wool producers are improving — the commodity price has doubled in the last two years and is currently at a six-year high — but the industry still suffers from years of economic neglect.
“We have not had enough profitability in the industry for so long, there’s been no investment in facilities, structures, new barns and handling equipment. There just wasn’t the revenue to do it,” Roeder said.
As Roeder herded and handled sheep at the Fort Ellis farm, he wore a hat decorated with an American flag in the shape of a lamb, a token of thanks from the Teton County Fair, where he’s spent more than a decade helping 4H participants raise and show their sheep and goats. His belt buckle, emblazoned with “Texas A&M,” commemorates his 1993 championship in intercollegiate wool judging.
He said he’s confident the wool industry isn’t going anywhere, and that a next generation of Montana sheep ranchers has plenty to learn, and to teach.
“Don’t ever put your fingers inside,” Roeder said, dropping his hand between a sheep and the pen’s metal railing. He pulled away just before the animal’s head butted the rail where his fingers had been.
“That’s instinct,” he said.

Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:53:00 UTC
03:53:00 KST

Eurovision bars countries at war from hosting
August 12, 2026
Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event.
Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition.
What did the Eurovision organizers say?
Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said.
The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected.
Why is the Eurovision changing the rules?
The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026.
Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza. Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran.
The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before.
Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf.
Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
What else is changing about the Eurovision?
Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists.
Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices.
The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live.
Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent.
Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga."

Putin threatens to seize foreign ships in response to EU detentions of Russian oil tankers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:50:17 UTC
03:50:17 KST

Vladimir Putin promised a “mirror” response to detentions of Russian vessels by European Union member states, according to a report by the Interfax news agency. He made the remarks during a visit to the final stage of Pacific Fleet exercises in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk.
“They recently came up with the possible seizure of our vessels and sale of property stolen from us,” Putin said. “Of course, this [detention of Russian vessels] is nothing other than piracy and robbery. And if this begins to be implemented in practice, we will be forced to respond in kind…where we ourselves consider it necessary and appropriate — anywhere, including in the area of responsibility of the Pacific Fleet.”
Putin has previously described Western actions taken against vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet” as piracy. He used that term after the tanker Boracay (IMO: 9332810) was detained by the French Navy in September last year. The vessel was released several days later.
This past July, Putin reiterated that view, saying attempts to seize Russian tankers should be treated as piracy.
“In such cases, of course, it is necessary to act carefully, within the framework of international maritime law, but decisively — the way piracy and pirates should be fought,” Putin said at a meeting with the commanders of Russia’s Pacific, Northern, Baltic, and Black Sea fleets, along with those of the Caspian Flotilla.
EU countries periodically detain “shadow fleet” vessels involved in transporting Russian oil, but later release them. In June, the UK detained a Russian tanker in the English Channel for the first time, with British forces and law enforcement personnel boarding the sanctioned tanker Smyrtos (IMO: 9389100).
The EU has authorized its member states to sell Russian oil and petroleum products that their authorities have seized or confiscated, and proceeds from these sales cannot be transferred to Russian citizens, companies, or organizations. The new rules are contained in an EU Council regulation that took effect July 24.

Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.
Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.
On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.
A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”
Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.
The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.
On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.
But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.
The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.
Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

A country in a state of war will not be able to host Eurovision – updated contest rules

Unknown Publisher

03:45:29 KST

A country in a state of war will not be able to host Eurovision – updated contest rules
Kyiv • UNN
The European Broadcasting Union has updated the Eurovision rules, according to which the winning country automatically loses the right to host the contest in the event of an armed conflict or geopolitical tensions. An alternative host will be determined after a security assessment.
The European Broadcasting Union has updated the rules for holding the Eurovision Song Contest. Now, the winning country automatically loses the right to host the contest if it is involved in an armed conflict or faces a tense geopolitical situation. This is stated on the official Eurovision website, reports UNN.
The winning broadcaster automatically loses the right to host the contest if an armed conflict, a tense geopolitical situation, or any other circumstance significantly affects the safety, security, or stability of its country or the immediate region
If necessary, the European Broadcasting Union may commission an independent security assessment of the winner’s region. Following such an assessment, the Union will consult with the Advisory Group to determine whether the winning country is capable of safely hosting the contest.
If it is determined that the winner cannot serve as the host, the EBU will appoint an alternative host broadcaster. The appointed host broadcaster will assume all rights, obligations, and responsibilities related to staging the Contest, including responsibility for organizing, producing, and staging the event. The host broadcaster will organize the Contest in its own name and will not be required to hold the event on behalf of another participating country
It should be noted that in 2022, the Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra won the international song contest "Eurovision 2022" with the song Stefania. The contest was held in Turin, Italy.
The following contest was supposed to take place in Ukraine, but it was relocated to the United Kingdom because of the hostilities.
We remind you
Bulgaria became the winner of the Eurovision Song Contest 2026 for the first time in history; it was represented by DARA with the song Bangaranga. The contest final took place on Saturday evening, while Ukraine’s representative Leleka finished in ninth place.
