Ex-Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, architect of growth, dies of illness at 98
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji has died, according to state media. The impatient, sharp-tongued reformer helped ignite China’s explosive economic boom by forcing wrenching change on state industry in the 1990s and leading the country into the World Trade Organization.
The official Xinhua news agency reported that Zhu died of illness in Beijing at around 11 a.m. on Wednesday. He was 98 years old.
Once sent into rural exile to do manual labor for praising reforms in other communist countries, Zhu pushed through a dizzying array of changes as premier, China’s top economic post, from 1998 to 2003.
Photo: AP
Zhu clashed with Communist Party conservatives and state industry bosses as he pushed state-owned companies to become efficient and profitable. That cost millions of layoffs, but helped propel China to overtake Japan as the second-largest economy behind the United States in 2010.
Building on former leader Deng Xiaoping’s 1979 reforms, Zhu is credited with supplying the resourcefulness and tenacity to push through history-making changes such as China’s WTO membership, which helped to transform China into the world’s biggest exporter.
Those changes helped to keep economic growth above 8% a year from 2000-2010, peaking at 14.2% in 2007.
Named premier in 1998 at age 69, Zhu became a popular figure by criticizing official bungling and graft and accepting blame when the government fell short. His demanding style earned him the nicknames Boss and Zhu Fengzi, or Madman Zhu.
“I have prepared 100 coffins here — 99 for corrupt officials and one for myself,” Zhu said in 1998, according to the party newspaper People’s Daily.
Zhu ranked No. 3 in the party hierarchy behind President Jiang Zemin and Li Peng, chairman of the ceremonial legislature, the National People’s Congress. But he was a technician without his own power base. Zhu complained that allowed officials to ignore his orders.
Zhu made his name as a deputy premier in the 1990s by crushing inflation. He enforced price controls and cut off loans to money-losing state companies, rebuffing resistance by local leaders — a pattern Zhu would repeat as he fought conservatives over the pace of reform.
Zhu led efforts to secure WTO membership following marathon negotiations that began in the 1980s. That status would enshrine free trade as a national commitment, giving Zhu a tool to force local officials to stop protecting favored companies.
Zhu’s campaign was nearly derailed when he went to Washington in 1999 with market-opening concessions to win U.S. endorsement of the WTO bid. The Clinton administration rejected the offer as inadequate while his political enemies at home accused him of offering too much, but Zhu survived and China went on to join the body in December 2001.
Zhu launched China’s home ownership boom in 1998 with an initiative to sell apartments owned by state companies. Families rushed to buy, and within a decade the majority of urban housing was privately owned.
Still, Zhu was less an advocate of free enterprise than a skilled bureaucrat who carried out party orders to whip state industry into shape.
Zhu showed no interest in privatizing the economy. He played a key role in drafting plans in the 1990s to turn banks, airlines, oil companies and other enterprises into profit-oriented corporations but to retain government ownership.
Born Oct. 23, 1928, in Mao Zedong’s home province of Hunan, Zhu paid an early price for his willingness to take risks and speak out.
After a start as an economic planner, his career went into a 22-year eclipse when he was labelled a “rightist” in 1957 for praising reforms in Hungary and Yugoslavia. He was banished to the countryside during the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution to do manual labor.
Rehabilitated in 1979, Zhu rose swiftly, becoming deputy Shanghai party secretary in 1987 and mayor the next year.
As mayor in 1989, Zhu gained a reputation for moderation when he placated protesters and pledged not to call in the military.
“He managed to defuse, with considerable subtlety, a tense political situation that could have developed into localized violence or worse if the military had felt it necessary to intervene,” wrote Australian diplomat Shelley Warner in the 1991 book “The Pro-Democracy Protests in China: Reports from the Provinces.”
Zhu’s boss, Jiang, would soon be called to Beijing by Deng and made party leader. Zhu was named deputy premier in 1991 and joined the party’s ruling Standing Committee in 1993.
Zhu broke with the leadership’s stance of infallibility by admitting and taking blame for official failings.
In 1998, after summer floods killed 4,150 people and officials were accused of embezzling money meant for anti-flood dikes, Zhu complained some barriers were no stronger than bean curd.
Three years later, he apologized on national television for his Cabinet’s failure to protect the public after an explosion in a schoolhouse in southern China killed at least 42 people, most of them children.
Zhu enlivened the party’s bland image by cracking jokes in public, sometimes at his own expense. Laughter erupted at a 1999 news conference when he said a recent photo “made me look like a dead man.”
One of Zhu’s proudest triumphs as deputy premier was to craft a tax system that required local officials to hand more revenue to Beijing. He said in 1996 that he deserved a Nobel Prize in economics for that.
Zhu rarely appeared in public after leaving office as premier.

Rare ‘Mario’ carts found in Wisconsin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

A few years ago, a pop culture store owner in Wisconsin told Jason Ganos, a well-known Nintendo game collector, that he had a box of Super Mario cartridges that had been sitting in storage for years. It stopped Ganos in his tracks.
It turned out to be an ultrarare collection of 97 “absolutely pristine” copies of Super Mario Bros. / Duck Hunt, a popular dual-game cartridge that was released in 1988, Ganos said.
After some initial research, Ganos found that the cartridges he held were not only a new variant of the game, but also the last known production date of it.
Photo: Jason Ganos, Nintendo Wire via AP
Most of the cartridges are to go up for sale tomorrow in an online auction that is to run until Sept. 9.
“I still don’t quite believe that any of this is happening,” Ganos said. “I just think it’s kind of serendipitous that this happened. It’s just still very bizarre to me.”
Ganos, a hardcore fan covered in Nintendo tattoos and who has operated Nintendo Wire, a news service for Nintendo announcements and nostalgia for more than 10 years, said he would not venture to guess how much the games are worth.
“It’s like pulling out like a Holy Grail,” Ganos said, later adding: “They’re gorgeous.”
The discovery came after Kevin Braun, the owner of One Stop Wonders in Waukesha, asked Ganos to help him sell some stuff, including common Nintendo games and Pokemon cards.
Braun mentioned the box of Mario cartridges that had been sitting in storage for years. He recalled buying them from a customer whose family had kept them for metal scraps, but thought they were not worth much.
The cartridges were made in 1993, long after the company discontinued the bundle in 1991. Braun and Ganos still are not sure why the copies were made, but assume they were either warranty replacements or part of a bundle with a box retailer that never panned out.
Knowing the potential significance of the possession, Ganos booked a flight immediately.
“I flew down to California with 97 carts in my carry-on luggage, sweating bullets going through TSA [US Transportation Security Administration], like why do you have 97 little circuit boards in your carry-on?” he said.
He anxiously made it through airport security to meet with video game experts to have the cartridges verified and graded, giving them a perceived value.
There had never been a cartridge rated a perfect 10 at Professional Sports Authenticator, Ganos said.
Five of the 97 Ganos possessed received a perfect score.
“I think there’s going to be historic significance to the tens,” Ganos said when talking about how much the games might sell at the auction. “Like No. 1, it’s so many people’s childhoods, and No. 2, there’s never been a 10 in an NES cart before.”
Ultrarare video game cartridges, especially ones with unique production history, can be sold for six to seven-figure prices in the collector’s market.
Ganos said the 97 carts are also unique because of their perfect condition, which, much like comic books or sports cards, often sell higher.
The cartridges could be worth hundreds, thousands or tens of thousands, he said.
Ganos and Braun are only auctioning off three of the perfect 10 scored cartridges at Golden Pop’s Culture Auction beginning tomorrow. They are both keeping one copy with a score of a 10, and a few others rated in the higher 9’s.
The games can be played if the buyer wants, but because they are pristine, Ganos hopes to keep them that way.
“Finding uncirculated stuff for me is just like super exciting,” Ganos said. “This game was the first video game I’ve ever played. Mario Duck Hunt was just such a big part of my life growing up.”
Braun and Ganos also plan to do a charity auction after they are finished with the current one.

Colombia declares three days mourning for victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

Colombia yesterday declared three days of mourning for victims of an earthquake that demolished buildings in the west of the country, killing more than 200 people.
The magnitude 7.4 quake on Monday was the strongest to hit Colombia in a century.
The government said flags would be lowered to half-staff on official buildings, as well as at Colombian embassies around the world, “in honor of all the dead.”
Photo: Reuters
Frantic attempts to find survivors continued, as authorities revised the death toll down to 216 after local officials in Cali corrected earlier figures.
In Pereira and in Cali, emergency crews used cranes, dogs and heavy machinery to search ruined buildings while volunteers formed human chains to clear debris by hand, hoping to reach people still trapped beneath collapsed structures.
The first two days after an earthquake are crucial for finding survivors under rubble, with some experts saying there is a 72-hour window, after which hopes quickly tail off.
There was joy on Tuesday when rescuers pulled out 32-year-old Daniela Largo.
“We were losing hope and then we received a call,” her mother, Sandra Milena Perez, said in Pereira.
A local resident heard cries for help beneath the rubble and joined neighbors in removing debris before professional rescuers arrived, Perez said.
From the air, neighborhoods in Cali appeared flattened, with piles of gray rubble replacing entire blocks of homes and apartment buildings.
Nearby, cars lay crushed beneath fallen walls and concrete slabs.
The quake overwhelmed parts of the health system, turning the rescue effort into one of Colombia’s largest disaster responses in years.
Many survivors spent the night outdoors, either because their homes were damaged or because they feared aftershocks.
“We lost everything, but we’re alive,” said 23-year-old John Tabasco, who was camped in a park in Pereira with his wife and seven-month-old son.
In Cali, part of the Hospital Universitario del Valle collapsed, forcing patients to be moved into a parking lot.
Thousands brought water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods, while long lines formed outside blood donation centers.
“It’s about wanting to help your community, your city and your country,” blood donor Ferney Cabrera said.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella on Tuesday declared a state of emergency and promised rent subsidies for affected families during a visit to Pereira.
The US announced US$15.5 million in emergency aid, while messages of support and offers of assistance arrived from around the world.

Recall ordered for batch of hypertension drugs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:24 UTC
01:38:24 KST

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) yesterday ordered a recall of a batch of hypertension drug, consisting of 87,360 tablets.
The FDA said it received notification of a defective drug product — Beniel F.C. Tablets 8mg, batch code 2KA31 — manufactured by Synmosa Biopharma Corp. The batch was registered with the Department of Health as Pharmaceutical Manufacture No. 057358.
The drug’s active ingredient is benidipine hydrochloride, a long-acting calcium channel blocker used to treat high blood pressure by relaxing blood vessels to improve blood flow.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
FDA Division of Medicinal Products senior technical specialist Liu Chia-ping (劉佳萍) said that the manufacturer initiated the recall because the tablets did not pass a dissolution test measuring their stability, meaning the quality and effectiveness of the drug might have been compromised.
The manufacturer has been ordered to complete the recall before Aug. 24, as well as submit an investigation report, and a corrective and preventive action report, the FDA said.
Article 91 of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act (藥事法) stipulates that companies that fail to comply with a recall order are to be fined NT$200,000 to NT$5 million (US$6,202 to US$155,058), it said.
Synmosa has two licenses for producing drugs with the same active ingredient, Liu said.
Other batches produced by Synmosa using the ingredient were not affected and the firm has sufficient inventory to ensure there would not be a shortage, she said.
The FDA urged hospitals and pharmacies to comply with the recall, and said people taking the drug should consult their doctor if they want to change their prescription.
Separately, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) on Tuesday said that a misdiagnosis resulted in the erroneous reporting of the first domestic case of typhoid fever this year.
The centers on Thursday last week reported that a woman in her 70s in central Taiwan was hospitalized last month with a persistent fever and diarrhea, and returned home after treatment.
An accredited laboratory at a hospital reported that it had detected Salmonella typhi, the bacteria that causes typhoid fever, in the woman’s blood, the centers said.
However, full-genome sequencing by a CDC laboratory showed that the bacterial strain was actually non-typhoidal salmonella, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said.
The hospital laboratory was ordered to correct its report as stipulated in the Quality Assurance Operational Requirements for Communicable Disease Diagnostic Laboratories and the typhoid case report was officially retracted on Monday, Lin said.
The CDC said it instructed accredited typhoid fever testing laboratories to strictly implement a “dual-person verification” mechanism for positive serum agglutination results and to release results only after confirming that laboratory data is accurate.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:24 UTC
01:38:24 KST

Yesiang Enterprise Co (鈺祥), the nation’s largest supplier of semiconductor chemical filters, yesterday said that revenue in the second half would significantly outgrow the first half, driven by rising demand for filters in advanced 2-nanometer chip plants.
Another key growth driver comes as a major customer begins to adopt the company’s high-end chemical filters at a new chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging plant in Tainan next month and at upcoming packaging facilities, to further improve production yield, Yesiang said.
“The company’s revenue growth started taking off in May, with sales growing more than 100 percent annually,” Yesiang chairman James Chuang (莊士杰) told an earnings conference in Taipei. “Driven by such strong growth momentum, we believe revenue will show significant growth in the second half.”
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
The company is seeing a dramatic spike in buyer urgency and intent, far outpacing the market pace from months prior, Chuang said.
In the first half, revenue jumped 53.2 percent to NT$1.16 billion (US$36 million) from NT$760 million a year earlier, the company said.
Beyond Taiwan, Yesiang also expects to supply chemical filters to a US chipmaking giant for the production of 1.4-nanometer chips, and is in discussion with Chinese memory makers about future orders, the company said.
Yesiang, which specializes in premium chemical filters used in sub-10-nanometer chip plants, is benefiting from strong customer demand for airborne molecular contamination prevention and chemical filters, due to high silicon purity requirements in the manufacturing process for advanced chips.
In addition to regular chemical filters, Yesiang plans to offer recyclable chemical filters later this year to help customers reduce chemical waste and carbon footprints, Chuang said.
The company expects recyclable chemical filters to account for a double-digit percentage of its revenue in December, Chuang said.
In the long term, the company aims to boost recyclable filter revenue share to about 50 percent, he said.
As recyclable filters deliver up to 80 percent in gross margin, Yesiang expects its overall gross margin this year to climb to a record high, surpassing its previous record of 56 percent.
Gross margin dropped to 37.8 percent in the first half of this year, from 42.6 percent in the same period last year, attributable to higher material costs, the company said.
Net profit surged 439.29 percent to NT$151 million in the first half, from NT$28 million a year ago. Earnings per share rose to NT$2.14 from NT$0.4.
Yesiang plans to apply for an initial public offering on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in October in preparation for a listing in the first quarter of next year.

16:38:21 UTC
01:38:21 KST

Nagasaki and Hiroshima suffered the devastation of atomic bombings and each year appeal to the world for peace, but it is puzzling that the two cities have taken starkly different approaches toward Taiwan.
At the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony on Thursday last week, Representative to Japan Lee Yi-yang (李逸洋) was seated alongside diplomats from other countries.
However, at the Nagasaki atomic bombing memorial ceremony three days later, the Nagasaki City Government designated seating for Taiwan’s representative outside the diplomatic delegation area. Lee declined to attend the event, with the head of the Fukuoka Branch of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Osaka, Chen Ming-chun (陳銘俊), attending in his place.
The Nagasaki City Government said that this year’s seating arrangements were the same as last year’s, with some overseas representatives being assigned to the general overseas section because space in the special guest section was limited. It said it had no intention to downgrade Taiwan.
However, the issue is not the seating arrangements, but the status accorded to Taiwan. If Hiroshima can seat Taiwan’s representative alongside diplomats from other countries, why not Nagasaki?
Taiwan and Japan have stood by each other through difficult times for decades. Following the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, Taiwan donated more than US$240 million in aid. Since then, anytime Japan has faced a major disaster, Taiwan has never once stood by idly.
In the past few years, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s investment in Kumamoto has deepened ties between the two nations, moving beyond friendship to economic, trade and strategic cooperation.
The purpose of recalling those ties is not to ask that Japan return the favor — rather, it is about recognizing that what is truly valuable between countries and their citizens is not keeping a tally of favors, but building trust in times of hardship and respecting one another’s dignity.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki inform the world of the suffering caused by atomic bombings, call for an end to war and to pursue peace.
However, peace does not just mean the absence of war — it also entails respect for freedom, democracy and human dignity. If a ceremony dedicated to promoting peace forces Taiwan, which faces threats from an armed hostile external force, to choose between its sovereign dignity and attending the ceremony, does that not run counter to the spirit of peace?
Taiwan is not asking for special treatment. It simply hopes that Nagasaki would grant it the same respect afforded to it by Hiroshima. Taiwan and Japan might not have official diplomatic relations, but they share a friendship that transcends formal diplomatic ties. True friends who have stood by one another through hardship should not allow political considerations to override mutual dignity, and a city that promotes world peace should have the courage to transcend political barriers and treat every friend who seeks peace equally.
If Hiroshima can do it, there is no reason Nagasaki cannot.
Wang Hui-sheng is a founding member of the East Asian Research Institute.

NCCU program weds language and learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:17 UTC
01:38:17 KST

In a classroom at National Chengchi University (NCCU) in Taipei, students answer their lecturer’s questions in Indonesian.
Down the hall, another class engages in a lively debate on Southeast Asian politics, discussing topics ranging from colonial history to gender equality.
Four years ago, that was a world unfamiliar to Ethan Huang (黃逸廷), a Taiwanese graduate of NCCU’s Department of Southeast Asian Languages and Cultures.
Photo: CNA
Curious about foreign cultures and encouraged by his family, who saw growing opportunities in Southeast Asia, Huang chose the relatively new program when applying to NCCU.
“I had almost no understanding of Indonesia,” Huang, who chose the department’s Indonesian track, said during an interview. “Everything about that part of the world was very vague to me.”
Today, the 22-year-old Huang speaks Indonesian confidently, has studied in Indonesia and hopes to build a career there.
His experience illustrates how the program introduces Taiwanese students to a region that has become increasingly important to Taiwan, especially as it continues to diversify its economy away from China.
At the department, students can choose among Indonesian, Thai and Vietnamese tracks while studying that region’s history, politics, society and culture.
Established as a bachelor’s degree program in 2017 and upgraded to a department in 2024, it is one of Taiwan’s few university departments specializing in Southeast Asian languages and regional studies.
For department chair Le Thi-Nham (黎氏仁), a Vietnamese academic who joined NCCU in 2018, language remains at the “center” of the curriculum.
“However, language is not enough,” she said.
Rather than simply producing graduates who can speak a Southeast Asian language, Le said the department aims to give them a broader, interdisciplinary understanding of the region, with many regional studies courses taught in English.
“You need to have a second major,” Le said, citing fields such as diplomacy, law, communications and business offered at NCCU.
By drawing on the university’s wider academic resources, students can combine their language training with professional knowledge and become “more competitive in the job market,” she said.
The department’s broader approach to Southeast Asian studies shapes its language instruction, with advanced courses moving beyond grammar and vocabulary to emphasize cultural context.
Farini Anwar (曾秀情), an Indonesian lecturer at NCCU and host of Radio Taiwan International’s Indonesian-language programming, teaches Indonesian-Chinese translation and interpretation.
She said the department’s third and fourth-year students generally have stronger Indonesian skills than students she has taught elsewhere in Taiwan, allowing her to focus on meaning and cultural nuance.
“The most important thing is culture,” Farini Anwar said. “Students need to learn how to translate between two different cultures so they can convey the real meaning.”
About 50 students graduate from the department each year, Le said.
She described graduates’ career paths as “very diverse,” ranging from public service — including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the National Immigration Agency — to banking, aviation and business across Taiwan and Southeast Asia.
Opportunities are expanding as trade between Taiwan and ASEAN member states grows.
Bilateral trade reached US$181.5 billion last year, up 32.54 percent from a year earlier and up 104 percent from 2019, according to the International Trade Administration.
For Le, however, the department’s role extends beyond supplying talent for a growing regional market.
She described education as “diplomatic soft power,” saying that teaching and research can help Taiwanese better understand Southeast Asian societies while allowing people from the region to learn more about Taiwan.
Taiwan’s ties with Southeast Asia should be viewed not only through economics but through cultural exchange and personal connections, she said.
Students can then carry what they learn beyond campus, sharing it with family and friends and gradually changing how Taiwanese society views a region still sometimes seen through stereotypes, particularly those associated with migrant workers.
For Huang, the social ties Le described grew alongside his command of Indonesian.
By his third year in the program, when his language skills had improved, he was able, for example, to communicate fluently with staff at an Indonesian restaurant in Taiwan.
“That was when I felt my Indonesian had reached the level I wanted,” Huang said.
Greater fluency opened the door to Indonesian community circles in Taiwan, where migrant workers and others shared stories with him about work, family and daily life that most Taiwanese rarely hear.
Those encounters helped Huang look beyond news reports that often portray migrant workers primarily through stories of “hardship.”
A semester-long exchange program at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta and travel across Indonesia exposed him to the country’s religious, linguistic and cultural diversity.
“You can’t look at Indonesia as a single entity,” Huang said. “There are hundreds of ethnic groups, languages and cultures.”
He shares those lesser-known sides of Indonesia with friends, hoping to broaden their understanding of a country he once knew little about himself.
“The language itself may fade if I don’t use it,” he said. “But my understanding of Indonesia will never disappear.”

Luxon secures party backing after challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon yesterday said he had the “full support” of his ruling National Party after surviving a leadership challenge called with less than three months until a general election.
Luxon, who has led New Zealand since 2023, has been unable to reverse his party’s slide in the polls, with a series of gaffes, divisions within his ruling coalition, and rising living costs and unemployment denting his popularity.
He called an emergency meeting on Tuesday after media reported growing speculation that his leadership was no longer tenable.
Photo: AFP
Following hours of closed-door talks with party grandees, Luxon said he had secured their backing.
“There was a confidence vote in my leadership this morning at our caucus meeting, and I have the full support of our caucus,” he told journalists.
“Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election,” he said.
The leadership challenge was brought by New Zealand Minister of Defence Chris Penk, who has since been fired, Luxon said in a statement.
Luxon’s office distributed a statement from Penk, in which the challenger said he would quit parliament altogether.
It was Luxon’s second confidence vote since April, when he made it through a vote after reports National members were displeased with the party polling under 30 percent.
Luxon was flanked by two rumored leadership contenders as he faced journalists — New Zealand Minister for Transport Chris Bishop and Minister of Education and Immigration Erica Stanford.
Stanford had appeared to have growing support to take on the leadership and would not pledge her backing to prime minister, while former tobacco lobbyist Bishop has long been said to have interest in the top job, but on Tuesday told reporters he backed Luxon.
Leaving the caucus meeting, members said they were “united” and “100 percent behind the prime minister,” but, as in April, they would not say if Luxon had unanimous support.
Details of who had prompted the leadership rumblings at first remained a mystery.
Nobody publicly confirmed plans for a leadership bid or expressed intentions to oust their leader, and those whose names were reported speculatively by news outlets denied it.
Several hours after the vote, Luxon named Penk as his challenger and said his now former minister’s position was “untenable.”
Penk, 47, was also the minister for building and construction, and responsible for the security services and space portfolios. A former lawyer who served in Australia’s navy, Penk entered parliament in 2017.
He did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in the statement Luxon’s office attributed to him, Penk said he had “reflected on my political future with my family tonight” and would not seek reelection in November, effectively ending his political career.
“I am proud of the progress I have contributed to as a Minister this term,” Penk’s statement said. “However, I have decided it is the time for me to seek other opportunities to serve New Zealand.”
The statement did not criticize Luxon or reference his leadership bid.
Meanwhile, Luxon’s political opponents lambasted him and his party.
“Backstabbing and infighting just means more delay and more distraction for New Zealand,” said Chris Hipkins, the opposition leader and leader of the Labour Party. “If National can’t govern itself, how can New Zealanders trust it to govern the country?”

Taiwan condemns ‘dangerous’ drill for political manipulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

The Indonesian Navy yesterday said that joint naval exercises that China said took place east of Taiwan were routine and not related to “war fighting,” after Taipei expressed alarm and called them dangerous.
China in June began coast guard patrols off Taiwan’s east coast, causing anger in Taipei and concern in Washington and some other Western capitals.
The drill, which China described as a “navigation exercise,” was the first time the country has carried out such an operation with a foreign military in those waters.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
China’s military said Chinese and Indonesian navy vessels concluded the drill in the waters east of Taiwan yesterday morning.
The exercise included maritime communications, formation maneuvering and replenishment at sea, and demonstrated the two sides’ willingness to cooperate pragmatically and jointly safeguard regional peace, the Chinese military added.
The Indonesian Navy said earlier yesterday that its ship, the I Gusti Ngurah Rai, would conduct “passing exercises” with countries while on its way back from a visit to Russia which were not related to “war fighting.”
These were a “universal naval tradition conducted when transiting through another country’s maritime area,” Indonesian Navy spokesman Tunggul said, without directly mentioning China.
Late on Tuesday, the Mainland Affairs Council said the drill was a “military provocation” and Beijing should “immediately stop this dangerous behavior.”
“This is, in reality, political manipulation, ‘exercises in name, expansion in fact,’ aimed at creating a false impression before the international community that the Chinese communists have jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan,” it added.
A senior Taiwanese security official said that China was characterizing a normal “passex,” or passing exercise, interaction as some kind of joint operation with military significance.
“In fact, navies from various countries do this routinely, and Taiwan is no exception,” added the official, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the matter.
Taking questions at the legislature yesterday, Major General Wu Tien-jen (吳天任), assistant deputy chief of the general staff for intelligence, said the Indonesian warship was on its way home via Japan and not there specifically to take part in the drill.
The ship was 70 to 80 nautical miles (129km to 148km) off Taiwan’s east, in the Pacific, he added.
“Militarily this does not have a direct impact on Taiwan,” he said. “It has a geopolitical significance.”
China’s state-backed Global Times cited military expert Zhang Junshe (張軍社) as saying the move shows the country’s sovereign rights over the waters east of Taiwan.
“Inviting foreign vessels to conduct training in waters under China’s jurisdiction is entirely normal and reasonable,” Zhang added.
Taiwan is holding its annual Han Kuang war games, where it simulates how to beat back an attempted Chinese attack.
China’s announcement came as US Undersecretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby met with Indonesian Minister of Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin at his Jakarta office on Tuesday.
Like most countries, Indonesia has no formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but Taiwan is home to more than 300,000 Indonesian workers.

School health amendments advance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:15 UTC
01:38:15 KST

The Legislative Yuan’s Education and Culture Committee yesterday gave initial approval to amendments to the School Health Act (學校衛生法) requiring the government to assist schools in stocking menstrual products and teaching students about menstruation and mental health.
Education and Culture Committee coconvener Lo Ting-wei (羅廷瑋) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) yesterday said the amendments had passed initial review, with some provisions reserved for cross-caucus negotiation.
Proposals by legislators on the committee to introduce a clear ban on the use of beta-agonists in school meals was reserved for further discussion.
Photo: CNA
At the suggestion of Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Rosalia Wu (吳思瑤), Lo forwarded the agreed provisions of the amendment to the floor.
Under current regulations, schools at the high-school and lower levels must offer health-related courses, including healthy eating education, while institutions at the junior-college level and above may offer such courses as needed.
The amendments would require the government to assist schools in stocking menstrual products to ensure menstrual equity and require schools to include mental health education in health-related courses.
Schools may provide guidance on, manage or restrict items or conduct affecting students’ health according to their age, stage of learning and campus needs, and may establish management guidelines, the amendments say.
They would also add hearing impairment to the existing list of conditions for which schools must strengthen prevention and treatment, including poor vision, dental cavities, hepatitis, scoliosis and parasitic infections.
The amendments would also ban e-cigarettes and new tobacco products on campuses and add tobacco-like and nicotine products to the list of products schools may not sell.

Burmese army escalates raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

The Burmese military has increasingly used low-cost aircraft such as motorized paragliders and gyrocopters in escalating aerial attacks that kill civilians in its conflict with armed, anti-government groups, a UN investigation said in a report released on Tuesday.
Separately, a major ethnic armed group fighting the government in Rakhine state said that 20 civilians had been killed in strikes by the military so far this month.
The Burmese government did not immediately respond to the UN probe or the allegations by the Arakan Army. In the past, the military has said it only attacks legitimate targets of war, accusing the resistance forces of being terrorists.
Photo: AFP
The report by the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IMM) details a year-long investigation into alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the Burmese military and affiliated militias, as well as the opposition armed groups.
It found that abuses escalated around the country’s army-organized elections in December last year and January.
The IIMM said it observed a notable escalation in aerial attacks in the months preceding the elections and that they have continued unabated afterward, with investigators also documenting a pattern of deliberate arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence.
Civilian casualties are worsened by the military’s increasing use of “double-tap” aerial attacks, in which a second strike follows the first, apparently targeting first responders, people helping the wounded and those trying to flee, the IIMM said.
The Burmese military was increasingly using motorized paragliders — also known as paramotors — as well as gyrocopters and drones to carry out low-altitude airstrikes with unguided explosives, the report said.
In incidents in the upper Sagaing region, paramotor pilots allegedly cut their engines as they approached targets, allowing them to glide silently and leaving civilians little or no warning to flee or seek shelter, it said.
The report came as the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group fighting the army in Rakhine, said that about 20 civilians were killed and 22 injured in airstrikes across three townships from Aug. 1 to Tuesday, including one attack involving up to eight aircraft that lasted about an hour.

North Korea yesterday fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off the Korean Peninsula’s east coast, South Korean and Japanese authorities said, days ahead of major joint military exercises by Seoul and Washington long denounced by Pyongyang, and a day after the US and 40 other countries warned of the dangers of ballistic missile testing without advance notice, in a joint statement issued a month after China launched a nuclear-capable missile in the Pacific.
The missile was launched from the North’s Wonsan area at about 6am, the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said, six days after North Korea fired another ballistic missile from the same area.
The launch came ahead of South Korean and US military drills, dubbed Ulchi Freedom Shield, set to run from Monday next week to Aug. 27, aimed at countering Pyongyang’s evolving nuclear and weapons capabilities.
Photo: EPA
Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification in Seoul, said the launch was likely part of North Korea’s existing weapons development schedule, but the timing could also have been selected to send a message ahead of the exercises.
“Even if it was a test of a weapon under development, choosing when to conduct it requires a political decision,” Hong said.
There was no immediate statement from North Korea on the Wonsan launch, but Pyongyang yesterday afternoon criticized the nuclear ambitions of South Korea and Japan.
South Korea said North Korea also fired a ballistic missile from Wonsan on Thursday last week, but Pyongyang did not report that launch in state media.
That test might have failed to achieve its intended objective, Hong said.
In Taipei, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it welcomed the US and 40 other countries’ shared call for transparent, routine missile-launch notification mechanisms to reduce miscalculation and unintended escalation.
“Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests,” the joint statement issued on Tuesday by countries from Europe and the Indo-Pacific region said.
“It increases the risk of miscalculation, undermines global stability and security, and is incompatible with the responsibilities that come with possessing long-range missile capabilities,” the countries said.
The statement called on all countries to provide at least 24 hours’ notice of launches, including the class of missile being launched as well as the planned launch window, area and direction.
Beijing gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing an intercontinental ballistic missile on July 6, flexing its military might in a region where it has long sought to expand its reach.
The rocket appeared to land in a patch of ocean somewhere between the Solomon Islands, Nauru and Tuvalu, monitors have said.
Taiwan condemned the launch and China’s failure to provide sufficient and appropriate advance notification, calling the move irresponsible and destabilizing.
China’s accelerating military expansion, coercion, “gray zone” activities and military intimidation threaten Taiwan and pose serious challenges to peace and stability across the Indo-Pacific region, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Taiwan will continue working closely with the US and like-minded partners to safeguard regional peace, stability and prosperity, it added.

Japan’s 2026 defense white paper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:11 UTC
01:38:11 KST

The Japan Defense White Paper provides important clarity on the direction of Japanese defense policy. It captures a transition under way as Japan revises its three 2022 strategic documents, having reached the planned defense expenditure of 2 percent of GDP while confronting a rapidly deteriorating security environment in the Indo-Pacific region.
The paper is no longer simply an annual stocktaking of Japan’s defense efforts. It points toward a new concept of national security. Japan now sees defense capacity as extending beyond the size and modernization of the Japan Self-Defense Forces, bringing together foreign policy, intelligence, economic, technological and industrial capabilities into a “comprehensive architecture for national defense.”
That represents significant progress from the earlier emphasis on territorial defense under the protection of the Japan-US alliance.
Military capability remains central. China is identified as the core strategic challenger, while North Korea and Russia are increasingly seen as interconnected problems because of their growing military cooperation.
However, Japan is reconsidering the basis on which military power should be built.
The paper’s emphasis on “new ways of warfare” reflects lessons from Ukraine and conflicts in West Asia. The growing use of relatively inexpensive uncrewed systems, together with rapid advances in artificial intelligence, cyber, space and electromagnetic warfare, is changing the character of conflict. Japan recognizes that expensive conventional platforms might have short technological lifecycles and be insufficient in a prolonged, rapidly evolving conflict.
The paper gives greater importance to cost-effective uncrewed systems, including aerial, surface and underwater craft, alongside the SHIELD architecture for littoral defense. The Japan Air Self-Defense Force is also being reconfigured into the Japan Aerospace Self-Defense Force with wider responsibilities, including cyberspace. The underlying shift is from platform superiority to technological adaptability, to the ability to innovate, replace systems quickly, replenish ammunition and modify capabilities after battlefield experience.
That brings Japan’s defense industrial base to the center of the strategy. Defense production and technological capabilities are no longer peripheral chapters, but integral elements of defense capability. Japan must be able to replenish ammunition and equipment and maintain platforms during a prolonged conflict.
This is particularly significant because Japan’s defense industry has been relatively limited since World War II, as companies withdrew from defense production and Japan relied heavily on the US’ security umbrella. Tokyo is seeking to make defense production economically sustainable rather than dependent solely on the restricted procurement requirements of the Self-Defense Forces.
The most important conceptual change is the incorporation of economic security into defense policy. Economic security is increasingly linked to resilient supply chains, the development and protection of advanced technologies, and the ability to sustain defense production and technological capabilities. Japan seeks greater autonomy, but through selective resilience rather than self-sufficiency or separation from the US-led alliance.
Japan wants to ensure that its technologies, industrial capacity and supply chains remain available during a crisis. At the same time, it wants to remain a dependable alliance partner. Defense spending is increasingly viewed not simply as a response to a deteriorating security environment, but also as an instrument of industrial policy. Larger procurement can sustain companies, create employment, improve regional economies and generate technological spillovers into civilian sectors.
The white paper also gives greater attention to start-ups and dual-use technologies, seeking to connect the defense establishment with academia, researchers, venture capital and civilian innovators.
Moreover, defense exports have acquired greater significance. Simplifying export restrictions can create economies of scale, sustain production lines, and build maintenance and support partnerships with other countries.
None of that represents a retreat from the US alliance. The paper regards the alliance as the cornerstone of Japanese security. Yet a subtle shift is visible. Japan is developing greater domestic capabilities to reduce the risks of excessive dependence on any single partner. Larger stockpiles, better domestic production, improved technological capabilities, and cooperation with the UK, Italy and the Philippines, as well as fellow Quad countries — India, Australia and the US — are creating a more diversified security architecture.
This is not strategic autonomy in the traditional sense, nor preparation for a rupture with the US. Rather, Japan is seeking to make the alliance more effective by increasing its own ability to contribute. Japan could evolve from being primarily a provider of bases and financial support to being a provider of technology, defense production and operational capabilities to a wider network of partners in the Indo-Pacific region.
The real significance of the white paper is that it moves beyond the defense reinforcement and implementation themes of the past few years. It begins to articulate a broader conception of national power, integrating economic security, industrial capacity, dual-use innovation, supply-chain resilience and defense exports with military strength.
The importance of the approach will be clearer when Japan’s revised National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program are released. The white paper nevertheless suggests that Japan is moving toward a model in which military strength, economic resilience, technological superiority and industrial capacity are increasingly inseparable.
Gurjit Singh is a former Indian ambassador to Germany, Indonesia, ASEAN, Ethiopia and the African Union. He is the author of The Durian Flavour: India and ASEAN After a Decade of the Act East Policy.

Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday said that net profit for the second quarter grew 35 percent year-on-year to NT$59.98 billion (US$1.86 billion), a record for a single quarter and beating the NT$58 billion average analyst estimate.
Earnings per share rose to a record NT$4.27 from NT$3.19 a year earlier, Hon Hai chief financial officer David Huang (黃德財) told an online earnings conference.
Gross margin fell to 6.12 percent from 6.33 percent due to changes in product mix, but operating margin improved to 3.75 percent from 3.16 percent due to better expense control, Huang said, adding that the figure is expected to stay above 3.2 percent for the full year.
Photo: Screen grab from the Internet
Last quarter’s strong performance was mainly driven by continued artificial intelligence (AI) server spending by major US cloud service providers, whose capital expenditure is expected to exceed US$1 trillion next year, Hon Hai rotating chief executive officer Michael Chiang (蔣集恆) said.
“AI server revenue contributions are expected to continue next year,” Chiang said.
Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn Technology Group (富士康科技集團), is Apple Inc’s primary iPhone assembler and makes servers powered by Nvidia Corp’s AI accelerators.
The company expects AI server rack shipments to grow by a high double-digit percentage sequentially this quarter, with AI server revenue also rising quarter-on-quarter, Chiang said.
For the full year, Hon Hai forecasts AI server rack shipments to more than double from last year, he said.
The company aims to begin shipments of AI server racks based on Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform next quarter and expects them to become a major AI server product next year, Chiang said.
Hon Hai aims to capture a 50 percent share of the Vera Rubin-based AI server market next year, he said.
The company is also positive about its general-purpose server business and is looking to achieve double-digit annual growth this year, Chiang said.
Hon Hai has secured new customers for the application-specific integrated circuit-based AI servers, he said.
This quarter, the company expects strong growth in its cloud and networking products business, on the back of continued ramp-up of AI server racks, Chiang said.
Revenue from smart consumer electronics is expected to grow significantly this quarter on peak-season smartphone demand, while computing product revenue is expected to decline slightly due to memory supply constraints, he said.
Revenue from components and other products is expected to stay flat, he added.
Last quarter, cloud and networking products accounted for 51 percent of Hon Hai’s NT$2.53 trillion revenue, followed by smartphones at 29 percent, computing products at 15 percent and others at 5 percent, the company said.
Capital expenditure totaled NT$80.9 billion in the first half, up NT$3.7 billion from a year earlier, and is expected to continue rising as Hon Hai expands capacity in Taiwan, the US, Mexico and Vietnam, Huang said.
The company spent NT$173.8 billion last year.

At least 15 people were killed and 27 remain missing when an overcrowed ferry on Lake Kariba capsized, authorities yesterday. Han Kuang focuses on battlefield responsiveness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:07 UTC
01:38:07 KST

The Han Kuang Exercise yesterday tested the ability of units to repair damaged vehicles, redeploy forces and adapt to changing battlefield conditions without waiting for orders as the annual drills entered their final day.
Army Logistics Command’s First Theater Support Center established forward repair sites at civilian workshops in Penghu, allowing damaged but mobile combat vehicles to be quickly repaired and returned to service.
More severely damaged vehicles were towed to the sites by M936A2 trucks for field repairs, in a demonstration of how military and civilian repair capabilities could be combined to sustain theater logistics during wartime.
Photo: CNA
First Theater commander Lieutenant General Liu Wei-hsin (劉暐欣) said the battlefield would not conform to military plans and that commanders at every level must be prepared to adjust as circumstances change.
The military is requiring battalion-level units to use the “Rapid Decisionmaking and Synchronization Process,” helping commanders to respond rapidly and independently to shifting developments on the battlefield.
In one scenario, an infantry battalion commander responsible for defending an inland area ordered wounded personnel evacuated to the rear after the unit came under long-range enemy fire, without waiting for orders from higher command.
An artillery battalion commander in another scenario dispatched drones to reconnoiter an important beachhead and ensure that enemy forces had not infiltrated the area.
An infantry battalion defending the southern flank of a designated “red beach” used psychological operations to force an invading force toward prepositioned Taiwanese firing positions.
Armored forces were redeployed to Pingtung, where they immediately established camouflaged defensive positions, demonstrating the ability of units to respond to unforeseen developments.
Liu said the exercises were designed to ensure that units could continue operating if communications were disrupted or the chain of command became unresponsive.
He said he had ordered commanders to use the Android Tactical Assault Kit to establish a common operating picture, allowing them to adjust plans while maintaining awareness of available resources and intelligence on enemy movements.
The Ministry of National Defense ordered a Patriot missile company to redeploy from the Fourth Theater to the Second Theater to defend Chia Shan Air Force Base in Hualien, a key air base.
The redeployment demonstrated the mobility of PAC-3 units and reflected adjustments to defense deployments in response to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s growing ability to project air power, including carrier-based fighter groups and long-range aircraft, the ministry said.
In Matsu (Lienchiang County), Matsu Defense Command simulated an enemy landing under aerial cover. Drones were used to identify enemy staging areas before Taiwanese forces engaged approaching vessels.
Shoreline units used 40mm automatic grenade launchers and T74 medium machine guns against simulated landing forces, while drones were used to attack landing craft.
Armored units in the Fifth Theater practiced a cross-theater redeployment, moving M60A3 tanks, armored fighting vehicles and M109A2 howitzers with the assistance of civilian vehicles.
Separately, the Army’s Eighth Army said it would conduct a rocket artillery exercise late next month involving the Thunderbolt-2000 (LT-2000) system.
Military sources said the exercise was particularly important following a 2022 accident, in which an MK45 rocket failed to eject from its pod and exploded on the rack, destroying the launch vehicle.
The LT-2000 is expected to play an important role in defending southern Taiwan against an amphibious assault, the sources said.
With deliveries of the US-made M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) underway, the military has multiple long-range strike options, with HIMARS able to hit targets from about 70km to 300km and the LT-2000 providing fire support from about 45km to the beachhead.

Social Darwinists to tech bros: tracing the long fight against equality in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

The historian Kim Phillips-Fein’s new book is published amid celebrations of the 250th anniversary of the declaration of independence and its truth “self-evident, that all men are created equal.” Country of Lords, however, is a history of Neo-Aristocrats, Social Darwinists, Tech Utopians and the Long Fight Against Equality in America.
Concise and hard-hitting, the book arrives at a time of glaring social and economic inequality, Phillips-Fein seeing Elon Musk “emerging as a trillionaire very much on people’s minds, with a deep level of discomfort, both fear and anger about what this portends.”
“It’s always hard to know what’s going to be happening when you have written a book,” she said. “But I think those questions about economic equality and the impact of extreme levels of economic hierarchy and concentration, and the questions, ‘Can you still have a democracy any longer? What are the ways that you can counter that? What alternate visions are there if you want to live in a world that’s not characterized that way?’, are present.”
Photo: AP
RIGHTS FOR THE POOR
Phillips-Fein studies conservatism and “questions about capitalism and democracy.” Her first book, Invisible Hands, was a study of businessmen who fought the New Deal of the 1930s. Her second, Fear City, about the New York economic crisis of the 1970s, was a finalist for the Pulitzer prize. Hers is a major voice. It’s also unique. Not many books start with founder John Adams and end with Peter Thiel of Palantir, Musk’s fellow techno-fascist. Might such company seem unfair on Adams, the Boston lawyer who was part of a great revolution but feared what was unleashed?
“I hope this comes through,” Phillips-Fein said. “Adams is very different from [steel magnate] Andrew Carnegie and [Yale professor] William Graham Sumner and the late 19th-century social Darwinists, and the pro-slavery advocates. He’s also definitely very different from people who are saying extreme levels of economic inequality are good.” Adams, however, was “very ambivalent and skeptical of egalitarian claims … during and after the French Revolution: a deep sense of you can have too much egalitarianism.”
Photo: AFP
“In his writing, he does also give a strong kind of conservative temperament and foundational sense of the problems of arguing for greater equality and a deep wariness and sense of pessimism about a politics that claims to do that.”
And so Adams takes his place in Country of Lords. Other subjects include preachers of race-based inequality from George Fitzhugh, a Confederate theorist of slavery as natural good, to Theodore Lothrop Stoddard, a hack journalist who had a huge bestseller in 1920 with The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy, “part of a larger intellectual subculture of ‘scientific’ racism … in the aftermath of world war one.”
There is also Carnegie, the Scottish-born tycoon who flourished in the Gilded Age of the late 19th century.
“What makes Carnegie so interesting is that he at least allows himself to have some sense of ambivalence,” Phillips-Fein said. “He says that while the concentration of wealth is absolutely necessary and inevitable, and the people at the top … should have the ultimate say over resources, he is deeply aware that this is politically dangerous, that … it creates an unstable society in which the poor and the working class might actually hate the wealthy, and that’s not in the interest of the wealthy in the long run. Also, he has a sense that human brotherhood is lost, or some kind of community that had existed.”
Carnegie’s father was a Chartist, seeking working-class rights. Carnegie’s major outlet for doubts about his wealth came through philanthropy, prominently the construction of libraries for working people.
“He had a very deep sense of paternalism,” Phillips-Fein said. “He was very invested in the idea of business as a romance and kind of a space of adventure and conquest and feudal benevolence. I think Carnegie’s answer was ultimately that the wealthy should have their money but they shouldn’t bequeath much to their descendants, they should invest it in massive philanthropic projects, and this was better than raising wages or other things like that … It is his level of guilt and ambivalence that I think does make him appealing, if also troubling. I think it raises a set of questions that he certainly was never really able to resolve.”
The 1892 Carnegie Steel strike and its violent suppression devastated Homestead, Pennsylvania, and left Carnegie disillusioned. Now, in Washington, Carnegie Science is the Qatari embassy. At Mount Vernon, the Carnegie library hosts an Apple Store.
INEQUALITY
Country of Lords is also a primer on modern inequality. In the early 1900s, Henry Ford mixed mass auto production with vicious racism. In mid-century, William Shockley was a proto-tech mogul “who went completely off the rails.”
“He was a co-inventor of the transistor and he figures in different histories of Silicon Valley because he ran this company and wanted to maintain a tremendous amount of control, and as a result a bunch of the employees quit and founded their own firm [two eventually founding Intel] … So after Shockley Labs fell apart, Shockley started to become drawn to racist science, pseudoscience and IQ testing in particular. I don’t think anybody really knows exactly what triggered this, but he starts to talk a lot about it publicly in the mid-60s. He was at Stanford at the time. He was supposed to be teaching physics and engineering.”
Shockley, Phillips-Fein says, was really “a uniquely horrible person, and probably quite unhappy as well.”
If that sounds familiar, also like Musk, Shockley wasn’t unique. Linked to the meritocratic movement of the mid-century, he was “not isolated. He is actually part of what is a growing, troubling community of people who coalesce in the late 60s, early 70s, and who are really responding, not always directly, to the context of the civil rights movement.
“It was obviously focused on overturning racist legislation that undergirded segregation, but it also made claims about the distribution of resources, saying the reasons for Black poverty are not innate, they reflect centuries of legal and political structures that have upheld white wealth and laid the foundation for exploitation of Black workers and working-class people, and the political disfranchisement has resulted in this distribution of resources. In other words, that’s nothing to do with merit at all.”
In such soil, Phillips-Fein finds the roots of “the tech titans of today,” rejecting liberal ideals.
“They are very skeptical and hostile towards elite institutions, or at least, have a very broad relationship to them,” she said. “So Peter Thiel embraces this set of ideas about competition drawn from the economist Joseph Schumpeter. He writes about how companies in a normal marketplace are competing at the margins … but every so often someone will come along and create a new invention, usually that winds up dominating the marketplace and changing it, and whoever does that first will completely change the marketplace.
“Thiel has the same idea. He kind of writes about how, ‘I was growing up, I wanted to be the best, I wanted to go to these elite institutions. I went to law school, I had the straight and narrow path, but then I realized that all that was wrong, and actually you had to disrupt everything, create your own monopoly, a monopoly of one: nobody else can ever be you,’ and then the people who are kind of blessed with this genius to recognize how to create something completely new in the world, those are the people who will deserve to win in this race and deserve to command the resources of society.”
The Country of Lords endures.

What disease is forcing Russian officials to slaughter pigs in the Tyumen region? They won’t say, except to describe it as ‘very dangerous.’
In Russia’s Tyumen region, authorities in several villages of the Golyshmanovsky district have begun seizing pigs from farmers and killing the animals, citing an unidentified disease.
Village administrations and regional authorities have not identified the disease behind the seizures, according to the local news outlet 72.ru. Residents believe it may be African swine fever, though this has not been confirmed. Officials have described it only as a “very dangerous disease.”
Officials said the only way to stop the disease from spreading is through strict quarantine measures, including destroying entire herds at outbreak sites and conducting thorough disinfection. A disinfection checkpoint was set up August 7 at the entrance to the Golyshmanovsky district, local residents said, where vehicles are treated with a special solution to help contain the outbreak. Residents are barred from taking pig meat out of their villages for the duration of the quarantine.
Authorities have not disclosed how much compensation residents will receive for their seized livestock, local residents said. For many residents, livestock is a source of both food and income since — as they put it — “there isn’t much work in their area.”
“They took 22 head from me,” farmer Vladimir Buzin said. “They gave them shots, loaded them up, and took them away. I live off these pigs, and now they’ve taken them. The authorities don’t say exactly how much they’ll pay for them. Apparently, the compensation is supposed to be the market price for adult pigs, about 3,000 rubles per piglet. As for the market price — that’s completely unclear. If I get, say, 30,000 rubles, what good would that money do me? Right now I don’t even have money for hay for the cow or diesel fuel, can you imagine that?”
District officials held a meeting in Golyshmanovo, the district center, on August 10 to discuss the pig seizures. They said the measures were tied to a disease that is fatal to pigs but poses no threat to humans. District representatives did not specify a compensation amount, saying only that “the compensation is quite decent and provided for by law.”

The death toll from a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia has risen to 239, according to a damage assessment released Wednesday by the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).
The quake, centered in the area of San Jose del Palmar, affected 14 departments and 403 municipalities, said the assessment.
At least 3,755 people were injured, while 287 remain missing. The disaster has affected 24,324 families, or 49,214 people, according to the latest figures.
The tremor caused extensive damage to homes and public infrastructure. A total of 9,215 homes were destroyed, while 45,457 were damaged.
The government has declared a national disaster situation to strengthen the mobilization and coordination of institutional capacities to address the emergency.
The quake occurred at 7.34 am local time (1234GMT) Monday, with the epicenter located approximately 5 kilometers (3.1 miles) east of the town of San Jose del Palmar, according to data from the US Geological Survey. The agency reported that the quake originated at a depth of 107 kilometers.
A magnitude 5.0 aftershock struck at 8.18 am (1318GMT), approximately 16 kilometers west of San Jose del Palmar. The municipality, located in the Choco Department, has a population of around 4,800 and sits 1,288 meters (4,225 feet) above sea level.
The quake has triggered an emergency response across affected areas, with international assistance also offered to Colombia.

The National Hurricane Center in Miami said that no watches or warnings were in effect for coastal areas, and the storm is expected to dissipate Thursday.

“They laid down their weapons, raised their hands”: Russia has executed at least 345 surrendered Ukrainian soldiers on the ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:34:12 UTC
01:34:12 KST

Russian forces have executed at least 345 Ukrainian soldiers who surrendered since the start of the full-scale war, Ukrainian Ombudsperson Dmytro Lubinets said at a press conference at Ukrinform.
The figure is the latest point on a documented and rising curve of a systematic war crime. Ukraine's prosecutors and international monitors have tracked these killings from 268 confirmed by July 2025 to over 330 by March 2026. Financial Times investigation found the executions appear to be systematic military policy directed from Russian command, with intercepted orders to "shoot prisoners on the spot."
The victims had surrendered
Lubinets described people killed after they had given up.
"It means that they laid down their weapons, came out with raised hands, lay on the ground, and showed they were no longer fighting," he said, and Russian soldiers examined them and confirmed they were unarmed.
Then the soldiers killed them.
"We have recorded cases where they fully demand that the clothes be removed. And after that, they force them to lie on the ground the same way, and shoot the Ukrainian soldiers at point-blank range," Lubinets added.
Killing a surrendered soldier is a war crime
Lubinets stressed the legal character of the act. The killing of soldiers who have surrendered is a distinct war crime, he said.
The prohibition is absolute. Under the Geneva Conventions, a soldier who lays down arms and surrenders is protected, and killing a prisoner of war is a grave breach of international law. Common Article 3 of the Third Geneva Convention prohibits "violence to life and person, in particular murder of all kinds" against those who have laid down their arms, with no battlefield circumstance that permits it, per the ICRC.
The count keeps rising and accountability lags
Ukraine documents each case for eventual prosecution, but most perpetrators are in Russia, beyond reach, and Russian courts and media have glorified the killings rather than punished them.

Exclusive: Iraq's PMF to undergo major leadership changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:33:29 UTC
01:33:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Major changes expected within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces
Major changes are expected within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), influential sources within the group told The New Arab, including the replacement of its chairman, Faleh al-Fayyad, who was formally appointed in 2020, and chief of staff Abdul Aziz al-Mohammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
Mohammadawi emerged publicly and assumed his post after his predecessor, Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was assassinated in a US airstrike in January 2020.
The sources told The New Arab on Wednesday that other changes are also expected, representing the first steps towards further integrating the PMF into Iraq's regular security and military system.
The changes come amid US pressure on Baghdad to regulate the PMF's status and restrict the weapons of Iran-aligned factions incorporated into and funded by the PMF itself.
The sources told The New Arab that "the committee for restricting weapons to state control, which was formed in March, has finally reached several measures concerning the Popular Mobilisation Forces, including changing the PMF uniform and providing it with new clothing, insignia and ranks, under the heading of replacing its visual identity, so that it is closer to the visual identity of the Iraqi army and the rest of the security branches, and preventing the use of religious and sectarian propaganda during tours and security and military operations when the PMF carries them out".
They also spoke of "organising the status of older personnel, as the issue of retirement from the PMF remains complicated and confusing because this matter has not been regulated through clear legal procedures".
The sources added that "the latest directives call for the inclusion of army officers with senior ranks in the PMF ranks to restructure security duties, the deployment map and disciplined compliance with military orders".
"The directives also included redistributing fighters among brigades and provinces after an electronic database was restructured and made subject to military procedures, with no mediation from brigade commanders or factions incorporated into the Popular Mobilisation Forces as part of eliminating intermediary directives and establishing the final relationship of affiliation with the armed forces' leadership, rather than with the leaders and formations that emerged with the establishment of the PMF and which exploited the PMF for political and electoral purposes."
According to political sources who spoke to The New Arab, "Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, backed by Shia political movements and parties, is seeking to implement these measures after removing Faleh al-Fayyad, who is clinging to the post and unwilling to leave it, despite political efforts on more than one occasion to remove him".
The sources also referred to accusations made by political forces that Fayyad exploited PMF brigades and formed new brigades to support his electoral list and his party, the Ata Movement.
They noted that "the Asaib Ahl al-Haq group, which surrendered its weapons and announced its separation from the Popular Mobilisation Forces and its decision to focus solely on political activity, has renewed its demand for the position of chairman of the Popular Mobilisation Forces and for Fayyad to be removed".
They added that despite the persistent efforts and numerous media campaigns waged by Asaib against Fayyad, Zaidi's view is to replace Fayyad with a military commander from within the "Popular Mobilisation Forces" who believes in the Iraqi state.
Three candidates for the post are not affiliated with a political party or entity.
Regarding Abu Fadak, commander of the PMF's staff, the sources said that "he is among the security changes proposed by the Zaidi government, which are in line with changing plans and bringing in new blood".
"But the real reason behind his replacement is to comply with the US desire not to allow those it has sanctioned over allegations of corruption and terrorism to remain in positions in the Iraqi state," they said.
They expected that "the position of chief of staff of the Popular Mobilisation Forces may pose a difficult situation in the coming period because the post is considered the second most important position within the PMF, in addition to being of great benefit to the factions, particularly Hezbollah Brigades, which is close to Abu Fadak".
Over the past weeks, the Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement, led by Qais al-Khazali, has resumed discussing failures within the PMF as part of a campaign against Faleh al-Fayyad and efforts to push for his dismissal.
The campaign intensified after Saudi-US airstrikes targeted PMF headquarters in more than one Iraqi province at the end of July, killing and wounding about 60 PMF members.
This was followed by leaks claiming that "Zaidi had informed Fayyad to evacuate the headquarters before the bombing, after receiving information about the planned strikes, but Fayyad did not take any precautions to prevent the PMF fighters from being killed".
Asaib Ahl al-Haq used this issue as part of its campaign to remove Fayyad from his post.
Sheikhani: Fayyad should be questioned after PMF headquarters bombed
Commenting on the issue, Hussein al-Sheikhani, a member of the political bureau of the Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement, said Zaidi "had informed the leaders of the Coordination Framework of the details of the strike during a meeting attended by Fayyad, but an unclear matter that we do not know about prevented the latter from taking measures to protect the Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters".
He told The New Arab that "Parliament is required to question Fayyad after the incident in which PMF headquarters were bombed by Saudi Arabia and then move towards dismissing or holding those responsible accountable according to the results of the questioning and the official investigation".
First Deputy Speaker of Parliament Adnan Faihan, a leader in Asaib, had previously called for a committee to investigate whether the government had prior knowledge of the timing of the Saudi-US targeting and failed to take the necessary measures.
The committee was expected to submit its report within a week. However, the results have not yet emerged.
The restructuring of the leadership of the PMF appears to have already begun, particularly after the Interior Ministry announced the closure of 71 headquarters described as "fake" and claiming affiliation with the PMF.
This prompted the PMF to issue a clarification confirming that those headquarters had no connection to it.
This indicates the emergence of a dispute between the prime minister and PMF chairman Faleh al-Fayyad.
In a statement, the PMF said that "the measures to close and monitor those headquarters were carried out by the General Directorate of Security and Discipline at the Popular Mobilisation Forces as part of the work of the Permanent Committee for Restricting Weapons".
The Interior Ministry's statement did not mention the specific body that carried out the closure of the fake headquarters.
Security and political affairs researcher Abdullah al-Rakabi said that "the security changes Zaidi made in the security agencies over the past weeks excluded the Popular Mobilisation Forces, given the sensitivity of the organisation".
"But the coming period may witness major changes within the PMF institution, particularly the position of chairman, as there are political parties that have objected to Fayyad's presence in his post for about 10 years," he said.
"His dismissal may also not cause political problems and is not difficult because Fayyad does not have political backing. It appears that the same applies to PMF chief of staff Abu Fadak."
Speaking to The New Arab, he said that "there are many political disputes over Fayyad. As for Abu Fadak, he is rejected by the US, and the two may be replaced before Sept. 30 as part of the US-Iraqi agreement to end the factions' weapons and the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq".
 
How were the Popular Mobilisation Forces established?
The Popular Mobilisation Forces are an umbrella organisation bringing together more than 70 armed formations and factions in Iraq.
The roots of its establishment date back to June 2014, when the Iraqi government decided to organise volunteers to repel Islamic State's invasion of Mosul and its surrounding areas.
This came before religious authority Ali al-Sistani issued a fatwa calling for "defensive jihad", urging those capable of carrying weapons to volunteer in the security forces.
This prompted thousands to join the armed formations later known as the "Popular Mobilisation Forces", which also included factions that were already active.
In February 2016, the Popular Mobilisation Forces were reorganised under a cabinet order.
In November of the same year, the Iraqi parliament passed the Popular Mobilisation Forces Law No. 40, which made it part of the armed forces and placed it under the authority of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
The move came amid objections and a boycott by lawmakers from Sunni political forces.

In central Gaza, Israeli military vehicles and drones opened heavy fire toward homes east of the Bureij refugee camp, according to Palestinian sources.
In the central Gaza Strip, two Palestinians were wounded by Israeli army fire east of the al-Bureij refugee camp while they were on Salah al-Din Street, according to a medical source.
Israeli military vehicles and drones also fired heavily toward civilian homes east of al-Bureij camp.
The developments came days after Palestinian sources told Anadolu that Israeli airstrikes and targeted killings in Gaza had declined, although Israel has continued to violate the ceasefire agreement.
The latest incidents also came despite Israeli media reports that Israel was implementing on the ground a 15-point plan approved by the Board of Peace and accepted by Hamas. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, on Sunday rejected the plan.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire have killed 1,259 Palestinians and wounded 4,148 others, according to Health Ministry figures released Wednesday.
The ceasefire agreement was reached to halt Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which began Oct. 8, 2023, and has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded more than 174,000 others, most of them women and children, according to Palestinian authorities.
The war has also caused widespread destruction across the enclave, damaging about 90% of the civilian infrastructure, with the UN estimating reconstruction costs at about $70 billion.

IDF strikes Gaza for second straight day as US gives Netanyahu ‘room’ ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
