How to Tell If You’re Trauma Dumping or Just Venting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:07:59 UTC
01:07:59 KST

You won’t find the term “trauma dumping” in a psychology textbook, but it’s gained popularity online to describe the act of unloading overwhelming feelings onto someone else without their consent. It’s like an extended, one-sided version of venting, says Cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety and trauma therapist in Los Angeles.
It’s also treated as one of the worst social sins you can commit—which can make people afraid to talk about their grief, trauma, or anything else too painful to package neatly. Yet social support is one way people cope with hard experiences. Conversations about tough topics don’t have to be concise, comfortable, or perfectly balanced to be healthy.
“It’s not about not talking about problems,” says Stephanie Mahalec, a therapist in Los Angeles. “Talking about problems is a very important part of relationships. It’s just how you talk about it.”
Here’s how to tell when trauma dumping might be reaching unhealthy levels in a friendship or relationship, according to therapists—and how to repair.
There’s no room for the other person to set a boundary
Asking whether someone has time to listen is considerate. It can be as simple as: “Do you have a minute? Can I vent about something?”
Dr. Hans Watson, a psychiatrist in South Jordan, Utah, recommends taking into account the time, place, and audience. Is this a workable moment? Is this an appropriate setting? Is this someone you ordinarily talk to about personal things?
With some relationships, that understanding is already in place. If you and a close friend routinely call each other when life falls apart, you probably don’t need to renegotiate the terms every time. And if you forget to ask permission during an especially painful moment, that alone does not make the conversation a trauma dump. “One conversation or one trauma dump is not a problem,” Groskopf says. “We’re all human.”
The larger concern is whether the other person has a meaningful way to say “not now,” slow the conversation down, or stop it—and what happens when they do. If every limit is ignored, negotiated away, or treated as proof that they don’t care, the relationship has lost room for one person’s boundaries.
The listener has a responsibility, too. Someone who’s overwhelmed may not notice shorter replies, broken eye contact, or glances at the clock. “If you’re that dysregulated, you’re not going to notice how someone else is feeling,” Mahalec says. That’s not necessarily selfishness; it can be part of what happens when a person is emotionally flooded. Rather than expecting them to decode subtle cues, the listener may need to say plainly: “I care about you, but I can’t give this conversation my full attention right now. Can we talk later today?”
Only one response will do
Wanting reassurance is normal. So is asking someone to listen, offer advice, sit beside you, or remind you that you’re not alone. The warning sign isn’t that you want comfort; it’s that the other person becomes responsible for producing one exact response that will make the feeling disappear.
If you need them to agree with you, reassure you repeatedly, or validate you in one very specific way, “you’ve unintentionally handed them the responsibility for changing your emotional state,” Groskopf says. That’s not reasonable to expect from anyone.
You might notice yourself explaining the story again, adding more context, or calling someone else because the first person didn’t say the thing that finally made you feel better. “It’s easy to start believing that one more detail or one more piece of context will finally make the other person understand the situation enough to change how we feel,” Groskopf says. “The strategy isn’t working, so the brain keeps trying harder and harder.”
That doesn’t mean there’s something wrong with telling a painful story more than once. Grief and trauma often need to be spoken about repeatedly. The question is whether you’re inviting someone to witness what you’re feeling—or making them responsible for ending it.
The friendship has become one permanent emergency
All close relationships go through periods of imbalance. When someone is grieving, ill, traumatized, or otherwise struggling, they may need far more support than they can give. People who love them often want to provide it.
So don’t judge the relationship by one conversation—or even one very difficult stretch. Look at the broader pattern. Do you contact this person only when something has gone wrong? Are they expected to be available whenever you become overwhelmed? Is there room for them to talk about their own life? Do the two of you still know each other outside of distress?
Groskopf says that when the same person repeatedly becomes the only place you go for emotional relief, both people can settle into roles without realizing it: One is always in crisis, and the other is always expected to steady them. Eventually, “the friendship starts to revolve around emotional crises,” she says.
How to seek support without silencing yourself
None of this means swallowing your pain, waiting until you can discuss it calmly, or saving every difficult thought for a therapist. “The urge to get it all out is so incredibly healthy,” says Jenny Martin, a psychologist and founder of Gemstone Wellness, a trauma-informed practice in Chicago. “The urge is correct.”
Some relationships can hold the full story. When enough trust and intimacy exist, Martin says, even an intense account of “real trauma and pain” can make sense and be welcomed. Mahalec also points to the value of co-regulation: Being with someone calmer can help an overwhelmed nervous system begin to settle. You don’t always have to regulate yourself before reaching for another person.
A few strategies can make that connection easier—without requiring you to communicate perfectly.
Say what you need
Before or during the conversation, tell the other person what would help. You might say: “I don’t need advice; I just need someone to listen.” Or: “I’m overwhelmed and don’t know what I need yet. Can you stay with me for a few minutes?”
Naming what you want relieves the listener of having to guess. It also makes room for an honest answer about what they can offer.
Ask about timing
Groskopf suggests asking: “Do you have the bandwidth for something really heavy right now?” Martin offers another option: “How much energy do you have for holding space for hard stuff right now?”
Think of these questions as tools, not tests you have to pass before you’re allowed to speak. If you’re too overwhelmed to ask gracefully—or only realize afterward that you never checked in—you haven’t committed some unforgivable relational offense. Watson points out that everyone occasionally gets difficult conversations wrong. What matters is being willing to listen, adjust, and repair.
Give your pain more than one place to go
Needing more support than one friend can provide doesn’t mean your story is too much or that it belongs only in therapy. It means you deserve more than one place where you can tell it.
Depending on what feels right, that might include several friends or relatives, a support group, a faith community, or a therapist. Different people may be able to offer different things: company, practical help, lived experience, distraction, advice, or space to tell the entire story.
The goal isn’t to protect everyone else from your feelings. It’s to keep you from becoming isolated—or dependent on one person being available every time the pain surges.
Use a private voice memo as a bridge
When you want to get your thoughts out in private, Martin recommends opening your phone’s voice recorder and saying everything you need to say. She uses the strategy herself. On one recent evening, after a particularly difficult day, she retreated to her hammock and let herself unload.
“I sat out in my hammock under the moon, and I just cried and talked into an audio memo,” Martin says. “It allows me to purge and wring out so much that is simmering in my body. It organizes and releases what’s fluttering around that needs out.”
But Martin doesn’t view the recording as a replacement for human connection. Afterward, she says, it’s sometimes important to recognize: “I also deserve a real human to share this with. How do I make that next step happen?”
Keep the recording private unless someone agrees to receive it. Voice messages “remove so much of the consent that naturally exists in a conversation,” Groskopf says, because they can arrive while someone is working, picking up their children, or finally having a good day. Before sending one, try asking: “Do you have the capacity for a long voice note right now?”
If you’re the person listening
Supporting someone doesn’t require being endlessly available or absorbing more than you can handle. But it is your job to communicate your boundary—not the distressed person’s job to read your mind.
Begin with a pause rather than a correction: “Can we stop for a second?” Then acknowledge what you heard before explaining your limit. Martin suggests: “I want to be the best version of your friend, and I know I’m not the right place for this level of pain. But when you’re ready, I want to help you find the right place.”
You can also set a boundary around timing rather than the subject itself: “I want to hear this, but I’m running on empty tonight. Can I call you tomorrow morning?” Or around what you can offer: “I can listen, but I don’t think I’m equipped to give you advice about this.”
A boundary doesn’t have to communicate that someone’s grief is frightening, inappropriate, or too heavy to shoulder. It can communicate: “I care about this, and I want to show up in a way I can sustain.”
If you wish you had handled the conversation differently
If you recognize afterward that you may have trauma-dumped, circle back. But don’t apologize for having needed help—that was never the problem.
“What’s not necessary is apologizing for the fact that you needed support,” Groskopf says. “It’s about repairing and recognizing the part where the consideration of the other person got lost.”
The repair can be simple: “Hey, I’ve been thinking about our conversation. I never checked whether you had space for all of that. Thank you for listening. How are you doing?”
Hard conversations can be awkward, repetitive, lopsided, and still deeply loving. The goal isn’t to express pain perfectly. It’s to build relationships sturdy enough to hold both the pain and the boundaries around it.

    "Sigfrido Ranucci is a victim three times over: a victim of a serious, dangerous attack, of betrayal, of being exploited by a friend in a delirious show of madness (if the facts are definitively established); and, last but not least—and perhaps most seriously—of a massive and persistent campaign of media and political lynching that, through conjecture and insinuations, has sought to portray the victim as the more-or-less-willing beneficiary of the attack." attorney Roberto De Vita said. 
    "We are now awaiting the verdict regarding those who have been charged with aggravated defamation for knowingly contributing to the vicious smear campaign against the most prominent figure in investigative journalism in Italy—an action that is as dangerous to democracy as an attack". 
    Carabinieri police have also arrested four people accused of carrying out the attack, in which a bomb was detonated in front of the gate to the journalist's home in Pomezia, near Rome, on October 16, 2025, destroying two cars parked on the street, his and his daughter's, and damaging a wall. 
    They were allegedly paid several thousand euros to carry out the attack. 
    Lavitola has been at the centre of many top political and business corruption stories over the years. 
    These include: a Monte Carlo house whose purchase sank former Berlusconi protegé Gianfranco Fini's political career; the alleged buying and selling of Senators to bring down a centre-left government; the attempted extortion of Silvio Berlusconi over a ring of escorts at his 'elegant dinners'; kickbacks for contracts in Panama; and scams involving publishing funds.

New space object ‘black hole star’ discovered by astronomers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:05:09 UTC
01:05:09 KST

New space object ‘black hole star’ discovered by astronomers
PARIS - Astronomers announced on Aug 12 they had discovered a new type of astronomical object called a “black hole star”, potentially solving a mystery involving strange red dots spotted in the early universe.
The object looks like a star the size of our solar system, but produces 100 billion times more energy than any star – a mighty blast of power closer to what is produced by a black hole.
The black hole star, which dates from 660 million years after the Big Bang, was spotted by a US-led team of astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope, according to a study published in the journal Nature.
Since history’s most powerful telescope went online in 2022, it has been spotting many extremely bright cosmic objects dubbed “little red dots” in the early universe that have baffled scientists.
“What exactly these objects are has been one of the most debated topics of the JWST era,” lead study author Rohan Naidu of Hawaii University said in a statement.
The team had been trying to find clues for a different mystery: why JWST keeps finding bright galaxies in the universe’s infancy, when it was thought to have been too early for them to have become so huge.
But while looking through the images, they spotted a little red dot.
‘Pure black hole star light’
“When we see something very red in the universe, we often assume that it is surrounded by dust, like soot or ash,” said Robert Simcoe, a study co-author from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
“The same way that the wildfire smoke from Canada recently made the sky in Boston look bright red, astronomical objects can also appear redder than their intrinsic colour when you see them through a veil of dust,” he added.
However when the team sifted through their data, they found that at certain wavelengths, the object’s light simply disappeared.
To their surprise, this suggested that it is not dust making this object appear red – it is hydrogen gas.
This explained the object’s colour, but not how it could be pumping out so much energy.
“You can’t be powering this by nuclear fusion, which is the energy source that sits at the heart of all the stars,” Naidu explained.
Using modelling simulations, they determined the most likely scenario was that the object is powered by a central black hole surrounded by a cocoon of gas that makes it resemble a star.
The team named the object MoM-BH*-1. The BH and asterix is for black hole star – and the number one suggests they believe there are more out there.
“Every little red dot is consistent with being a black hole star,” Naidu said.
“What is special about MoM-BH*-1 is, the black hole star is essentially completely outshining its surrounding host galaxy, such that we’re seeing pure black hole star light.” AFP

Eye on the sky: Millions across Europe hope to catch glimpse of rare total eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:04:46 UTC
01:04:46 KST

The eclipse, a first in mainland Europe since 2006, also cast its shadow through parts of Greenland, racing south to smother part of Iceland before arcing across the Atlantic Ocean towards northern Spain.
Day briefly turned to night in Spain on Wednesday, as the country witnessed its first total solar eclipse in more than a century, plunging it into eerie darkness in one of nature's greatest spectacles.
The spectral glow of the Sun's outer corona, shimmering out of the edges of the shadowy Moon, drew gasps and cheers from huge crowds, just 90 minutes after it first appeared in the remote Arctic region of northern Russia.
"This is crazy!" said one woman in Tarragona, on Spain's Mediterranean coast, as the crowd beside her applauded enthusiastically.
The eclipse, a first in mainland Europe since 2006, also cast its shadow through parts of Greenland, racing south to smother Keflavík, some 50 kilometres from Iceland's capital, Reykjavik, before arcing across the Atlantic Ocean towards northern Spain.
In Spain, the lunar shadow moved diagonally in a narrow path from the northern coast to the Balearic Islands, where tourists and locals gathered to watch on the beach, many dressed in swimming costumes accessorised with protective glasses.
"Spectacular, very beautiful, truly a unique moment," said Rosa Maria Zamora, 72, who came to watch the eclipse in Colmenar Viejo, around 30 kilometres north of Madrid.
Supplies of special viewing glasses were in high demand, with huge crowds turning out to watch a partial eclipse across Europe, with the event also visible in Canada, the northern United States and northwest Africa.
A partial eclipse began in parts of northern Spain shortly after 1930 CET, prompting gasps from waiting crowds and applause from South Korean tourists in a field in Lodoso, near the northern city of Burgos.
"How wonderful!" said one woman in the crowd in Colmenar Viejo.
On the summit of the Pic du Midi, in the French Pyrenees, heavy clouds parted minutes beforehand, allowing visitors to see the spectacle, which also drew crowds in London, Paris and across the continent.
Disappointing view in Iceland
Earlier on Wednesday, a total eclipse plunged western Iceland into complete darkness, though heavy cloud cover and rain blocked the sight of the sun disappearing behind the moon.
Total darkness swept over Keflavík, some 50 kilometres southwest of the capital Reykjavik, at 5:47 pm local time, according reporters at the scene.
It was the first time the rare phenomenon was visible in Iceland's capital Reykjavik since 1433 and attracted thousands of tourists and locals across the country.
Astronomer and popular scientist Saevar Helgi Bragason was among the most eager spectators.
He said he had been "waiting for this day for more than 10 years" after a partial solar eclipse over Iceland on 20 March 2015.
Speaking to the AFP news agency just before the event, he said he was filled with "excitement and heartbreak" because of the unfavourable weather forecast which predicted that clouds would obscure the view of the moon blocking out the sun.
"It's almost like I've lost someone."
The total eclipse lasted the longest over the cliffs of Latrabjarg in the westernmost part of Iceland, about 2 minutes and 13 seconds, while further south in the centre of Reykjavik it lasted for just over one minute.
Hotels in Reykjavik and the rest of Iceland were fully booked, with one hotel in the western village of Breidavik receiving its first booking for the event 14 years ago, according to national broadcaster RUV.
A fleeting event
Throughout human history, eclipses have stirred amazement, fear and reverence, as they appear to momentarily halt the normal course of nature.
The shadow or "umbra" cast by the alignment of Sun and Moon creates a strange twilight during which temperatures drop, shadows appear at strange angles and some animals go to sleep.
But the phenomenon is generally fleeting: in parts of Russia and Greenland, the total eclipse lasted under two-and-a-half minutes.
The partial eclipse, which occurs as the Moon starts and finishes crossing the Sun's path, dimming its light, was expected to last around one hour and 45 minutes.
The event, which was livestreamed by both NASA and the European Space Agency, presented scientists with a rare opportunity to study the Sun's atmosphere and its outermost layer, as they seek to uncover secrets about solar winds and our star's magnetic field.

Oil leaking from grounded tanker started reaching Oman mainland: UN shipping agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:04:26 UTC
01:04:26 KST

Gokhan Ergocun and Mucahithan Avcioglu
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
- Caroline Bezengi tanker was carrying around 130,000 tons of crude oil, equivalent to roughly 800,000 barrels
- Tanker, grounded off Oman on June 30, is currently around 22 nautical miles offshore of Sharbithat
Oil leaking from a tanker grounded off Oman’s coast has begun reaching the country’s mainland, the International Maritime Organization said Wednesday.
The UN shipping agency told Anadolu it is closely monitoring the leakage from the crude oil tanker Caroline Bezengi, which grounded off Oman on June 30 and is currently around 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) offshore of Sharbithat.
The vessel was carrying approximately 130,000 tons of oil, equivalent to about 800,000 barrels, at the time of the incident, the agency said.
“Oil has been leaking from the vessel for some time,” the organization told Anadolu.
 
The agency said seasonal monsoon conditions had restricted access to the tanker and delayed salvage operations.
The spilled oil is drifting offshore northeast of Oman’s Al-Qibliyyah Island, while some has reportedly reached the mainland, according to the organization.
It said oil-spill contingency planning was in place to respond to the incident and limit its environmental impact.
The organization said it had been in contact with the Omani government since the tanker grounded and would continue supporting the ongoing response efforts.
 
Spill previously estimated at 390 square kilometers
Oman’s Environment Authority said earlier this week that the slick covered approximately 390 square kilometers (150 square miles) northeast of the Al Hallaniyat Islands and was advancing toward the mainland.
 
At the time, the pollution was estimated to be around 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) from the coast, with authorities saying nearby desalination plants and tourism facilities faced no immediate threat.
The islands lie within a protected marine reserve that supports wildlife, including the endangered Arabian Sea humpback whale and Socotra cormorants.
The Caroline Bezengi is a roughly 274-meter (899-foot) Suezmax tanker built in 2001. It has been sanctioned by the UK and EU over its involvement in transporting Russian-origin oil.
The vessel is also believed to be part of Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of older tankers used to move crude outside Western shipping and insurance networks.

‘A hostile world’: As fear and mistrust reshape everyday life in wartime Russia, some are still finding ways to build community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:04:11 UTC
01:04:11 KST

‘A hostile world’: As fear and mistrust reshape everyday life in wartime Russia, some are still finding ways to build community
Inside Russia, loneliness has become one of the war’s less visible but pervasive consequences. Many people are afraid to interact with others, because even an innocent conversation about peace could cost them their freedom — and so they remain alone with their pain. Others have lost interest in public life, seeing little opportunity to make a difference, and have focused on their families instead. It’s not only people with antiwar views who complain of isolation and fear, but also people who support the war. And yet some people do manage to find a way out of this impossible situation. The independent journalists’ cooperative Bereg reports on how. Meduza is translating the story in full.
Note: This article contains explicit language.
‘It feels like we ended up in a hostile world’
Oleg’s family in the Moscow region woke up one night in June 2026 to explosions and drones roaring over their house at four in the morning. Going back to sleep was out of the question — it was too frightening.
That morning, Oleg says, there were “no sirens, no alerts” warning of the attack — as if even the warnings themselves were banned in Russia.
Oleg, who is about 40, owns a small clothing manufacturing business. He had been mentally bracing for a morning like this since the start of the full-scale war — but he still wasn’t ready.
It might seem like it’s only now hitting us [the scale of the fallout from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine]. But for me personally, it hit on the very first day in 2022. For four years I’ve periodically dreamed about bombings. Now it’s just moved into reality.
Oleg isn’t a political activist, but the full-scale invasion devastated him — and he had almost no one to talk to about it.
“There were a couple of run-ins [on the street] over the peace sign sewn onto my clothes,” Oleg recalls. “At first they’d say something really negative, like “I don’t like this shit” or “I’m against this.”” He managed to turn those complaints into “conversations about hippie culture.”
One coworker, the entrepreneur says, “turned out to be a Putinist”: “He started saying that the West wants to seize us and always has, and that they “brought down the Soviet Union”… I had a rough idea [of his views], but I didn’t know how far they went. I didn’t try to start conversations like that — so as not to spoil the relationship.”
Before the war, Oleg was outgoing and made friends easily. Now he focuses entirely on his family and avoids meeting new people.
Many Russians are tormented by their inability to speak freely about the situation in their country — a condition that could be called “political loneliness,” though not everyone Bereg spoke with for this story agrees with the term.
Censorship and fear for their freedom and their lives have forced Russians into silence, and many are afraid to discuss politics or the war in any form. Because only state rhetoric is voiced openly, many come to feel that alternative views are unpopular — producing an acute sense of isolation.
Natalya (name changed at her request), an instructor at Vladimir State University, describes her wartime feelings as “the fear of being misunderstood and breaking off relationships with people who used to be close.” “I’ve become cautious about certain topics, as if I’m carefully choosing my words so as not to misjudge a person’s position and become disappointed in them. And I’ve already become disappointed in many.”
Taisiya (name changed at her request), a Moscow resident in her 50s, feels much the same as Oleg and Natalya: “It feels like we ended up in a hostile world where nobody shares your views at all. And it’s no longer clear whether you can talk about anything, or what it might lead to. It weighs on you psychologically.”
‘I didn’t think it was illegal to answer questions about organizations designated “terrorist”’
In February 2023, a stranger sent 24-year-old Polina Yevtushenko a friend request on VK.
Nikolai Tsarev, who said he was from Samara, sent a friendly message asking about her job at the mobile carrier Yota and her interest in drawing — details Polina had mentioned on social media. She replied, and the two began exchanging messages.
“Kolya asked whether I could draw him — and draw him with “Korzh” [a type of cake layer]. I thought he wanted a portrait with a cake. I told him I wasn’t very good at it but could try. Then we talked about music, and he said he liked [Belarusian musician] Max Korzh,” Polina Yevtushenko recalled of how it began, in a letter to Bereg. Afterward, their exchanges settled into “simple, everyday topics.”
Yevtushenko grew up in Tolyatti and had a daughter at 19, the independent Russian outlet Holod reported. She raised the child alone while building a career.
She didn’t hide her views and was outspoken on social media, posting at times in Ukrainian and using blunt Instagram hashtags like “NoToWar,” “PutinKhuilo,” “FreedomOfRussiaLegion,” and “RussiaWithoutPutin.”
“Tolyatti, don’t stay silent! No to war!” Yevtushenko wrote shortly after Russia announced its mobilization in fall 2022. Around that time, she wore a T-shirt with an upside-down “Fuck Putin” print and carried a backpack with a Ukrainian flag and the words “No to war.”
By the time Tsarev wrote to her, Polina had already quit Yota to launch her own business, an online store selling women’s sportswear that she planned to sell through Wildberries. She completed courses for young entrepreneurs and even won a grant from regional authorities to get it off the ground.
After a couple of weeks of messaging, Tsarev told Polina he was coming to Tolyatti on a business trip and suggested meeting up. He said he worked as a sales representative for a company that sold car-cleaning products, but Polina later recalled getting the impression he didn’t work anywhere at all — he was always free.
During their meeting, Polina noticed “small oddities” in her new acquaintance’s behavior. “His hands were shaking badly.” He asked strange questions. “Out of nowhere, with no connection to what we’d been talking about, he asked, “I read on your page about the [Freedom of Russia] Legion. What if I joined the legion?””
The question caught Yevtushenko off guard. It embarrassed her, but she answered anyway — she “didn’t think it was illegal to answer questions about organizations designated as terrorist.”
At later meetings, Tsarev kept steering the conversation back to the Freedom of Russia Legion.
“Tsarev” was actually Nikolai Komarov. He recorded their conversations on a dictaphone and passed the recordings to officers of Russia’s Federal Security Service, the FSB. He and Yevtushenko talked for about five months.
On the morning of July 12, 2023, Polina walked her 5-year-old daughter to kindergarten. As she stepped back through the gate, someone struck her in the back, and she fell to the ground. When she turned around, she saw more than 10 men in plain clothes.
“They put a plastic zip tie on my wrists and threw me into the car like a sack of potatoes. Then the men got in and put their feet on me. They didn’t explain anything. I thought they were criminals and that I was being taken away to be killed,” she later told Holod.
The next day, a court in Samara ordered Yevtushenko held in pretrial detention for two months on suspicion of “inducing” Komarov — “Tsarev” — to commit treason. Investigators alleged she had been persuading him to join the legion and fight against Russia.
Yevtushenko insists she did no such thing and says that would have been obvious if the court had reviewed the full recordings of their conversations. “The parts that could have exonerated me were left out, and you can hear it — the conversations simply cut off.”
The human rights group First Department also noted that one of the recordings presented in court captured Komarov rehearsing talking points about the legion out loud before meeting with Yevtushenko.
Komarov likely became a provocateur as early as 2017, when he volunteered at Navalny’s Samara headquarters. In 2020, he testified as a prosecution witness in an administrative case against Marina Yevdokimova, a former headquarters staffer who was running for a seat on the Samara district council at the time.
Prosecutors later added several more charges to Yevtushenko’s original charge. A court sentenced her in March 2026 to 14 years in prison; she does not admit guilt. The human rights group Memorial considers her a political prisoner.
‘Since 2022, meeting new people has become stressful and scary’
Antiwar Russians who spoke to Bereg say making new acquaintances has grown far scarier since February 2022 — especially in small towns.
Natalya, the Vladimir State University instructor, says her circle now consists of just a couple of friends and family: “Since 2022, meeting new people has felt stressful and scary — what if this is a spy or an FSB agent who’s going to report you? Even trying to meet people for a relationship feels dangerous.”
Natalya says she misses talking with like-minded people. People she once considered “reasonable” “stopped being that way” after the full-scale invasion began, and trying to talk war supporters out of their views, in her view, “isn’t worth it — it’s unnecessary and even dangerous.”
Finding like-minded people is even harder for older Russians.
Making new friends after 50 is difficult enough already, says Yulia (name changed), a 60-year-old Moscow resident. She has no idea how to meet people now that sharing your thoughts can be dangerous: “Some of the people close to me have left. It’s especially sad when children leave — it deepens the sense of despair, and it gets harder and harder to find meaning in what’s happening.”
Yulia works in the entertainment industry, where, she says, it’s “long since become impossible to discuss what actually worries you.”
Yulia doesn’t consider herself an activist. Before the war, she never went to rallies, though she spoke out on social media in support of political prisoners, called for fair elections, and urged her followers to donate to the independent Russian human rights monitor OVD-Info.
In the spring of 2022, she secretly hung green protest ribbons in courtyards and on playgrounds: “I was scared, but it was my own quiet protest.”
For Yulia, wartime has become a period when it’s hard to talk even with acquaintances. “I’m always carefully choosing my words, trying to figure out where it’s appropriate to say something and where it’s not,” she says. She calls it “a throwback to Soviet times,” since she has to “communicate in half-truths” even “with people who you know share your point of view” — in case outsiders overhear the conversation:
When you suddenly find out that the person you’re talking to shares your views, you take it as rare luck. It’s usually discovered by accident. Normally, people avoid those topics — it’s considered inappropriate. Not because it’s scary. But because you don’t want to spoil the relationship [with colleagues]. There’s nowhere to go — we see each other every day and we’ve grown used to this political hypocrisy.
Aesopian language is now used in Russia not just at work but within close circles too, according to Veronika Danilova, a sociologist at the NGO Arendt Labs and co-author of a recent study of Russian civic initiatives titled “Solidarity Under Pressure”.
“Many of our respondents talked about growing self-censorship even in conversations with friends, because there’s no certainty about anyone,” Danilova says. “This is noticeable even among those who used to be the most politically outspoken and who, as recently as 2024, expressed themselves much more freely.”
Yulia recalls cautiously joking about the regime in a recent conversation with a coworker she barely knew — and he told her: “God, I’m so glad to hear we’re on the same wavelength!”
She smiled for the rest of the day.
Natalya would like to find like-minded people but has no idea where in Vladimir she could meet others she could be herself with. She’s heard that local activists recently tried to launch a regional branch of the Rassvet party — an effort that ended with searches.
“Most of my friends and like-minded people who took an active position have either left the country or are in prison,” says Pyotr (name changed), who lives in a small city in northwestern Russia and remains politically active.
“The disunity and atomization of people inside Russia who oppose the war is a fact. But that’s a deliberate policy of the Kremlin,” Pyotr continues.
Left-wing politician and labor activist Mikhail Lobanov, who has continued his political work since being forced to leave Russia, says regional activists he knows have come under close scrutiny from security officials.
“They were essentially advised to disengage from everything, [meaning any political activity]. Some of those people left the country. And some really did withdraw from active political and social life.”
The situation facing independent civic projects has steadily worsened since 2024, when the Arendt Labs study came out, amid growing pressure from the state, Danilova says.
As recently as two years ago, human rights defenders looked to Belarus’s experience and expected Russian authorities to designate civic and political initiatives as foreign agents first, then as undesirable organizations, and only later as extremist. But the cases of the human rights groups Memorial and OVD-Info showed that “everything can happen much faster than that.”
Now many projects fear being hit immediately with the most discriminatory label of all, extremist status, Danilova concludes.
‘Today there’s a need to do something’
For several years, Taisiya has led themed walking tours through central Moscow. Along the way, participants come across plaques from “Last Address”, a project on building facades that preserves the memory of victims of Stalin-era terror.
“When you tell the history of Moscow — whether it’s culture, the history of theaters, or the history of science — you inevitably run into the subject of terror. If you don’t touch on the Stalinist repressions, many details and people’s motivations become impossible to understand,” Taisiya explains.
Once, after the full-scale war began, she was leading another tour when she noticed people in the group who had already walked the route before.
“Every time I see familiar faces on my tour of the sites of repression, I feel like a mom whose child is asking her to read the same fairy tale for the 10th time,” Taisiya says with a smile. Some people, she says, had come “probably five times already.”
Taisiya tried to understand why and settled on a simple explanation: “it seems that it’s important for people to be among their own”:
Today’s war relies heavily on repression inside the country. And right now, more than ever, it’s important to talk about the value of an individual human life, regardless of the merits of the person whose memory we’re preserving this way. That runs counter to today’s dominant trend, where people say that life, on the contrary, should be spent without a second thought. Our walks have become a kind of expression of solidarity.
Around the same time, at the start of the full-scale war, “Last Address” plaques on some buildings began disappearing. Unknown people were smashing and unscrewing them “whole districts at a time,” Taisiya says. The makers of the documentary Karton “Cardboard,” by the studio Razrez, found one of the people responsible for the vandalism: Gosha Tarasevich, leader of the nationalist movement SERB.
One of the regulars on Taisiya’s tours then suggested cutting out cardboard plaques and hanging them where the originals had been torn down. “A group of people from the tours took it upon themselves to look after the plaques. At first there were just a few of them, but the group gradually grew to a couple dozen.”
After one tour, Taisiya stopped at a cafe for coffee. When she came out, she ran into the same tour participants she had just said goodbye to, walking down the lane with a notebook and pen, checking whether the plaques were still in place.
When the volunteers held a workshop on cutting out cardboard duplicates, 40 people showed up, according to Taisiya — they barely fit in the room.
She’s struck that volunteers with no obligations to one another keep the project going on their own. In wartime, under censorship and persecution, she believes people want to make at least some contribution to a common cause:
For all this to keep working, some kind of energy is needed — and apparently that energy exists here. I think this is exactly today’s need for people to go offline and do something. There’s still a large gap between staying silent and not staying silent. You can always find a way to express yourself somehow.
Sociologist Veronika Danilova also says there’s strong demand for participation in offline initiatives: “It’s getting stronger every year. It’s important for people to feel their own agency, no matter what.”
The nature of these projects has changed since the war began: many people gave up political work for small, often local civic initiatives, Danilova says. Projects that feel safe to Russians tend to center on the environment or culture — activists take part in neighborhood cleanup days or form book clubs, for example.
Little by little, members of these communities may “start carefully feeling out whether a given person is “one of us” or “not one of us,”” the researcher says, recounting her conversations with respondents in Russia:
Nobody will ask directly, “Are you against the war or for it?” It’ll be careful leading questions, for example about Trump’s policies.
Right now, Danilova says, people’s main efforts are focused on “survival and preserving themselves and their organizations.”
‘I wouldn’t want anyone to get the impression that we’re a secret cell’
It’s an April day in downtown Moscow, and dozens of people are learning to juggle right there on the street. Nearby, tables hold Easter breads, painted eggs, and steaming samovars, while children laugh and run around. One participant has brought along several stray dogs, hoping to find them owners.
That’s what another Sunday looked like this spring on Danilovskaya Alley, between Pokrovsky Boulevard and Solyanka Street. Since the summer of 2020, weekly “Khokhlovsky vigils” have taken place here — an open-ended street protest to preserve the historic character of the Ivanovskaya Gorka neighborhood.
The vigils take their name from Khokhlovsky Lane, where a large business center is under construction. Participants are demanding that construction stop and that the historic garden of the Jurgenson estate, destroyed in the 1930s, be restored. The Institute of the International Labor Movement was later built on the site in Soviet times; it has now been torn down to make way for a business center twice the institute’s size.
Participants believe the construction violates the law on protected zones around cultural heritage sites.
“Put simply, you can only build something that regenerates the historic setting of the landmarks at a given site,” Dmitry Charakhchyan, a lawyer who takes part in the vigils, explained. “And it’s obvious that the historic setting of the landmark was the Jurgenson garden, and by law that’s the only thing that can be recreated here. No business center was ever part of the setting of the cultural heritage sites, and one can’t be built right in the middle of the estate.”
Gatherings on Ivanovskaya Gorka happen every Sunday, rain or snow. So far, organizers have held 300 free concerts, tours, lectures, exhibitions, and workshops there.
Some events draw 200 people, says Maria (name changed at her request), a preservationist activist. The crowd isn’t limited to Ivanovskaya Gorka residents, she says — Muscovites come from outlying districts, too.
Although the standoffs pursue exclusively peaceful goals, police have shown up several times with utterly absurd complaints, Maria recalls: “They had questions about whether a samovar counts as an open flame. They were told a samovar is a closed flame.”
Officers were offered tea, and in the end everything ended fine. Maria adds that breaking up the Petrushka puppet theater actors performing for protesters that day would have been “downright Pinocchio-esque.”
The people who take part, she says, “are defending people’s right to a cultural living environment”: “People are always drawn to the chance to talk with like-minded people. But I wouldn’t want anyone to get the impression that the gatherings are a secret cell. We try hard not to be that.”
* * *
The study by Danilova and her Arendt Labs co-authors confirms that many Russians are coping with loneliness by seeking out communities where they can share common values with someone.
“The viewpoint they [war opponents] might gravitate toward isn’t represented in public discourse, and they’re desperately looking for places where they can feel like they’re among their own and relax, if only a little,” Danilova says.
But Russians who are ambivalent about the war, or who even support the invasion, feel isolated, too, and “suffer from a sense of being judged.”
In interviews with respondents in Russia, Danilova and her colleagues found that people who provide humanitarian aid to mobilized soldiers and service members, or who weave camouflage nets for the front, describe the same isolation and fear as antiwar Russians. Some even hid from coworkers that they were helping the Russian military.
“People in general try not to state their position outright, to sort of blur it. You’d think [pro-war] views like that are represented absolutely everywhere. But people are anxious and feel like outcasts,” Danilova says.
In her view, this stems from political repression that after 2022 spread far beyond the openly oppositional, while the “rules of the game” governing public life in a Russia at war remain unclear. As a result, self-censorship and a “survival logic” are spreading through society regardless of political conviction.
In some fields, such as historic preservation or environmental activism, many experts deliberately distance themselves from politics, try to bring together people with different views, and avoid sensitive topics, Danilova says: “This strategy is based on the premise that we all share the same air, the same planet.”
“When you’re united by the goal of protecting something with objective value, you learn to negotiate with each other and get something done together,” says Maria, the preservationist activist from Ivanovskaya Gorka:
It’s a very important skill — if what you’re building isn’t a sect or a party, but a machine made of people. And, generally speaking, that’s the foundation of civil society. After all, you don’t always only interact with people who share your views on every issue.
Politician Yulia Galyamina, designated a foreign agent in Russia, decided not to leave the country after the war began, despite her suspended sentence and the risks that come with it.
In conversation with Bereg, Galyamina stresses that antiwar views are, first and foremost, about a desire for peace — and so rest on the idea of dialogue. That’s why, she insists, “you need to learn to have a dialogue with people who have a different outlook on life.”
The inability to talk about political topics “without starting to hate the person you’re talking to over their different view” is a real problem in Russian society, one “that needs to be worked on,” Galyamina believes.
(Galyamina’s own posts may illustrate the point: her post about the unacceptability of killing children on either side of the border prompted a wave of sharp criticism from antiwar Russians living abroad.)
Galyamina acknowledges that the arsenal of collective political action in today’s Russia is “limited.” But it still exists — Russians retain the ability to “express their political identity without directly clashing over the topic of the war.”
“If by politics we mean working together for the common good, then all sorts of things fall under that. You can unite around values like opposing violence, protecting the environment, or fostering intellectual development,” Galyamina says, adding as a caveat: “That doesn’t mean the only people there will be ones with antiwar views.”
As an example, Galyamina cites a recent trip to the village of Yeski in the Tver region, where she met volunteers with all kinds of political views, all working toward the same goal — helping the “Conservation” project prepare for the restoration of the local Church of the Epiphany, where 19th-century murals are set to be restored.
The word “activism” itself has become toxic in today’s Russia, Danilova concludes: “For example, people who protect the environment, cultural heritage, or animals today extremely rarely call themselves activists. They’re more likely to say “I volunteer,” “I help out sometimes,” or “I’m interested in this.”” They’re afraid to call themselves activists outright, so as not to draw unwanted attention.
‘Lots of “foreign agents,” current and future’
“People sit in the kitchen, eat pilaf. They drink wine, talk. Pet the cat. Then they move to the living room and put on a movie with a projector,” says Boris (name changed for safety reasons), a philologist and YouTuber, describing evenings at a Moscow apartment where the owner runs a home film club.
Usually about 15 people gather — journalists, lawyers, human rights activists, film school students, and musicians of all ages — and they barely fit in the small kitchen.
According to Boris, in his acquaintance’s apartment you can find “lots of ‘foreign agents,’ current and future.”
People get into the screenings by invitation only. The first time Boris found himself in the apartment, he couldn’t shake the parallels with the Soviet dissident movement:
In principle, I get that feeling anywhere there’s a kitchen where people smoke and talk about something — because I come from a family of dissidents. But this era seems worse to me than the Brezhnev one. Back then there were at least some rules of the game, but now it’s total randomness.
The films participants watch are often “socially significant in nature.” One evening they discussed Pavel Talankin’s much-talked-about film Mr. Nobody Against Putin. Another time, an independent journalist showed his own documentary about a Russian contract soldier who went off to fight in the war against Ukraine.
Strictly speaking, a film about a contract soldier who says he’s fighting for the money isn’t an antiwar statement, Boris reasons. But what the subject says still points to the conclusion that this is “not at all the people’s war that propaganda tries to present it as to the public”:
The people who get together [at the home film club] are — at least for now — in Russia. And in the films we watch, what interests the group is more the view of the war and all this disaster from inside Russia. And really, what can people who stay in Russia and hope not to end up in prison actually do? Document it.
Still, these evenings are far from always devoted to “social topics,” Boris says. The club is “just a gathering of people who have something to talk about and who want to visit each other.” “Nothing illegal happens” there, Boris reasons, and he’s “never once heard any serious sedition” that might draw “some kind of interest from the authorities.”
That’s not because the guests lack such thoughts, he says, but because the people there already understand each other: “The most seditious thoughts, it seems to me, are these loud, declarative manifestos… But when you’re among your own, you somehow don’t feel the need for them.”
‘We don’t announce events, we invite people only in person’
After leaving Russia, politician and former Moscow State University instructor Mikhail Lobanov said private film clubs, where antiwar-minded participants gather, have sprung up across Russia.
But discussion venues aren’t limited to people’s homes, he says — they also persist within universities. “These kinds of projects keep operating, just in a safer mode, in a non-public space,” Lobanov explains.
Veronika Danilova says one of the conditions that has kept civil society alive in wartime Russia is the shift of initiatives into non-public spaces: “More and more activities are going underground or semi-underground — that is, they’re effectively invisible from the outside.”
The authors of the Arendt Labs study quote one Russian activist they managed to interview (the study doesn’t specify her field of activity):
Recently, officers from Center E started coming around, and we realized… that’s it, it’s not safe and it’s not fun anymore. So we decided to go back underground, gave up public spaces, and want to meet in different places. […] We’re gradually giving up social media. We don’t announce events, we only invite people personally. Or through activist chats — but that’s rarer now, because it’s not as safe anymore.
“It’s clear that what we used to see — movements like FBK [the Navalny-founded anti-corruption organization] — have become extremely unsafe,” Danilova says. But that doesn’t mean people who remain in Russia, whether by choice or because they have no way to leave, are disengaging from civil society altogether and becoming “either a neutral mass or pro-Putin.”
The number of politically active people, especially the young, in major cities “hasn’t dropped much,” Lobanov believes. That, he says, is what led to the “Radical Democracy” project, aimed at “the emergence of a strong political force on the democratic flank.”
Galyamina adds that independent book and philosophy clubs are operating in Russian cities, and that exhibitions and theatrical productions are being staged, some not even in theaters — one, for example, took place in a parking lot.
Some events and institutions are easy to get into and operate openly; word of mouth spreads information about others. “How does it all work here? Like this: there’s one facade, and life underneath is different,” Galyamina says.
Authorities have been continuously ramping up pressure since 2022, but civic activity persists regardless, Danilova says: “People are simply looking for safe forms of participation and are flocking to them.”
This will keep happening, she’s confident — Russians will keep finding new ways to interact: “It’ll be harder for outside observers to pick up on from the outside. But that doesn’t mean it will all disappear.”
‘There’s caution in actions and words. There’s no fear’
“From outside, life in Russia looks like some kind of black hell. In reality, there’s a great deal of life here,” Yulia Galyamina is convinced. “Someone less optimistic will tell you that everything is awful. Because it’s true: a lot of it is awful. There’s no gas, no internet, everyone’s fed up. But on the other hand — people come together, talk to each other, do things together.”
Galyamina believes important shifts in public mood have taken place over the past year and a half to two years: “The emotion of fear has given way to something more like irritation and a feeling of ‘being fed up with everything.’” And finally, plenty of people are willing to talk about how “fed up” they are — so people freely complain to each other about the internet, gas, and prices:
Everyone is irritated by absolutely everything. And everyone wants all of this to finally be over, the war above all. Because all of this is because of the war. Of course, not everyone understands that it’s because of the war. But I think most people do understand that.
“Almost everyone speaks negatively about the current government, about prices, gas shortages, and internet blocking, and actively shares local problems in their area,” confirms Pyotr, the activist, who is close to one of the regional election campaigns and talks often with residents and volunteers.
Pyotr adds: “It’s very obvious that people are deeply tired of staying silent and being afraid.”
* * *
Over the course of the war, each person Bereg spoke to has developed their own approach to dealing with neighbors, coworkers, and acquaintances.
Oleg, from the Moscow region, who woke up in June 2026 to a Ukrainian drone attack, tries not to step outside his own bubble: “I don’t really talk to many people [right now]. I’ve sort of sealed myself off in my own little world,” he says. “It’s not interesting to talk now — with the elephant in the room. It ends up feeling awkward somehow.”
People with opposing views, Oleg believes, are “someone you need to protect yourself from.”
Natalya, the instructor from Vladimir, and Yulia, the Moscow resident in the entertainment industry, have both given up looking for like-minded people or new friends.
“I don’t plan to do anything about it. It was the same way in Soviet times, so for people my age it’s nothing surprising. I have a few people I’m on the same wavelength with. I know how to be selective about who I talk to,” Yulia says. She avoids risky, dangerous conversations to “protect herself for the sake of her children.”
The trial and prison have turned upside down the life of Yevtushenko, who used to be open to the world. “In my conversations with Kolya, I went along with his topics simply because I couldn’t do otherwise, even when I didn’t want to talk about it,” she later wrote from prison. “Excessive suggestibility and the desire to please others needed to either be controlled or rooted out entirely.”
Now Polina believes that “you don’t always need to be nice to everyone,” and that with some people you shouldn’t be at all, “for the sake of your own good and your own freedom.” “You shouldn’t try to be good to everyone. There are people who take advantage of that for their own ends,” Yevtushenko concludes.
Some people are looking for a way out of isolation by finding at least some common ground with their ideological opponents. Lobanov’s former colleagues who stayed in Russia to teach have told him that by the third or fourth year of the full-scale war, a “kind of mutual adjustment” had taken place at universities between supporters and opponents of the war: “Over time, a sense emerged that this is all going to last a very long time, and that everyone is, in some sense, in the same boat.”
Those who keep doing local activism — activism they’re so afraid to call by that name — are making new friends. Volunteers tell Taisiya, the tour guide, about “frightening times, general depression, and despair,” always adding: “But look at the people we’ve met!”
“Going out on the street feels a little scary, sort of. But there’s usually more support than not — from young people and older ones alike. Someone always stops and says: oh, I know ‘Last Address,’ you’re heroes! Thank you… And that’s inspiring,” Taisiya says.
Politician Yulia Galyamina hasn’t lost her optimism either. “People believe in Russia, they believe in its future,” Galyamina is confident. “Because otherwise, why restore a church?”
Pyotr, the activist, says he’s “very lucky”: he has “a wonderful girlfriend, friends, and parents who also don’t support everything that’s happening right now.”
“I still believe this clusterfuck will end, and the beautiful Russia of the future will inevitably arrive,” Pyotr says. “There’s caution in actions and words, but there’s no fear. I’d even say I’m afraid of fear itself, since it paralyzes any productive action.”

Ukraine finds American Nvidia Jetson micro-computer in Russia’s new missile that can’t reportedly tell truck from a bus with children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:03:44 UTC
01:03:44 KST

An American AI computer has turned up inside Russia's newest cruise missile. Ukrainian specialists has found an Nvidia Jetson micro-computer in Russia's new S-71 "Monokhrom" cruise missile, the Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reports.
S-71M “Monokhrom is the first fully autonomous long-range strike system designed to engage not only stationary but also moving targets. The system is designed to independently decide whether to destroy a target based on threat priorities. A significant problem for such autonomous systems is determining exactly what they are attacking — a military truck or a bus carrying children.
The discovery is the latest evidence that Russia's newest weapons still run on Western technology. Ukraine has already documented hundreds of foreign components in Russian missiles and drones reaching Moscow despite sanctions.
The AI chip is the standout find
The use of the Nvidia Jetson may indicate the application of AI technologies in the missile. This capability would let the weapon process visual or sensor data onboard to identify targets or navigate, functions that depend on exactly the kind of compact AI computing it provides.
The chip sits among many foreign parts. In total, 35 electronic components used by Russia in the missile were identified, making Monokhrom another Russian weapon built substantially from foreign electronics.
The same parts show up across Russia's arsenal
HUR's analysis linked the missile to Russia's wider weapons program. The identified components included parts of a passive radar seeker that Russia has begun installing on Geran-2 drones to detect and strike Ukrainian air-defense systems and radars.
Other finds tied the missile to Russia's newest strike systems. They included a Chinese Honpho TS130C-01 camera from the jet-powered Geran-4 drone and components of the active homing seeker of the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
The finding sharpens the sanctions case
HUR framed the discovery as an argument for tighter enforcement.
"The discovery of an Nvidia Jetson in a new Russian missile once again demonstrates the need to strengthen sanctions pressure and coordinate the efforts of the civilized world," HUR said.
HUR specialists and Ukrainian research institutions continue to study Russian weapons and trace the origin of their electronic components to strengthen measures to block them.

Poland rekindles Musk feud over Starlink snub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:02:48 UTC
01:02:48 KST

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski on Wednesday threatened to reconsider Warsaw’s $50 million-a-year spending on Elon Musk’s Starlink network, joining a growing government backlash over new roaming restrictions set to hit Polish customers later this month.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, stop discriminating Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services,” wrote Sikorski on X.
The foreign minister's anger follows Starlink’s decision to exclude Poland from a shared European roaming zone that covers more than 30 countries, including Germany, Czechia, Slovakia and Lithuania. Customers within the zone can take their terminals across borders without triggering international-use restrictions. But Polish users will now face extra requirements when traveling.
Advertisement
“Note: Poland is not included in the Europe region above. Accounts registered in Poland are treated as Poland-only for home-country use,” reads Starlink’s current guidance.
Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski also went after Musk, accusing Starlink's parent company SpaceX of treating Poles as second-class customers and demanding it spell out the regulatory basis for the change.
“Poland is not a second-tier market. Polish customers are not second-tier customers,” Gawkowski wrote on X. If SpaceX blames “local regulatory requirements,” Warsaw expects it to point to the specific rules rather than offer “general explanations,” he added.
The new rules have applied to new customers signing up for Starlink since July 14, 2026 and will extend to existing Polish users on Aug. 17.
This isn't the first time Sikorski and Musk have fought over Starlink. Last year, Musk told the Polish minister to “be quiet, small man,” after Sikorski warned that Warsaw could seek alternative providers for the satellite service it's financing for Ukraine.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to POLITICO's request for comment.

The Polish government has appealed to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, to reverse its decision to exclude Poland from its European roaming area. It says that Polish users, who will now face greater costs when travelling, should not be treated as “second-tier customers”.
Starlink, which provides users with portable terminals that act as receivers for internet connections from its network of satellites, offers a “Roam” service that lets customers continue using their connection outside their home country without extra charges as long as they remain within their designated region.
One region is Europe, in which Starlink has included 36 countries and territories. However, the firm makes clear that “Poland is not included in the Europe region”, meaning users registered in that country are not included in the Roam system.
The company offered no explanation for Poland’s exclusion from the system. Some media reports have suggested that it is because terminals registered in Poland are used in Ukraine. However, Ukraine is itself not included in Starlink’s European “Roam” region.
The company’s decision prompted an angry response from Polish government ministers. “I do not agree with a global technology company treating Poles worse than other Europeans,” wrote digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on X, the social media platform owned by Musk.
“If Elon Musk’s SpaceX wants to operate in Poland, benefit from the Polish market, and earn from Polish customers, it must treat them fairly and on equal terms,” he added. “That is why I have appealed to SpaceX for the urgent restoration of equal terms for the company’s Polish customers.”

Primaries in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin show Democratic voters crave change, not just ideology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:00:17 UTC
01:00:17 KST

Democrats remain mixed over what ideological direction the party should take. But across a series of closely watched primaries, the results point to demand for change among Democratic primary voters.
In marquee Senate primaries in Michigan and Minnesota, progressive candidates defeated two members of Congress with significant backing from party leaders. Wisconsin voters narrowly rejected a democratic socialist but still chose a 40-year-old county executive who is seeking to become the state marquees first Black governor.
And in Connecticut, voters ousted one of the longest-serving Democrats in Congress for a challenger who campaigned on generational change.
The results so far this month deliver no clear ideological mandate. Instead, they add to mounting evidence from this year's primaries of a Democratic appetite for turnover that is cutting across the party’s traditional divisions.
"If leaders in our party don't recognise that we need to make changes, then the changes are going to come from the ground up," Luke Bronin, a former mayor who defeated 14-term Connecticut Representative John Larson in Tuesday's primary, said in his victory speech. "That's a message our party needs to hear."
The November elections will test whether the trends seen in Democratic primaries carry into general-election contests against Republicans. Beyond that looms the 2028 presidential race, when a new generation of leaders will compete to shape a changing Democratic Party.
Progressives are ascendant, but Wisconsin shows their limits Democratic socialist Francesca Hong hoped to ride the wave of recent progressive victories, including Abdul El-Sayed’s upset in neighboring Michigan's US Senate primary a week earlier, to the Democratic nomination for governor in Wisconsin.
Instead, she narrowly lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a more moderate Democrat who had dropped out of the race only to reenter in its final weeks and win the backing of outgoing Governor Tony Evers.
Hong's defeat also came after a number of her past comments resurfaced, including support for defunding the police and a call to cancel Thanksgiving that she said was a joke. And unlike El-Sayed, Hong did not receive the backing of some of the nation's most prominent progressive leaders, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Different outcomes for progressive candidates
The result illustrates a tension for the party's ascendant left flank.
Candidates running on populist economic messages have found growing success with Democratic voters. But some positions associated with the progressive movement’s recent past remain vulnerabilities — particularly among voters worried about electability in November.
That tension was evident on Tuesday for Sarah Atkins Hoggatt, 61, who said she agreed with Hong on issues including Medicare for All but worried that Hong’s deeply progressive politics and the democratic socialist label would make it harder for her to defeat Republican Tom Tiffany.
"I voted for someone who I think has a better chance" to beat Tiffany, said Atkins Hoggatt, who sells construction materials and drainage systems. She voted for Crowley.
"I didn't vote my heart," she said.
Progressives scored a much clearer victory in Minnesota, where Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan resoundingly defeated centrist Representative Angie Craig. Craig had the backing of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and several senators from battleground states.
Flanagan had her own powerful allies, including Sanders, Senator Elizabeth Warren and outgoing Minnesota Senator Tina Smith, who rallied with her in the campaign's final weeks.
Her campaign highlighted Craig's support from wealthy donors and criticised her vote for an immigration bill backed by President Donald Trump.
As in Michigan, the winning progressive candidate was significantly outspent.
"For months now, I have been telling you that this campaign was about the many versus the money," Flanagan said as she celebrated her victory in Minneapolis. "Well guess what? The many just won."
The contrasting results in Minnesota and Wisconsin mean the November general elections will provide another test of the candidates' electoral support beyond Democratic primary voters.
Flanagan is 46 years old. Crowley is 40. And El-Sayed is 41. But nowhere was generational change a more prominent campaign theme Tuesday than in Connecticut.
Bronin, 47, defeated the 78-year-old Larson. A central theme of Bronin's campaign was the need for a new generation of leadership in Washington, an argument that helped him win the state Democratic Party’s endorsement months before his decisive primary victory.
"The goal is to shake things up in Washington DC, and we are just getting started," Bronin said after his victory. He was a sophomore at Yale when Larson was first elected to Congress in 1998.
Larson became the seventh Democratic House incumbent to lose a primary this year, many of them to younger challengers. The defeated incumbents and the Democrats replacing them span ideological lines, making the wave of losses difficult to explain simply as a shift to the left.
The push for generational turnover has taken on greater urgency since Democrats' defeats in 2024, when concerns about President Joe Biden's age ultimately ended his reelection campaign and forced the party into an uncomfortable reckoning over a generation of leaders who had remained in power for decades.
Bronin himself has connected his challenge to that experience. Earlier this year, he argued that Democrats needed "new members of Congress, new Democratic leaders who have the energy and courage and clarity of mission that this moment demands."
That sentiment was evident among voters in Larson’s district as well. Dan Schnaidt, a 73-year-old Democrat, told The Associated Press months before the primary that he appreciated Larson's service but believed it was time to move on.
"It's time for new blood, for new ideas," Schnaidt said.
El-Sayed's win
The generational divide extends to the electorate. While Hong fell just short in Wisconsin, her performance also showed significant support among younger voters.
Cody Chandler, a 35-year-old software engineer, voted for Hong and called her "probably the most exciting candidate I've seen." Unlike in elections past, Chandler said, he voted for the candidate he most wanted to win rather than the one he considered most electable.
Jesse Heer, a 32-year-old Madison business owner, also backed Hong, citing her focus on affordability as the top reason for his vote.
That support showed up geographically. Hong won Madison, home to the University of Wisconsin’s flagship campus, by nearly 7 percentage points, though it wasn't a big enough of a margin to help her win the nomination.
A similar pattern was seen in El-Sayed's victory a week earlier in Michigan.
El-Sayed won Washtenaw County, home to the University of Michigan, by nearly 25 percentage points and Ingham County, home to Michigan State University, by 23 points. He also won Grand Rapids, with its large population of younger, college-educated voters, by nearly 26 points.
Jordan Snyder, a 20-year-old Michigan voter who supported El-Sayed, said she backed him because of his progressive positions and because she viewed him as trustworthy.
"People are feeling like a lot of the people that they've trusted that have been in government haven't really been living up to expectations," Snyder said.

Switzerland is a country of stunning landscapes and historic cities. In this episode, Lilly Douse explores one of Europe's most picturesque destinations.
Set in the heart of Europe, Switzerland welcomes millions of international visitors each year. The Alps cover 60% of the country, which is also home to more than 1,500 lakes.
Lilly starts her journey in Zurich, Switzerland’s largest city, known for its charming Old Town and beautiful lake.
Her first stop is the Polybahn, a historic funicular that has been carrying passengers up the hillside for over a century. At the top, she takes in panoramic views of the city.
The viewpoint sits next to ETH Zurich, one of Switzerland’s most prestigious universities. A centre for science and technology, it once taught Albert Einstein.
Zurich is home to more than 1,200 fountains and numerous public gardens. One of them is Lindenhof Tree Court, an ancient hilltop public square considered to be the birthplace of the city.
Zurich is also closely linked to one of Switzerland's famous exports, Swiss chocolate. Inside Switzerland’s Chocolate Museum, Lilly visits the world's largest chocolate fountain and learns how to make her own chocolate creation.
After exploring the city, Lilly takes a boat across Lake Lucerne and checks into the historic Bürgenstock Resort. The Qatari-owned resort sits 500 meters above the lake and can be reached by a 150-year-old funicular.
Lake Lucerne covers more than 100 square kilometres and is surrounded by mountains. Here, Lilly follows one of the popular hiking trails famous for its dramatic views.
Switzerland is a country of rich heritage and stunning natural beauty. With Zurich’s historic Old Town and its nearby lakes and mountains, the country offers the perfect mix of culture and Alpine luxury.

Josh Kushner, Bob Iger agree to buy Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5B: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:00:05 UTC
01:00:05 KST

Halis Sünnetci
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Billionaire investor Josh Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and former Disney CEO Bob Iger have agreed to buy the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion, ESPN reported Wednesday.
The price would set a record for the sale of a US sports franchise.
Kushner and Iger confirmed the agreement in a statement to ESPN.
“As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world. We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss,” it said. “Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles.”
The transaction requires approval from the NBA’s board of governors, which is due to meet next month in New York.
The agreement comes less than a year after Mark Walter acquired a controlling interest in the Lakers from the Buss family in a transaction that valued the NBA team at $10 billion.
Walter, the founder and CEO of holding company TWG Global, became the Lakers’ majority owner in October after the league approved the acquisition.
The sale would represent a $2.5 billion increase in the Lakers’ valuation in less than a year.
Kushner is the founder of venture capital firm Thrive Capital, which has backed major technology companies including Spotify, Instagram, Stripe and OpenAI.
Iger served as Disney’s chief executive from 2005 to 2020 and again from 2022 until earlier this year. He and his wife, Willow Bay, are controlling owners of the National Women’s Soccer League club Angel City FC.
The Lakers have won 17 NBA championships and are among the most valuable and widely recognized franchises in sports.

Mecca Agreement could be starting point for regional stability, security: Palestinian president
