Why the UK faces a prisons crisis amid row over release of cop killers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:23:34 UTC
23:23:34 KST

Why the UK faces a prisons crisis amid row over release of cop killers
The killers of Police Constable Andrew Harper had been set to partake in early release scheme as prison system stands on the verge of collapse.
The UK’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has become embroiled in a row about an early prison release scheme to alleviate overcrowding in England and Wales, which ignited furious public outcry when it emerged that two of the killers of Police Constable (PC) Andrew Harper could benefit from the plan.
Under the Sentencing Act 2026, which was passed under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, prisoners in England and Wales who are serving fixed, determinate sentences will be released as early as one-third of the way through their jail time in order to free up space. The scheme is set to begin in October this year.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Infantino sets deadline for FIFA offer in Kushner-backed World Cup plan
- list 2 of 3Police arrest dozens at London rally supporting Palestine Action
- list 3 of 3UK left-wing MP Diane Abbott reinstated by Labour Party after suspension
Prison services are devolved in Scotland and Northern Ireland, but are still centrally controlled in England and Wales.
Here is what we know about the row and why England and Wales are facing a prisons crisis.
What has Burnham said about prisons since taking over as prime minister?
Burnham, who took over as prime minister last month after Starmer’s ousting just two years after winning a landslide election, paused the early release scheme for review following public backlash over the news that some rapists and child-grooming convicts might be freed. The family of slain PC Andrew Harper, who was killed in 2019, also protested.
Harper died after being dragged by a car driven by the two killers who were escaping from a burglary. They were convicted of manslaughter.
Following this review, Burnham said on August 4 that the Sentencing Act would no longer apply to those guilty of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences. That brought the number of inmates eligible for early release to around 5,000, rather than the previously estimated 6,000. However, the exemptions do not include those convicted of manslaughter, as well as other charges.
Burnham has also moved the start date for the scheme back by one month to October, and has announced extra supervision of those released and more support for victims.
Adding the crime of manslaughter to the list of exclusions to prevent the release of PC Harper’s killers would result in blocking the early release of around 1,000 inmates, according to estimates published by British media.
While there have been calls to add manslaughter of an emergency worker as an exception, this is not a specific offence, and the government has said that such an amendment would not be legally feasible.
Experts say the British prison system is on the verge of collapse, as it has one of the highest imprisonment rates in Western Europe, and successive governments have grappled with unpopular options to solve the emergency.
Burnham has vowed to take concerns on board, but ultimately, he said he would see the policy through. “I am doing all I can,” he wrote on X. “But it is simply not possible to prevent all offenders from being released early without the prison system collapsing.”
What happened to PC Andrew Harper?
Twenty-eight-year-old PC Harper from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, was killed in 2019, just four weeks after getting married, as he responded to reports of a burglary. As three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire, his ankle became caught in the getaway car’s tow-rope loop, and he was dragged along a country road for more than a mile (1.8km), suffering fatal injuries.
Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, two of his killers who were convicted of manslaughter, were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Under usual rules, they would have to serve at least two-thirds of their sentences before they could be considered for release.
Under the new scheme, however, they would be eligible for release in June 2027, just halfway through their sentences.
A third killer, Henry Long, was given a longer sentence, which requires his case to be seen by the Parole Board before any release can be granted.
The police officer’s widow, Lissie Harper, has pleaded for Cole and Bowers to be denied early release. Chris Bushnell, a former police dog handler who was at the scene of PC Harper’s death, told media in the United Kingdom that he was “shaking” when he was informed that the officer’s killers might be eligible under the scheme.
Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC she was in “turmoil” over the conflicting reports that Cole and Bowers could be eligible for release next year.
Some 900,000 people have signed a petition to prevent the killers’ early release. On Wednesday, 50 police chiefs also signed a letter urging Burnham to pursue every legal option to prevent their release.
How has PM Burnham responded to this case?
Andy Burnham is under increasing pressure to block the release of the killers of PC Harper, and is reportedly actively seeking ways to be able to do this.
On social media, the prime minister said he fully appreciated the “anguish” felt by Harper’s family and said the scheme could be mitigated by expanding prison places in other ways, including removing foreign offenders more quickly and repurposing some women’s prisons for male offenders.
“However, I recognise that, even with all these changes, there will be concerns from many victims about who will still be released early for other offences,” Burnham said on Tuesday.
He added that he was “confident” that the release of the most serious offenders, including Harper’s killers, could be prevented. However, it remains unclear how he intends to do that.
Why is there a prisons crisis in the UK?
Britain’s prisons are nearing the breaking point, experts say, while the prison population is projected to keep rising.
According to the Institute for Government, an independent British think tank, the prison population has doubled over the past 30 years despite falling crime rates. This is largely due to longer sentences being passed and a growing number of people being recalled to prison following release.
As a result, men’s prisons are currently 97 percent full, according to the think tank. Building new prisons would not solve the problem in time, given that it can take an average of seven years to construct and open a new, operational facility, with projects often suffering delays. Additionally, lack of adequate staffing is a long-running problem for British jails.
The think tank said public campaigns calling for the creation of new offences or the introduction of longer sentences have also contributed to the overcrowding.
In 2020, the Conservative government led by Prime Minister Boris Johnson increased the length of sentences for certain serious offences by one-third, while in 2022, the Conservative government of PM Rishi Sunak did the same for a wider group of offences, despite there not being enough capacity in prisons to absorb the increase.
According to independent UK charity Prison Reform Trust, years of rising sentence lengths have driven the prison population close to the limits of available capacity.
“The current crisis is the result of successive governments relying increasingly on imprisonment, while population growth has outpaced the construction of new prison places,” Alex Hewson, the charity’s senior policy and communications officer, told Al Jazeera.
Research conducted by the organisation found that between 2024 and 2025, almost three-quarters of prisons (72 percent) in England and Wales were overcrowded. More than 21,600 people – one-quarter of the prison population – were being held in overcrowded accommodation.
The Howard League, a British charity advocating for penal reform, said overcrowding, coupled with chronic staff shortages, means prisons cannot engage everyone in activities that help rehabilitation. This means more people are locked in an overcrowded cell for 23 hours a day with nothing to do, raising the risk of self-harm, violence and reoffending.
What is Burnham’s government doing about this?
Under the Sentencing Act 2026, up to 5,000 inmates serving a standard prison sentence will be eligible to be released earlier than their originally set date.
According to the new rules, prisoners convicted of less serious offences who would have been expected to serve 40 percent or 50 percent of their sentence in prison will be eligible to leave after having completed one-third of their sentence. A second group, currently set to be released after two-thirds of their sentence is served, will leave after half.
Being released does not end the sentence. Those convicted continue to serve the rest of their sentence in the community, under conditions set by probation, and can be recalled to prison if those conditions are breached.
Hewson, at Prison Reform Trust, said these changes are expected to provide “the single biggest reduction in demand for prison places”.
“With places projected to run out in the autumn [September through November], there are no easy alternatives waiting in the wings,” he added.
“Other options, such as tackling growth in the recall population, reducing the use of remand, or making greater use of community-based alternatives to custody, could also help, but none offers an immediate solution on the scale required,” Hewson continued.
“In the long term, the only sustainable answer is a justice system that reserves prison for the most serious cases, reverses decades of sentence inflation, and does more to reduce reoffending in the community.”

Iran is not anti-imperialist. It is a state calculating survival

Iran is not anti-imperialist. It is a state calculating survival
Regardless of its current hostile rhetoric, the Islamic Republic will likely reach a settlement with the US and Israel.
More than five months into the US-Israel war on Iran, the prospects for a deal that would end the confrontation remain unclear. Earlier this week, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were no direct negotiations with the United States.
Meanwhile, hostile rhetoric and calls for revenge continue to emanate from Tehran. Some Western commentators, especially on the right, have claimed that Iran is incapable of striking a deal because of its anti-American ideology. But that is a flawed assumption.
One just needs to look at the Iranian constitution and its recent history to discover that the Islamic Republic is not governed solely by ideology. The regime, in its present form, would not shy away from reaching a settlement with the US and even Israel, if it fell in line with its guiding principle: regime survival.
The limits of Iranian anti-imperialism
In January 1988, Iranian Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini settled an internal dispute over the scope of velayat-e faqih, the guardianship of the Islamic jurist, by declaring that the Islamic government ranks above all other rulings of Islam, including prayer, fasting and pilgrimage. The following month, he ordered the creation of a body to resolve deadlocks between the parliament and the Guardian Council by determining what was in the interest of the governing system.
The revisions to the constitution in 1989 gave it a permanent place as Article 112: the Council for Discerning the Expediency of the System.
The message was explicit. Preservation of the system — hefz-e nezam — was the highest religious obligation, and an organ was established to license departures from religious law whenever the system required them.
In the following years, this principle was clearly applied in how the Islamic Republic deployed official ideology, including its hostility towards Washington and Tel Aviv.
Today Tehran presents its anti-imperialist doctrine as a moral commitment grounded in opposition to domination, colonialism and Western hegemony. That self-presentation has earned it sympathy well beyond its borders, including among people who acknowledge its repression at home while treating it as an indispensable pillar of resistance abroad.
But Iran’s anti-imperialism is positional rather than universal. It opposes domination when the Islamic Republic is the object of it, but it has not consistently opposed domination as a political relationship.
The doctrine of “forward defence” has often treated Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Palestine as arenas in which Tehran deters enemies, projects power and acquires leverage. The anti-imperialist principle is therefore applied selectively.
Iran invokes sovereignty and self-determination when resisting external interference in its own affairs, while its regional strategy has often compromised those same principles elsewhere by subordinating other societies to its own security interests.
This behaviour is not peculiar to Iran, nor does it make Iran uniquely cynical. Realist theory has long held that survival is the primary end of states, from which other objectives are derived. On that reading, Iran is not an aberration. It is an ordinary state with an unusually elaborate justificatory apparatus.
That is exactly the point, and it is what makes a bargain thinkable.
The Islamic Republic’s commitments operate on two levels. Enmity towards the US and Israel, support for allied movements and the rejection of accommodation all guide policy. Above them sits a second-order norm that determines when the first-order commitments may be revised. That norm is hefz-e nezam, and Article 112 is its institutional expression.
Survival is the core; anti-imperialism is the protective belt, and belts can be loosened.
A settlement with the enemy
The Islamic Republic speaks the language of principle honoured regardless of cost while governing by calculation of consequence. That gap is not hypocrisy so much as a structural feature of any state that rules in a doctrine’s name, but it leaves a standing problem. It must compromise without appearing to have compromised.
The record shows how this is possible. In July 1988, Khomeini accepted the ceasefire with Iraq, saying publicly that doing so was more lethal to him than poison.
During that war, with the immediate danger coming from Saddam Hussein rather than the “Great Satan”, Tehran accepted American weapons routed through Israeli channels and entered secret dealings with Washington in what eventually would be known as the Iran-Contra affair. After the 9/11 attacks and the US invasion of Afghanistan, Iranian and American diplomats cooperated at the Bonn conference to shape the post-Taliban government.
None of this made Iran pro-American or pro-Israeli, and none of it shows that its doctrine was decorative. It shows that apparently absolute prohibitions have an off-switch, and that the switch is labelled survival.
This year the mechanism has operated under far greater strain. Strikes by the US and Israel on February 28 killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the first day of a war whose declared aims included forcing regime change in Tehran. Within days, the Assembly of Experts for Leadership installed his son Mojtaba in a hereditary succession that the republic’s own doctrine disparages — another first-order norm surrendered to protect the core.
On June 17, President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU), which included an end to hostilities, sanctions relief, access to frozen funds and reconstruction support. Mojtaba Khamenei endorsed it in writing while recording his misgivings. Again, the core held, but the belt was loosened.
The memorandum left much unresolved, and renewed fighting exposed its fragility. But its existence remains significant. Under existential pressure, the Islamic Republic accepted direct arrangements with Washington and made confrontation itself negotiable.
How can a state enter such an arrangement without renouncing the identity that legitimises it? Not by announcing that anti-imperialism has been abandoned, but by revising what it means. Ali Khamenei supplied the vocabulary in 2013 when he spoke of “heroic flexibility”, invoking a wrestler who gives ground without forgetting his opponent’s capabilities. Concession becomes strategic patience, and retreat becomes the preservation of the struggle.
Supporters largely follow, and not out of confusion. Where an institution interprets its own doctrine, that doctrine cannot constrain it, and a follower who defers to the leader’s reading is applying the principle as the system defines it. So the leadership can cross its own red line without losing its base, because much of the base crosses along with it.
The MoU follows the same logic. Anti-imperialism was not abandoned but reinterpreted as preserving Iran’s capacity to resist under changed conditions.
The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action signed in 2015 had already framed negotiation not as surrender but as another means of defending Iran’s interests. The same logic could support a future settlement involving the US and, indirectly, Israel, without recognition or reconciliation, if mutual restraint is judged better for the system’s survival than continued confrontation.
An agreement with the enemy reduces the risk of war and eases economic strangulation, both of which matter enormously to ordinary Iranians. But relief abroad does not mechanically produce liberty at home.
The state has already invoked wartime conditions to expand arrests, expedite prosecutions and accelerate executions. That repressive apparatus was not built by sanctions and will not be dismantled by their removal. Sanctions relief may ease hardship for Iranians, but without political reform it could also leave the state with greater resources to sustain the institutions of repression.
Therefore, the usual debate offers a false choice between confrontation that breaks the Islamic Republic and diplomacy that moderates it. A third and more likely possibility is already visible: an accommodation with the US that preserves the system but brings it no closer to democracy. One form of domination eased, another consolidated. Iran better protected from foreign attack; Iranians no less exposed to their own state.
Anyone still asking whether the Islamic Republic would trade its enmities for its survival should read Article 112 again. The answer has been in the constitution since 1989.

6 must-watch matchups that could play key role in setting the 2026 College Football Playoff field
From early-season heavyweight clashes to conference rivalry games, the road to the College Football Playoff could come down to a handful of marquee matchups. Here are six must-watch games that could shape the playoff race in 2026:
Ohio State at Texas, Sept. 12
Steve Sarkisian and Ryan Day match wits again as both teams get an early-season measuring stick game after failing to meet expectations in 2025. A Week 1 loss to the Buckeyes left the Longhorns fighting an uphill battle with little room for error throughout the rest of the season. Texas ultimately fell short of the 12-team CFP while the Buckeyes lost their last two games, the latter in the CFP quarterfinals.
Julian Sayin vs. Arch Manning will get the headlines but last year’s 14-7 win by Ohio State is a reminder that the best-prepared defense may rule the day. The Buckeyes are reloading on defense — including three spots on the line — while Texas has four of its starting o-linemen back.
Both teams have stacked schedules — Texas faces the likes of Tennessee, Ole Miss, LSU and Texas A&M and Ohio State has Indiana, Oregon, USC and Michigan — so a win here helps set the tone.
LSU at Ole Miss, Sept. 19
One of the most intriguing games of the year, an emotionally charged revenge game on paper for Ole Miss, as Lane Kiffin returns to Oxford for the first time since his awkward departure for LSU last December. Trinidad Chambliss is a Heisman contender again for the Rebels. Will Leavitt says he couldn’t be happier after transferring in for the Tigers.
Besides the obvious tension, the matchup could help shape the playoff race early. As contenders but not necessarily favorites in the SEC, Ole Miss and LSU could find themselves fighting for an at-large bid. A win here could make all the difference come playoff selection time, especially with both teams facing schedules that leave little room for error.
Georgia at Alabama, Oct. 10
The SEC’s two most dominant programs over the past decade meet in Tuscaloosa, with plenty of recent history hanging over the matchup. Georgia had its 33-game home winning streak snapped by Alabama with a 24-21 defeat in 2025, but the Bulldogs later got revenge with an SEC championship game rout.
Both teams now enter the season with plenty at stake. Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer faces pressure to keep the Crimson Tide in national title contention following Ty Simpson’s departure for the NFL. Kirby Smart looks to finally secure a regular-season win against Alabama. This one could have major implications beyond just SEC standings.
Ohio State at Indiana, Oct. 17
Indiana was untouchable in 2025, as coach Curt Cignetti and a haul of transfers — including quarterback Fernando Mendoza — put together a perfect 16-0 season and claim the Hossiers’ first national title. The final four wins were a murderer’s row: Ohio State, Alabama, Oregon and Miami.
It will be difficult to go through the Big Ten unscathed. A road win here would reassert the Buckeyes as a top dog in a rugged conference.
Miami at Notre Dame, Nov. 7
It’s safe to assume grudges are still being held in South Bend after Miami beat the Fighting Irish in the opener and then finished ahead of Notre Dame in the rankings to claim a playoff spot this past season.
Both teams enter the season with extra motivation to win it all and rosters capable of pulling it off. While Miami can return to the playoff by winning an Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC) title, this is one of the few statement-making opportunities for the Irish, who have a relatively low strength of schedule.
BYU at Utah, Nov. 7
Morgan Scalley’s debut season as Utah coach will include an edition of the Holy War that could play a big role (again) in the Big 12 race and the playoff berths available the first week of December. There’s new staff in place and new faces, too, including two replacements for NFL draft picks on the offensive line.
BYU held on to coach Kalani Sitake, has quarterback Bear Bachmeier and RB LJ Martin back, and is coming off a 12-2 season loaded with big wins and only a pair of losses to Texas Tech. The Cougars will be itching to erase that runner-up finish and crack the CFP.
Honorable mention
Oklahoma at Michigan (Sept. 12), Houston at Texas Tech (Sept. 19), SMU at Louisville (Sept. 19), MIami at Clemson (Oct. 3), USC at Penn State (Oct. 10), Texas at Texas A&M (Nov. 27).

Mini-Mozart heist blights anniversary tribute as thieves make off with 210 statuettes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Mini-Mozart heist blights anniversary tribute as thieves make off with 210 statuettes
SALZBURG, Austria (AP) — More than 200 gold statuettes of Austria’s most famous composer disappeared from his hometown of Salzburg, officials said Wednesday, leaving a tribute to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart on his 270th birthday considerably less crowded.
The Mozarteum Foundation on July 15 unveiled 320 statuettes, barely 50 centimeters (less than 20 inches) high, showing Mozart with his dog. They were designed by German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl.
Within two weeks, more than 80 of the polymer figures had disappeared. By Wednesday, a total of 210 were missing.
“The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves,” Hörl told the German news agency dpa. He said he did not believe visitors stole the works but rather that it was an “organized theft.”
Hörl intended to sell the statues for about 100 euros ($114) once the exhibition was over, meaning whoever ran away with 210 mini-Mozarts has not become an overnight millionaire.
The mini-Mozarts populated not only the garden of the composer’s former house, but also his living quarters as well as several pavilions.
While the organizers put aside some spare statuettes in case of theft, there were too few to compensate for the actual losses. And in a further stroke of bad luck, the manufacturer of the statues was away on holidays, so there was no quick fix.
The exhibition of statuettes, now more widely spaced, is scheduled to remain on display until Aug. 30.
For Hörl, who is known from his sculptures made from polymer, the theft of his artworks is nothing new. At an installation in Bayreuth, Germany, a complete array of statues of Richard Wagner was stolen within 10 days.
“That’s just the nature of public space. That means when you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn’t complain about what is happening there,” Hörl said. “It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is.”
Mozart was born on Jan. 27, 1756, in Salzburg, where the Mozarteum Foundation offers concerts, maintains Mozart museums and supports research on him.
“I didn’t want to do a monument of Mozart. There are already enough of these. But I wanted to show his human side, that he was a normal human being despite his genius,” Hörl told The Associated Press.
To give the statues a human touch, Hörl depicted the composer with his favorite dog, Pimperl. Mozart and his family were known to take long walks with their dogs in the Mirabell Garden, next to where they lived.

Google unveils latest Pixel phones with slimmer cameras and more AI features
Google on Wednesday unveiled its latest lineup of Pixel phones, with slimmer cameras that include more a powerful zoom and artificial intelligence features designed to help users accomplish things with fewer taps and swipes.
With the improvements, the search giant hopes to give users a reason to buy new models and expand the number of people using its AI tools.
“Google continues to tout new software features, primarily around AI, as the reason to upgrade,” said Forrester senior analyst Andrew Cornwall. He noted the company has added a way to extract photos from videos, a teleprompter, video stabilization, and an improved speech-to-text feature.
While the Pixel phones are not as popular as Apple’s iPhone, Google has been steadily increasing the amount of AI on its Pixel phones since 2023.
Apple, meanwhile, has been lagging behind. It announced new AI advances in June, focusing on how the technology can help with people’s day-to-day lives, with a focus on privacy and security — using Google’s Gemini AI model to do so.
Google said in a presentation to reporters last week that the new phones will double the previous storage size, starting at 256 gigabytes, and feature 30 hours of battery life and faster wireless charging. The company has eliminated the 128 gigabyte Pixel 11, which had been its lowest-priced option at $800.
Beginning Wednesday, U.S. customers can order the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL, starting at $900, $1,100 and $1,300, respectively. The Pixel Pro Fold, meanwhile, starts at $1,900. That’s a $100 increase for each phone from last year’s prices.
New features include live translation for videos, podcasts and voice messages. In the Pro models, a tool called HiLight lets you assign a color to your favorite contacts and have the phone light up in that color when they call and your phone is placed face down. It complements Pixel’s “Flip to Shhh” feature that puts the phone in “do not disturb” mode when it is placed face down.
Google is also offering a free six-month subscription to its AI Pro plan to anyone who buys the more expensive Pixel 11 Pro or Pixel 11 Pro XL models. The company is hoping to hook more people on the AI Gemini tool kit, which it assembled to compete against OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
Camera upgrades include a new mode called Magic Capture, which automatically takes a series of photos and video with a single tap of the shutter button. Google said the cameras also feature improved light sensitivity and, for Pro models, Instant Night Sight captures shots in dark environments faster, so you don’t have to hold your phone still while waiting for exposure.
Google also introduced a tracking device for the first time. Called Pixel Tag, it will cost $30 for one or $100 for a four-pack and is compatible with phones running Android 9 or higher.

Hungary’s government plans interventions on Danube River to keep nuclear plant running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:23:01 UTC
23:23:01 KST

Hungary’s government plans interventions on Danube River to keep nuclear plant running
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Authorities in Hungary will begin taking steps to raise the level of the Danube River this week in order to ensure the country’s only nuclear power plant can continue operating, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Wednesday.
Persistent drought and successive extreme heat waves in recent months have deprived one of Europe’s largest rivers of water, bringing Danube levels to record lows and pushing the Paks nuclear power plant to the brink of shutting down for the first time in its 44-year history.
The Soviet-built plant, which uses water from the Danube to cool its four reactors, is currently operating at little more than 10% of its 2,000 megawatt capacity due to low water levels. It supplies Hungary with around a third of its electricity.
In a video posted to Facebook on Wednesday, Magyar said authorities would begin building a bed sill — a low concrete or stone structure built into the riverbed to slow the current and raise upstream water levels — on Thursday on a section of the Danube just upriver from the plant.
Delivery of some 145,000 cubic meters of rocks used in its construction would begin on Wednesday evening, Magyar said, adding that the intervention could raise the level of the Danube by up to a meter (3 feet).
Meanwhile, two 80-meter (262-foot) barges will be transported to the site near Paks and may be sunk in order to raise the Danube up to a further 20 centimeters (8 inches) at the plant’s cooling pumps. A decision on whether to sink them will be made on Friday, Magyar said.
“We can no longer consider this extraordinary situation as a one-time natural extreme,” he said, adding that the work must be carried out quickly to avoid a full Paks shutdown.
Magyar referred to the construction of the bed sill as a “long-term” solution which could ensure that water levels never fall below the threshold at which reactors at Paks must be powered down.
He said that after a recent temporary rise in water levels, they were expected to begin falling again in coming days which, without external intervention, could lead to the complete shutdown of the Paks plant.
“The Danube has given us days, not months,” he said.
Similar measures were taken in Romania last week when authorities sank four barges laden with rock into the Danube in an attempt to redirect water downstream toward the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which had already shut down one of its two reactors due to low water levels.
On Wednesday, Magyar said the Paks plant operating at its current output is costing Hungary’s economy up to 50 billion forints ($158 million) per month. By contrast, he said the planned interventions on the Danube will cost around 6 billion forints ($19 million).

Burnham to consider ban on disposable barbecues as wildfires rage in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:20:10 UTC
23:20:10 KST

The government will look at banning disposable barbecues as wildfires continue to rage across the UK, Andy Burnham has said.
Disposable barbecues have been the cause of a number of serious fires over the last few years, but campaigners were critical of the prime minister’s failure to link those fires more broadly to the climate crisis.
In July this year, firefighters called to Cannock Chase found an area the size of a football field blazing in the summer heat. The heathland in Sherbrook Valley, part of a special area of conservation, was home to adders, toads and other wildlife, which were thought to have suffered severe damage, though no people were harmed. The cause of the fire was identified as a disposable barbecue.
This was one of two fires in the area that were particularly concerning, Staffordshire council officials said, because Cannock Chase is home to protected wildlife, including ground-nesting nightjars. Fires can destroy nests, chicks and vital heathland habitat, causing damage that can take many years to recover from.
Disposable barbecues, which can be carried into public areas, present a number of problems: they remain hot, sometimes for hours, after they are used, making them extremely difficult to dispose of safely, and when they cannot be carried away, people are forced to leave them or place them into bins where they carry on smouldering.
Burying the barbecues, as some try to do, will not stop the danger as these trays of charcoal can reach 450C and will carry on burning underground, where they can still ignite fires long after use. On beaches, the buried coals and metal grills are also a hazard for walkers, and in fields for farm animals.
Over the last few years they have been identified as the cause of a number of serious fires including:
- 
  Macclesfield, Cheshire, July 2026: a large woodland fire that was tackled by dozens of firefighters. Cheshire fire and rescue service said a discarded barbecue was the probable cause
- 
  Three separate fires in one day around London, July 2026: in Feltham, 6 hectares of heathland close to houses were damaged. The London fire brigade urged people not to use disposable barbecues and to properly extinguish cigarettes after crews tackled three grass fires.
- 
  The Trossachs, Scotland, May 2025: covered 2 hectares in the Glen Finglas region of the national park. Glen Finglas is the biggest Woodland Trust site in the UK. The barbecue understood to have sparked that fire was found with a burger still on the grill.
The National Farmers’ Union is now calling for a ban. Although Burnham has said he may consider a ban, government ministers have been set against such measures.
Jon Pearce, the Labour MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, 50 miles from Cannock Chase, has been working on ways to bring forward a partial restriction on the devices in legislation, which would avoid some of the problems of a blanket ban.
He said: “It is hugely welcome that the prime minister has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues. He is right that the message needs to go out loud and clear that people should not be using disposable barbecues in public places at this time.
“But we need to be in a better place next summer. Last year was the worst on record for wildfires. This year will surpass it. We need to accept our climate has changed and put in place measures to adapt, and one of those is banning the use of disposable barbecues in public places.”
Portable barbecues could be exempt, he said, as they were taken away after use. “The irony of ‘disposable barbecues’ is that they are actually very difficult to dispose of. They can cause bin fires, and unless you stay around for a long time until it has totally cooled down, there is still a fire risk.”
Other igniters for fire include lightning strikes, carelessly tossed cigarettes, campfires, rubbish and bottles. But it is clear that disposable barbecues pose particular problems. Research for the government published last year found more than 1,600 fires were caused by barbecues in England from 2020 to 2024, though it did not specify whether those barbecues were disposable, and the cause of a majority of the nearly 4,500 fires listed was put down as unknown.
The Greenpeace political campaigner Angharad Hopkinson said: “To truly protect the public, the government must also address the fossil-fuelled elephant in the room that is driving extreme temperatures. The climate crisis is staring us in the face, threatening our national security and straining our resilience to breaking point.
“Burnham has acknowledged the dangers of these conditions by convening Cobra; now he must match that urgency with a real long-term plan to end our reliance on fossil fuels – the ultimate driver of climate change – once and for all.”

PYONGYANG, August 12. /TASS/. North Korea intends to develop the capabilities to strike back in the event of a threat to its security as South Korea implements its nuclear submarine program, First Deputy Foreign Minister Jang Kum-chol said.

Jang Kum-chol also linked South Korea’s plans with the US policy in the region. According to him, Seoul's acquisition of nuclear submarines may become a preparatory stage for turning military cooperation between the United States, Japan and South Korea into "a second AUKUS."

‘Probably most severe weather event that any of us here can remember’: 3 dead, 800,000 without power in US Midwest

Berk Kutay Gokmen
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
At least three people were killed, and nearly 800,000 customers lost power as severe storms swept across the US Midwest on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Two deaths occurred in the state of Indiana; one person died in a suspected weather-related house explosion in Portage, while a boy, 4, was killed when a tree fell on his home in Jennings County, according to NBC News.
“Contributions are probably wind and the storms that came through this county earlier today,” Jennings County Chief Sheriff’s Deputy Cody Low said about the child’s death.
Another person died in Roseville, Ohio, after emergency crews were unable to reach the victim, said Gov. Mike DeWine. A state of emergency was declared following widespread flooding, with flash flood warnings affecting 16 million people Wednesday.
In Portage, severe weather and trees blocking roads delayed firefighters responding to the house fire. Police Capt. Rob Maynard described the storms as “probably the most severe weather event that any of us here can remember.”
Sixteen inmates at a prison in Grafton, Ohio, were taken to hospitals after lightning struck as they returned from dinner; one was airlifted, said authorities.
The National Weather Service confirmed two tornadoes near Chicago, both producing EF1-level damage. Nearly 800,000 customers in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky remained without power Wednesday morning. Most of them in Ohio and Indiana.
Utility provider AEP said the Columbus, Ohio, area experienced gusts of more than 80 mph (129 km/h) and trees falling on power lines. It said it had more than 2,000 workers trying to restore electricity, including crews from other states.

A video recently released by the Russian Defense Ministry features a female drone pilot reporting the details of a successful battle against Ukrainian forces. Women are being increasingly accepted for combat roles in the country, marking a shift in gender roles.
The short clip published on Monday showed a first-person-view drone operator named Yekaterina, whom the ministry described as a “delicate girl with an iron character.” She explained the role that short-range unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) played in the liberation of Belitskoye, a town in the Donetsk People’s Republic, that Russian forces reportedly completed three weeks ago.
The ministry previously said the battle required coordinated efforts by multiple drone units supporting assault troops. It produced several similar videos praising pilots who participated in the operation.
Women have been accepted in the Russian armed forces for decades, but most of them served as communications and logistic specialists or medics. Nurses operating close to the front line are regularly exemplified for their courage.
During World War II however, a wide range of combat roles were open to women, producing notable examples like acclaimed sniper Lyudmila Pavlichenko and the all-female pilots of the night bomber regiment known as the Night Witches.
The mass introduction of drones during the Ukraine conflict and the creation of dedicated Unmanned Systems Troops within the armed forces has apparently shifted Russian generals’ attitude to female troops.
In March, the military’s official publication, Krasnaya Zvezda, printed an article about the life journey of a female drone pilot with the callsign Bayana. A childhood fan of radio-controlled cars and planes, she enlisted in a private military company in 2024 to pursue her chosen career as a drone ace, the report said. The option to enroll in Russian UAV forces has since been opened for women.

Fatboy Slim will perform in Estonia for the first time in November
Dance music legend Fatboy Slim will perform on November 21 at the Põhjala factory in Tallinn. The artist, appearing in Estonia for the first time, chose the concert venue himself.
Fatboy Slim, whose legal name is Quentin Leo Cook, is a pioneer of dance music whose career took off in the early 1990s. The DJ from the United Kingdom is one of the trailblazers of the big beat genre, and his work played a major role in bringing electronic dance music into the mainstream.
He began his musical path in 1985, not behind a DJ booth but as a bassist in an indie band. Three years later the band broke up, and Cook bought his first controller, synthesizer and sampler. Around the same time he released his first remixes, and "Dub Be Good to Me," released in 1990 by the sound system collective Beats International, which included Cook, reached the top of the charts. Two years later the collective disbanded.
The musician decided to try his hand as a guitarist in an acid jazz band, but he quickly realized he was a poor guitarist. That was followed by Pizzaman, a house music duo with John Reid. Three songs from their only album, "Pizzamania," reached the charts. In 1995 he started the Fatboy Slim project, and the debut album "Better Living Through Chemistry" was released in 1996.
A turning point in Fatboy Slim's career came in 1998 with the release of his second album, "You've Come a Long Way, Baby," which included songs such as "Praise You," "Right Here, Right Now" and "The Rockafeller Skank." He has released four studio albums as Fatboy Slim, the most recent being "Palookaville" in 2004.

Newer drones haven’t dethroned the FPV, and Russia fears our bomber drones, Ukrainian commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:16:29 UTC
23:16:29 KST

Ukraine's first-person-view (FPV) drones are not being displaced by newer unmanned systems, a Ukrainian officer told Ukrinform. They remain a central tool for precision strikes, while Ukrainian forces claim a separate advantage in larger bomber drones.
Unmanned systems have become a defining weapon of Russia's war against Ukraine, and both sides race to out-innovate each other, a contest in which a cheap UAV can down a platform costing dozens of times more.
FPVs remain central
"Since FPVs appeared in service, they have become a leading means of precision engagement. This trend will continue," said Captain Anton Bobrovskyi, who commands a company training unmanned-systems specialists at the 199th Training Center of the Air Assault Forces.
Bobrovskyi conceded that Russia also uses drones effectively and that Ukraine learns from it, but said Ukraine keeps a lead in one category: bomber drones.
Ukrainian drone that downed Russia’s rarest spy UAV just bagged its anti-drone interceptor too
Ukraine's bomber-drone advantage
Russian forces fear Ukrainian bomber drones, according to Bobrovskyi. He said Ukraine outmatches Russia many times over in such systems, and that Russian troops who encounter one often do not know what to do with it.
The distinction matters because bomber drones work differently from single-use FPVs. Rather than flying into a target and exploding, larger bomber drones carry and release munitions, then fly on. Euromaidan Press has documented the growing role of these systems, including reusable platforms capable of returning to base after dropping their payloads. Developers have also adapted them to fly through Russian electronic warfare, with upgraded Vampire drones built to resist jamming.
Bobrovskyi said Ukraine's advantage does not mean Russia lacks comparable technology. Instead, he argued that Ukrainian forces and society initiated many of the current battlefield drone trends and have kept the initiative in using them.
Each new drone class draws a countermeasure, so the side that keeps iterating fastest holds the battlefield initiative. How long Ukraine's bomber-drone edge lasts will depend on its ability to keep protecting and upgrading those platforms.

Around 700 flights canceled at Italy’s Catania airport due to Mount Etna eruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:13:25 UTC

Necva Tastan Sevinc
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
By Necva Tastan Sevinc
ISTANBUL (AA) — Around 700 flights have been canceled at Catania airport on the Italian island of Sicily due to Mount Etna’s ongoing eruption and the release of volcanic ash, local media reported Wednesday.
Between Aug. 8 and 11, around 400 departing flights were canceled, while another 52 cancellations were scheduled for Wednesday, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
More than 250 flights were redirected to other airports, including over 100 to Comiso, around 50 to Palermo on Tuesday alone and another 22 to Trapani.
SAC, the company that manages Catania airport, said all arriving and departing flights had been suspended until 4 pm local time (1400GMT) Thursday because of volcanic ash in the atmosphere.
The closure of airspace sectors affected by the ash cloud was also extended, it added.
Passengers were urged to check the status of their flights with their airlines before traveling to the airport.
Comiso airport, in the province of Ragusa, has meanwhile resumed full operations after temporarily suspending flights due to ash contamination.
The disruption comes at the height of Sicily’s summer tourism season, affecting thousands of residents and visitors.
Italian Civil Protection Minister Nello Musumeci said the latest disruption had revived long-standing concerns over Catania airport’s vulnerability due to its proximity to Mount Etna.
Mount Etna, located on Sicily’s eastern coast, is among the world’s most active volcanoes.

China’s C919 makes first international flight as it takes aim at Boeing and Airbus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:11:18 UTC
23:11:18 KST

China’s homegrown C919 passenger jet has finally ventured beyond the country’s borders, making its first scheduled international flight from Beijing to Mongolia.
China’s C919 jet has officially left home soil for the first time, taking its first scheduled international passenger flight from Beijing to Mongolia.
The milestone marks a major step for China’s homegrown answer to Boeing and Airbus, although the jet still has plenty to prove before it can seriously challenge the aviation giants overseas.
According to flight tracker FlightRadar24 the flight, operated by Air China, took off from Beijing Capital International Airport and touched down around two hours later in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia.
The flight is the latest step in China’s plan to establish the state-owned Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China, aka COMAC.
It hopes it will act as a direct competitor in a global field currently dominated by United States-based Boeing and Europe’s Airbus.
Currently, though, the C919 still uses foreign components and it has also not been able to secure certification from major aviation regulators in Europe or the US, meaning it’s very limited in its ability to win over customers.
COMAC had initially aimed to have its jets entirely made in China by 2025 and to capture 10% of the country’s domestic market, but those goals have since passed.
The airline hopes the Beijing to Ulaanbaatar service will eventually operate daily and has been showing off its planes to the industry, most notably at the Dubai Airshow last November.
Are COMAC’s offerings realistic challengers to existing jets?
The C919 can carry up to 174 passengers and is a similar single-aisle narrow-body set up to Boeing’s 737 MAX and Airbus’s A320neo.
As of now, China’s domestic airlines still rely on Boeing and Airbus aircraft and, in May, the nation ordered 200 of the former’s planes, as well as spare parts and engines, so it’s clear that there’s a need for western technology as COMAC gears up to fly.
According to CNBC, COMAC delivered 32 C919s by the end of last year, and a further eight in the first half of 2026.
That’s a tiny amount compared to about 100 narrow-body Airbuses delivered to China in 2025 alone, and also far away from COMAC’s goal of producing 200 of its planes every year by 2029.
There’s also the fact that building the plane is only half the battle. COMAC also needs to prove it can make enough C919s and keep them running reliably once they’re in the air.
That means strengthening its supply chain, increasing production and making sure everything from engines to tiny components is readily available. Even a shortage of one small part can bring production to a halt.
For now, the C919 still has a long way to go before it can take on Boeing and Airbus globally. But its first international commercial flight is a significant step for China’s aviation industry, and one that could mark the beginning of a much bigger challenge to the world’s two biggest plane makers.

====================================================================================================

Will MENA follow UAE's lead on social media bans for under-15s?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:09:59 UTC
23:09:59 KST

Breadcrumb
MENA social media bans: Can governments protect children without expanding surveillance?
From Canberra to Paris, governments are increasingly turning to social media restrictions and age verification systems in an attempt to protect children online.
Australia became the first country in the world to prohibit children under 16 from accessing several major social media platforms, while France has since passed legislation banning children under 15 from using social media, with implementation due to begin later this year.
In the UK, Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced plans in June to introduce similar restrictions that would prevent children under 16 from accessing platforms including Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, X, and Facebook by 2027.
But in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), where online spaces have long been shaped by government regulation, censorship and surveillance concerns, experts warn that child safety measures could take on a very different meaning.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) became the first Arab and Muslim-majority country to prohibit children under 15 from creating or operating personal social media accounts.
The UAE government said the policy aims to address concerns over children's exposure to inappropriate content, unsafe online interactions, excessive social media use and the collection of personal data.
Authorities have also been empowered to "take all necessary measures [against platforms] in the event of non-compliance", raising questions over whether other MENA governments will adopt similar measures.
Saudi Arabia has since emerged as a potential next adopter, with its Shura Council calling for age-verification requirements and restrictions on social media use by those under 16.
While countries including Indonesia, Malaysia and Turkey have previously tightened restrictions on young people's use of social media, outright bans on underage users still remain rare.
Nonetheless, governments worldwide have increasingly focused on protecting children from cyberbullying, harmful content and online exploitation; however, rights groups have warned that age verification systems can also create new risks, particularly in countries where privacy protections and independent oversight remain limited.
The New Arab examines whether MENA states are likely to follow the UAE's lead, and whether restrictions designed to protect children could also deepen existing patterns of digital control.
How MENA states have traditionally governed online spaces
The UAE is the first country in the Arab world to introduce a minimum age for social media accounts.
However, governments across the region have long maintained extensive frameworks governing online platforms.
These approaches have traditionally focused less on age restrictions and more on content monitoring, website blocking, government requests for user data and broad cybersecurity legislation.
Rights groups have highlighted that many MENA governments have enacted digital laws that grant authorities significant powers over online speech, often justified by national security, public order, or morality concerns.
In June 2023, the League of Arab States announced a unified social media regulation strategy reportedly influenced by the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and Germany’s Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG).
However, digital rights organisations have warned that regulatory models adopted from Europe do not automatically come with the democratic safeguards that underpin them, including judicial oversight, independent regulators and protections for freedom of expression.
"Historically, MENA states relied on site-wide content blocking rather than granular age verification. However, this is evolving," Ramy Raoof Halim, a Nonresident Fellow on Surveillance & Technology (MENA) at The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told The New Arab.
Halim said the UAE's introduction of social media restrictions for users under 15 reflects a wider shift towards identity-based systems.
"This means moving away from simple, self-declared age gates towards more stringent identity-based assurance," he said.
"Legislation specifically targeting child online safety is emerging but remains nascent. While some states have existing provisions within broader data protection or media laws regarding minors, these are often secondary to state-led censorship mandates."
He added that the UAE’s Child Digital Safety Law, which came into force in January 2026, marked a move towards more formal obligations for platforms to protect children.
As more than 20 countries worldwide consider restrictions on children's access to social media, experts say MENA governments are moving at different speeds on digital regulation.
Gulf states, particularly the UAE and Saudi Arabia, have emerged as regional leaders in developing digital regulation frameworks.
"The UAE has established a centralised 'Regulatory Intelligence Office' and sophisticated legal frameworks for child safety and data protection," Halim said.
"Saudi Arabia, through the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA), has aggressively modernised its data protection and AI governance infrastructure."
Asia Anwer, Digital Rights Researcher and Project Coordinator at the INSM Foundation for Digital Rights (INSM Iraq), said Gulf countries have made the most significant progress in strengthening digital regulation.
By contrast, she described Iraq's digital governance framework as "fragmented and underdeveloped."
"Gulf countries have rapidly expanded privacy and data protection legislation, while Jordan has recently implemented a comprehensive Personal Data Protection Law," she told The New Arab.
"Iraq, however, remains among the countries where digital rights protections continue to lag behind regional developments."
Palestine and the risks of identity-based verification
For Palestinians in Israeli-occupied territories, debates over online safety and digital regulation take place within a wider context of unequal access, surveillance concerns and restrictions affecting digital expression.
Lama Nazeeh, Advocacy Manager at Palestinian digital rights organisation 7amleh (the Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media), said existing digital policies demonstrate how political realities shape online spaces.
"The occupation that fragments Palestinian land now fragments Palestinian connectivity," she told The New Arab.
Nazeeh argued that Palestinians experience a form of digital inequality, with Israeli users, including settlers, having access to more advanced connectivity infrastructure while Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza face significant restrictions.
She said the destruction of telecommunications infrastructure amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza had further intensified these challenges.
"The genocide [in the Gaza Strip since 7 October 2023] that UN bodies have named is also waged on infrastructure," she said.
Nazeeh also warned that stronger age verification requirements could create additional barriers for Palestinians who already face difficulties accessing digital services.
"We have documented surveillance technologies tested on Palestinians and exported worldwide, and leaked evidence of mass coordinated takedowns," she said.
"We do not want to hand any actor a cleaner map of who is speaking."
She argued that identity-based verification systems could exclude people who lack recognised documentation.
"Many Palestinians lack the recognised identity documents these systems expect, which would deepen an exclusion they already face, having been shut out of basic digital and financial services," she explained.
"In Gaza, where most of the network is destroyed, layering verification burdens on people who can barely get online is its own cruelty."
Nazeeh stressed that protecting children online remains important, but warned that safeguards must not be built on systems that increase surveillance.
"Child safety is a real goal. It must not be built on architecture that surveils and excludes the most vulnerable users."
Morocco, Egypt and the politics of 'child safety'
Dima Samaro, Executive Director at Skyline International for Human Rights, cautioned that debates over children’s access to social media in the MENA region cannot be separated from the wider history of digital regulation.
"This is not a new wave of digital regulation," she told The New Arab. "It is an acceleration of something governments here have been doing for years, which is using technology law to consolidate control over what people can say, read, and organise around."
Samaro said governments across the region have repeatedly used different justifications to regulate online spaces.
"The justification changes, but the impulse does not. During COVID, it was a public health issue. Before that, it was national security or protecting public morality. Now, increasingly, it is children’s online safety."
She pointed to Morocco as a key example of how European-inspired digital regulation could be introduced in a country where concerns over freedom of expression remain.
Morocco has been developing legislation to regulate social media platforms by expanding the powers of its broadcasting regulator, HACA, while drawing heavily on the language of the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA).
The DSA aims to increase platform accountability, require greater transparency and protect users from illegal content.
However, Samaro argued that when similar frameworks are adopted elsewhere, the safeguards that underpin European regulation may not always accompany them.
"But what does not get borrowed is everything that makes the DSA meaningful in practice: the courts that can challenge it, the press that can scrutinise it, the civil society that can push back against it," she said.
"What travels across borders is the regulatory architecture. The safeguards that make it work stay behind."
She argued that Morocco's Gen Z 212 protests in late September 2025 demonstrated why governments across the region increasingly view social media platforms as both communication tools and spaces for youth mobilisation.
The movement, one of Morocco's largest youth-led protest movements in recent years, relied heavily on platforms such as TikTok, Discord, and Instagram to organise demonstrations.
According to Samaro, young Moroccans increasingly moved towards platforms such as Discord because they believed mainstream platforms were vulnerable to state pressure.
"Young people organised through Discord because mainstream platforms had a well-documented record of handing over user data and removing content at government request," she said.
"For a generation that watched content about Palestine and war crime documentation systematically disappear from Instagram and Facebook in real time, that lesson did not need explaining."
Samaro said the response to the protests highlighted why digital regulation cannot be viewed solely through the lens of child protection.
This included Moroccan authorities launching a crackdown that resulted in mass arrests and the deaths of three demonstrators.
Jordan subsequently blocked Discord, while Iraq banned Roblox, with both governments citing child protection and online safety concerns.
"At Skyline, we have documented how governments across the SWANA region blocked platforms like Discord and Roblox, citing child safety, while the timing and targets of these bans point clearly to a different motive entirely," she said.
"After Morocco showed what a generation could do when it organised on apps the state cannot monitor, other governments in the region moved quickly to block those same apps before their own youth could do the same."
Egypt offers another example of how child online safety measures could be introduced within a wider environment of digital restrictions.
In January, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi urged authorities to review age-based restrictions on minors' access to digital platforms, prompting Egypt's House of Representatives to begin drafting legislation to tackle what lawmakers described as "digital chaos".
The proposals have since been compared with child online safety frameworks introduced in countries including Australia and the UK.
However, rights groups have warned that introducing such measures in Egypt would take place against the backdrop of existing restrictions on online expression.
"If you already know who is saying what, and you have laws that criminalise criticism of the government, age verification is not protecting young people. It is making them easier to find," Samaro said.
Halim similarly argued that online regulation in Egypt and across the wider region is often influenced by state security priorities alongside efforts to address genuine digital harms.
He said governments frequently rely on broad cybercrime and counterterrorism laws that frame online activity as a matter of national security and public order.
"In Egypt, for example, there have been many cases where content creators on different social platforms are targeted with harsh sentencing and police arrests for violating ‘family values’," Halim told The New Arab.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE’s age verification model
Saudi Arabia is emerging as one of the countries most likely to follow the UAE's approach to regulating young people's access to social media.
Earlier this year, the country's Shura Council called on the Communications, Space and Technology Commission (CST) to establish age-verification requirements and usage restrictions for social media platforms used by those under 16.
Officials said the proposed measures could help address concerns over children’s exposure to harmful content and excessive social media use.
However, ALQST for Human Rights reported that both cybersecurity and counterterrorism laws have been used to restrict freedom of expression online.
"Saudi authorities also block access to many websites they deem to be in violation of Saudi law," the organisation told The New Arab.
The independent grassroots organisation, established to promote and protect human rights in the Gulf kingdom, added that Saudi authorities have prosecuted individuals over their online activity, including a journalist who was executed this year over posts published under a pseudonym.
The group also highlighted cases involving people sentenced for social media posts, including a British national who was detained in Saudi Arabia during a visit over content he had posted online while in the UK.
Meanwhile, digital rights groups have warned that stronger identity requirements could create privacy risks in countries where independent oversight remains limited.
"The concern about children's wellbeing online is real and deserves honest policy engagement," Samaro said.
"But age verification systems require identity documents to be tied to online activity. In countries with functioning independent institutions, that is a serious privacy risk that can at least be contested, litigated, and revised. In much of SWANA, the same system becomes a surveillance tool with a child protection label on the front."
She argued that many countries in the region either lack comprehensive data protection laws or have weak enforcement mechanisms.
"Most countries in the region either lack data protection laws entirely or have frameworks that are outdated, poorly enforced, and offer no meaningful barrier between the data platforms that collect data for age verification and governments that demand access to it."
The UAE's restrictions on under-15s include mandatory verification requirements involving digital identity checks and AI-supported technologies. Self-declaration of age will not be considered a valid form of verification.
Emirati authorities have said the policy aims to protect children from inappropriate content, unsafe online interactions, excessive use and the collection of personal information.
Lisa Dittmer, Amnesty Tech's researcher on children's and young people's digital rights, warned that implementing bans requires identifying users online.
"We know that the only way to implement these bans is through age verification," she told The New Arab.
"To ban children, we need to know who the children on the internet are. And that means in some way or another, we will need to identify people."
Dittmer warned that requiring users to submit identity documents could have consequences beyond child protection.
"One solution for that is actually identity documents. And that dramatically increases the risk of age verification being abused as a sort of smoke screen for de-anonymising people, for tracking them online, even if there are privacy protections in place."
She added that identity checks could discourage users from participating online.
"People knowing that they have submitted documents, that they have ID'd themselves at one point, there's a chilling effect, where people aren't quite sure what's being done with their data and how they’re being tracked and whether this data could be passed on to their governments."
Have social media bans worked elsewhere — and could they work in MENA?
As governments worldwide move to restrict children's access to social media, questions remain about whether such policies can achieve their intended aims.
Australia's landmark legislation, which came into force after becoming the first country to ban social media access for under-16s, has become a key test case for whether age-based restrictions can be effectively enforced.
However, researchers remain divided, as evidence on nationwide social media bans is still limited and long-term data on their impact are yet to emerge.
Early indications suggest that implementing such restrictions may prove more difficult than introducing them.
A study by software testing firm KJR, which previously advised the Australian government on age assurance, found that major platforms were not consistently verifying users’ ages months after the ban came into force.
KJR found that none of the 50 test accounts declaring the user to be 16 were asked to provide proof of age, raising questions over whether age verification systems can reliably prevent underage access.
The findings renewed criticism that users may bypass restrictions by entering false birth dates or using alternative platforms.
Amnesty Tech's Lisa Dittmer said banning children from social media entirely risks failing to address the wider problems associated with online harms.
"Simply shutting children and young people out will prove ineffective ultimately because children and young people are tech-savvy and they will know how to get around this," she told The New Arab.
Instead, she argued governments should focus on creating safer online environments through stronger platform accountability, improved design and digital literacy.
"It's a core issue around the world that these bans are being rolled out very fast without adequate consultation with children, young people, civil society and all the experts who have been doing research on this for decades."
Dittmer said that while concerns about children's online safety are legitimate, bans risk offering a simple solution to a complex problem.
"These teen bans seem to offer a simple solution but actually fail to address the core issues."
In the MENA region, Halim believes more governments are likely to introduce restrictions on young people's social media access, but warned that the motivations behind such policies may differ from those seen in Western countries.
"While Western models focus on protecting minors from algorithmic harm or commercial exploitation, MENA regimes may adopt these bans to consolidate control over the digital environment, using 'child safety' as a socially palatable justification for tightening access and enforcing state-managed digital identities," he said.
Halim said the effectiveness of any future restrictions would depend on several factors, including governments' ability to implement age verification systems, the availability of digital infrastructure and the role social media plays in young people's daily lives.
"Governments must balance their desire to restrict platforms with the necessity of these tools for economic modernisation and state-sanctioned messaging," he said.
He added that social media has become central to youth culture, political discussion and news consumption across the region.
“There is significant tension between the desire to protect traditional social values and the reality that social media is now the primary space for youth cultural expression, political discourse, and news consumption.”
For Skyline International's Dima Samaro, the challenge for governments is not whether children should be protected online, but whether those protections can be achieved without creating new risks.
"The answer to protecting children online is not less access and more restrictive regulation but better design, stronger platform accountability, and genuine investment in digital literacy and in helping families and young people in the region navigate online spaces safely," Samaro said.
She argued that governments should focus on addressing the underlying problems behind online harms rather than relying primarily on restrictions.
This includes requiring platforms to improve moderation systems, increase transparency, tackle harmful content and give users greater control over their online experiences.
A new digital divide?
The debate over social media bans in the MENA region reflects a wider global struggle over how governments should balance child protection with digital rights.
Few experts dispute that children face genuine risks online. Research has linked excessive social media use with concerns around mental health, cyberbullying, exposure to harmful material and exploitation of personal data.
However, rights groups warn that the methods used to address these risks matter.
As MENA governments debate whether to follow the UAE's lead, the central question remains whether new restrictions will genuinely protect children — or risk creating new systems of surveillance in a region where digital freedoms are already contested.

Groundhogs' play ends amid Alpine heat
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:09:52 CEST
23:09:52 KST

Rising temperatures in the Alps have
stifled the formerly playful behaviour of the Alpine marmot or
groundhog, according to a new study.
                                    
                                       
				The ongoing heat wave in the Alps is changing the lives of
marmots, who are giving up playing, according to the study
conducted in the Orvieilles research area, in Valsavarenche
(Aosta), in the Gran Paradiso National Park, and recently
published in open access in the journal Animal Behaviour.
                                    
                                       
				The research, titled "Too warm to play: temperature selectively
constrains social behavior in the Alpine marmot, Marmota
marmota," is by Park researcher Caterina Ferrari, Diego
Rastelli, Maria Paniw, and Achaz von Hardenberg.
                                    
                                       
				It is based on data collected as part of the long-term marmot
research project active in Orvieilles since 2006.
                                    
                                       
				Between June 2023 and June 2025, the researchers observed 83
marmots from 14 family groups, for a total of 189 hours of
observation, recording 667 social interactions.
                                    
                                       
				The results are particularly striking for play, a behavior
primarily associated with young individuals.
                                    
                                       
				Activity peaks around 12.8°C, then rapidly decreases as
temperatures rise, becoming almost nonexistent above 21°C.
                                    
                                       
				According to the researchers, this finding is particularly
significant because play, in Alpine marmots, is not simply a
recreational activity.
                                    
                                       
				It particularly affects the young and contributes to the
development of their motor and social skills.
                                    
                                       
				A prolonged decline could therefore have consequences that go
beyond the immediate response to heat, potentially affecting
individual development and important behaviors in adulthood,
such as territorial defense and reproduction.
                                    
                                       
				The research thus highlights an early and barely visible effect
of climate change.
                                    
                                       
				Rising temperatures can alter the way animals use their time and
interact with each other before having any noticeable effects on
survival, reproduction, or population size.

UK Officials Call for Military Dialogue With Russia to Be Restored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:09:16 UTC
23:09:16 KST

British defense officials are calling for direct contacts between the military leadership of the United Kingdom and Russia to be restored amid concerns about escalation.
The Times reported the matter.
The situation has escalated following a series of incidents involving British and Russian military personnel.
The last known conversation between Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov and his British counterpart took place in September 2022. At the time, Gerasimov spoke with the then-Chief of the Defence Staff Adm. Sir Tony Radakin.
Radakin subsequently tried several times to contact Gerasimov, but the Russian side did not respond to his calls. After Richard Knighton was appointed Chief of the Defence Staff, he also tried to establish contact with Gerasimov, but without success.
In June, the Russian frigate Admiral Grigorovich fired warning shots from small arms at a British yacht in the English Channel, after which the crew changed course.
Another incident occurred near the aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales in the Norwegian Sea. The Russian Tu-142 Yuri Malinin approached the ship at an unsafe distance while flying at low altitude. According to the British side, the aircraft also dropped a large number of surveillance devices into the water near the British aircraft carrier.
Former UK defense attaché to Moscow and Kyiv, John Foreman, said that Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting and Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton should restore direct contacts with the Russian military leadership.
According to him, even in the absence of a political agreement, the military should maintain communication channels to resolve dangerous incidents.
UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting, July 21, 2026. Photo: Jack Taylor/Reuters
The lack of direct communication is not the only problem. In 2024, the United Kingdom expelled a Russian defense attaché, accusing him of working for Russian intelligence. In response, Moscow expelled the UK military attaché, Adrian Coghill.
The two sides previously maintained a dedicated hotline between the UK Ministry of Defence and the Russian Presidential Situation Center. It still exists but is used less frequently than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The UK government says London is ready for dialogue with the Russian military leadership, but Moscow has so far shown no willingness to restore that dialogue.

Heatwave and jellyfish: a fifth of France's nuclear capacity offline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

France uses nuclear power to generate around 70% of its electricity. The country has seen nuclear power production disrupted by multiple heatwaves and droughts this year.
France recorded a more than 20% shortfall in nuclear power production capacity on Wednesday, a record deficit caused by environmental-related outages linked to drought, extreme heat and a jellyfish invasion.
France uses nuclear power to generate around 70% of its electricity. The country has seen nuclear power production disrupted by multiple heatwaves and droughts this year.
According to AFP calculations based on data published by energy group EDF since 2015, 20.4% of generating capacity was unavailable.
Between 9:45 am and 10:00 am, EDF's nuclear fleet recorded a new peak in outages due to "environmental constraints" or "external environmental causes," both in terms of the number of reactors shut down or operating at reduced output and in terms of lost generating capacity.
In total, 13 of the 57 reactors in EDF's nuclear fleet were affected. Eight reactors were completely shut down while five were operating at reduced power.
Much of the lost nuclear generating capacity was due to full or partial shutdowns at five of the six reactors at the Gravelines nuclear power plant after a swarm of jellyfish clogged pumps used to cool the units.
Experts say overfishing, plastic pollution and warming seas due to climate change have created conditions allowing jellyfish to thrive and reproduce.
Outside the Gravelines plant, the largest in Western Europe, the shutdowns or production reductions affecting other reactors are linked to extreme heat and droughts, depriving the plants of the water they need for cooling.
During droughts or heatwaves, lower river flow and higher water temperatures can force EDF to cut, or even halt, production in order to protect the environment and biodiversity.
The operator is then unable to discharge chemical or radioactive effluents or further warm rivers with its cooling water, which is returned to the river at a higher temperature.
"But there is enough leeway that this does not pose any supply problems in the short term," says Nicolas Goldberg, an energy expert at consultancy Colombus Consulting quoted by CNews.
