Ukrainian law enforcement officials charge Russia's Kursk detention centre staff with torturing and beating civilians
Ukrainian law enforcement officials have charged two employees of a detention centre in Kursk, Russia, with systematically torturing Ukrainian civilians. The suspects beat the illegally detained civilians with their hands and a baton, and tortured them with electric shocks.
Source: Prosecutor General's Office
Details: According to the investigation, two employees of Detention Centre No. 1 of the Federal Penitentiary Service Directorate for Kursk Oblast brutally mistreated at least five civilians.
They subjected them to electric shocks and beat them with their hands, feet and a plastic baton on various parts of their bodies. The violence was carried out systematically, in violation of the requirements of international humanitarian law.
The Russian detention centre employees have been charged with cruel treatment of civilians committed by a group of people acting in prior collusion under Article 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The crime is punishable by imprisonment of 8 and 12 years.
Background: During their captivity in Russia, Ukrainians have been subjected to torture and humiliation by Russian doctors and nurses. Those released from captivity have said they were denied medical treatment, beaten with stun guns and given medication only after obeying the command, "On your knees!"

Wall Street opens higher as US inflation meets expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:07:00 UTC
23:07:00 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
By Mucahithan Avcioglu
ISTANBUL (AA) - US stocks opened higher Wednesday after consumer inflation for July was in line with expectations.
The Dow Jones industrial average edged up 0.01% to 53,797.47 at the opening bell.
The S&P 500 rose 0.48% to 7,765.46, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.89% to 26,680.46.
The US Consumer Price Index increased 0.1% month-on-month and 3.4% annually in July, matching market estimates.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.2% on a monthly basis and 2.5% from a year earlier, also in line with forecasts.
Expectations that the US Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next month weakened slightly following the release of the figures.
Analysts said the inflation data, coupled with last week’s report showing weaker employment growth in July, reinforced expectations that the Fed could keep its policy rate unchanged at its September meeting.
Another consumer inflation report is due before the meeting; however, investors will closely monitor producer inflation data scheduled for Thursday.
Technology shares led the advance as corporate earnings indicated continued demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Shares of cloud-computing company CoreWeave surged more than 20% after its second-quarter revenue nearly doubled from a year earlier.
Super Micro Computer climbed more than 10% after the server maker reported financial results that exceeded market expectations.
Investors also continued to monitor geopolitical developments in the Middle East, particularly their effect on energy prices and the inflation outlook.

Ukraine needs underground storage amid growing strikes on fuel infrastructure - A-95 director
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:05:42 EEST
23:05:42 KST

Amid shrinking fuel supply channels and escalating Russian strikes on fuel infrastructure, Ukraine needs to build decentralized, small underground petroleum product storage facilities, according to Serhiy Kuyun, director of the consulting firm A-95.
"There’s only one way out - storage in underground facilities. Both the state and private players are apparently already working on this. At the same time, building this kind of infrastructure costs at least twice as much as above-ground tanks," he wrote on Facebook on Wednesday.
According to the expert, there is currently no state support even at the level of streamlining and speeding up approval of project documentation, let alone preferential lending and other incentives.
Kuyun said the goal in building underground storage should not be large facilities, since these are more vulnerable to complex missile strikes.
"But if every importer builds its own small storage facilities of 3,000-4,000-5,000-10,000 cubic meters, that would already be a much more resilient setup. In any case, it should be understood that this won’t happen quickly - a year and a half to two years, if started today," he said.
The expert said the need to build fuel reserves should be communicated to citizens, municipal institutions and state organizations, as well as private companies. "A dispersed reserve among consumers will help prevent panic buying and excessive instantaneous strain on the supply system in the event of a crisis," the A-95 director said.
According to Kuyun, Russia has carried out new strikes on the bridge in Mayaky (on the route from Reni to the mainland) and a jet-powered Shahed strike on an oil tanker truck on the same route.
"I think that when planning fuel supply strategy for the coming months, it’s better to write off the South (...). This means the entire burden will fall on the land border, which is already maximally overloaded. All this points to the system becoming less diversified, with the corresponding risks," Kuyun wrote.
He explained that the enemy is gradually cutting off Ukraine’s southern fuel supply route, dealing a triple blow: fewer supply channels, reduced consumption as "sea" exports shift to "wheels," and increased strain with reduced border throughput capacity for fuel imports.
At the same time, Russia is now attacking not only oil depots in Ukraine but also gas stations with fuel trucks.
As previously reported, the Oil and Gas Association of Ukraine (NAU) is petitioning the government to give the fuel industry access to loans at 10%, which could be achieved by extending Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 594 to all types of business, in order to build underground petroleum product storage tanks as part of the reconstruction of existing oil depots.
NAU president Yaroslav Starovoitenko said this at an online meeting with business organized by the parliamentary Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy earlier this week.

Russian Combat Drone Forum Postponed Over Fears of Ukrainian Attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:05:17 UTC
23:05:17 KST

Organizers of a major forum for Russian military drone operators have postponed this year’s event, citing intelligence that Ukraine was preparing an attack involving ballistic missiles and what they described as “terrorist bio-drones.”
The annual Dronnitsa meeting, scheduled for Aug. 29-30 in the city of Veliky Novgorod northwest of Moscow, brings together combat drone operators, technical specialists and volunteers involved in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The event was scheduled to be held some 120 kilometers (75 miles) away from President Vladimir Putin’s Valdai residence, the exiled investigative outlet Agentsvo reported. Previous reporting by exiled media has said Putin's alleged partner Alina Kabaeva and their two sons spend much of their time there and that the presidential residence is surrounded by air defenses.
Organizers said the decision was made following consultations with the Novgorod region’s leadership and Russian security services, who said protecting the forum would require diverting air defenses and security personnel from other locations.
“Exposing factories and bases in the Novgorod and neighboring regions for the sake of our own security would be wrong at this time, while holding the event under such risks would be overly presumptuous,” organizers said in a statement on Telegram.
Alexei Chadayev, the event’s principal founder, confirmed the decision, saying that Ukrainian forces “would not have targeted Dronnitsa itself” if the gathering had gone ahead. He did not elaborate.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify the organizers’ claims about a planned Ukrainian operation. There was no immediate comment from Ukrainian authorities.
Dronnitsa has been held annually in the Novgorod region since 2022. Its principal organizer is the Coordination Center for Assistance to Novorossiya, a group that supports Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.
According to its website, the gathering aims to promote a culture of “military unmanned aviation” and build a professional community of drone instructors and operators, as well as electronic intelligence and electronic warfare specialists.
Past events have focused on the battlefield use of drones, lessons learned from combat and the creation of specialized drone and counter-drone units. Organizers have also discussed the mass deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles and ways to apply Russian and foreign experience to the military development of the sector.
The event describes itself as a meeting place for people working “for the victory of Russian arms in the special military operation,” the Kremlin’s term for its war on Ukraine.
Dronnitsa also helped give rise to Ushkuynik, a research and production center in Veliky Novgorod headed by Chadayev. The center tests, modifies and certifies drone technology including the Knyaz Vandal Novgorodsky (KVN), a fiber-optic-controlled first-person-view drone.
Chadayev has described the KVN as one of the most effective drones in its class when comparing its development and procurement costs with the damage it has inflicted on Ukraine. His claim could not be independently verified.

President Vladimir Putin said Russia would seize ships belonging to European countries if they tried to sell cargo confiscated from Russia-linked vessels suspected of belonging to Moscow's so-called shadow fleet.
"This is nothing less than piracy and robbery," Putin said during drills by Russia's Pacific Fleet on August 12, referring to Europe's plans to tighten measures against vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade Western sanctions.
"If this begins to be put into practice, we shall be forced to respond in kind," he added, saying that Moscow would not limit its response to the waters where Russian ships were being detained. He did not provide other details.
Western governments have stepped up efforts to target the shadow fleet -- a network of opaquely owned or insured vessels that Russia has used to keep its oil exports flowing despite sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine.
Putin's statement came after the European Union last month passed a new sanctions package against Russia, including measures allowing member states to sell oil or other cargo seized from sanctioned or detained vessels.
According to European media reports, Swedish court documents showed that Stockholm was planning to transfer to Kyiv a seized Russian ship suspected of transporting grain from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Days before Putin's threats, the US Senate also approved a sweeping Russia and Iran sanctions package that would give President Donald Trump additional leverage to push Moscow toward negotiations with Ukraine by squeezing its war economy.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, energy revenues have remained a crucial source of income for the Russian state and its war effort. Kyiv has sought to curb Russia's ability to finance the war by calling for strict sanctions against its energy sector.
Among other things, the bill -- which has yet to be approved by the US House of Representatives -- targets Russia's shadow fleet, including vessels, owners, operators, insurers, ports, and other intermediaries involved in transporting Russian oil and sanctioned goods.
In recent months, the Ukrainian military has also intensified its long-range attacks on Russia's shadow-fleet vessels and energy infrastructure, a campaign Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described as Kyiv's "long-range sanctions" against Moscow.

Too many holes! Why badgers are digging up Britain’s lovingly maintained golf courses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:04:38 UTC
23:04:38 KST

Name: Badgers.
Age: European badgers live for five to eight years in the wild. They have been in the UK, where this story is set, for half to three-quarters of a million years.
Appearance: Black and white mustelid anarcho-syndicalists.
Hardly. Badgers are quite posh, aren’t they? Well, perhaps. But everyone has their breaking point, and now I must inform you that badgers have become embroiled in an aggressive form of anti-capitalist class warfare.
What turned them? The cost of living? The rise of the billionaire class? Close, but no. It was the drought.
How so? This has been a historically hot summer in the UK. England and Wales endured the driest July since records began (1836). All the grass is brown and dead. There are wildfires everywhere and 26 million people are living with a hosepipe ban.
It’s awful. Yes, especially for the badgers. Most of their food lives underground, and it’s much harder to get to it when the earth has been baked dry by the sun.
So what’s the solution? That’s easy: turn over a few golf courses.
Are they really into clubhouse sandwiches? Not when there are nice wet lawns to tear up.
Why do golf courses have wet lawns during a drought? The Water Use (Temporary Bans) Order 2010 permits exemptions for watering sports turf. That means that while you are carefully sharing your bathwater, your local golf course is hosing its lush greens.
Yes, but the badgers. Oh, right. Well, if you’re a badger and you need to dig up some worms, and all the ground is hard except for golf courses, where do you think you’re going to get your worms?
From golf courses? That’s right! Jim Croxton, chief executive of the British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association, says: “Badgers generally dig turf to find food and August is the beginning of the period when chafer grubs are generally present.”
Is it a widespread problem? Golf courses from Suffolk to Staffordshire to Worcestershire have reported greens being torn up by badgers, according to the Telegraph.
This sounds like a victimless crime. You would think so, but the golf courses are very upset about it.
How upset? A video of one ripped-up course posted to Facebook prompted the furious comment: “They’re a f*ckin pest, I’ve had countless ornamental lawns wrecked by these f*ckers.”
Quite right. Will nobody think of the ornamental lawns? Exactly. It’s clear that there needs to be an urgent change to the law.
To what? Well, it obviously isn’t fair that golf courses are exempt from the hosepipe ban in a time of national crisis.
But then the badgers would have nowhere to eat, and they would die. No they wouldn’t. Badgers are enterprising creatures. They’d find a way.
Do say: “The badgers have absolutely massacred hole nine.”
Don’t say: “Four legs good, golf clubs bad.”

This season, Ukraine reduced wheat exports but increased corn exports
Kyiv • UNN
As of August 12, Ukraine had exported 2.952 million tonnes of grain, 4.76% more than last year. Wheat exports decreased by 18.33%, while corn exports increased by 66.38%.
Since the beginning of this marketing year, which started on July 1, Ukraine has already shipped almost 3 million tonnes of grain for export, but has reduced wheat exports, the relevant ministry reported, citing data from the State Customs Service, writes UNN.
Details
According to the data provided, as of August 12, Ukraine had exported 2.952 million tonnes of cereals and leguminous crops in the 2026/27 marketing year. This is 4.76% more than on August 15 last year in the 2025/26 MY. At the same time, wheat exports this year were 18.33% lower than last year. Corn exports, by contrast, were 66.38% higher this MY than last year.
At the same time, a total of 280,000 tonnes of grain have already been exported in August.
In particular, in the 2026/27 MY, the following have already been shipped for export:
-  wheat - 1.239 million tonnes; 
-  barley - 333,000 tonnes; 
-  corn - 1.376 million tonnes. 
No rye has been exported yet this MY.
Flour exports amounted to 2,800 tonnes.

The Select Club: Which Countries Have Their Own Ballistic Missiles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:02:20 EEST
23:02:20 KST

The Select Club: Which Countries Have Their Own Ballistic Missiles
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is implementing a ballistic missile program. Although for us this is primarily a matter of effectively countering the enemy, the emergence of such a technology places Ukraine among the few countries that possess ballistic missiles.
Developing an indigenous ballistic missile is a technologically complex task. Far from all countries even have tactical-level ballistic missiles in their arsenals. Read about which countries have ballistic missiles in their arsenals in the UNN article.
Ukraine is on the path toward its own ballistic missile launch. This is fundamentally important in the war with russia, because ballistic targets are among the most difficult to intercept, and such missiles have the potential to carry a significant explosive charge and thus strike major targets on enemy territory.
However, the emergence of Ukrainian ballistic missiles also has a certain element of prestige and pride, because by obtaining its own missile of this type, Ukraine will join a fairly small list of countries possessing similar technologies.
Most countries implemented their own ballistic missile programs over many decades, whereas Ukraine is forced to do everything within incredibly tight deadlines.
Ukraine’s ballistic missile program
In July, the Ministry of Defense announced ballistic missile tests. It concerned the "Sapsan" operational-tactical missile system developed by the "Pivdenne" Design Bureau. Fire Point also has its own ballistic missile program. Its portfolio includes two missiles: the FP-7 and FP-9. The former has a stated range of up to 200 km, while the latter has a range of 855 km.
The FP-7’s range can be compared with that of the American ATACMS. Ukrainian troops need such tactical ballistic missiles to strike warehouses and enemy concentrations beyond the "kill zone" at a distance of up to 200 km.
According to Fire Point, the missile has undergone about 15 test launches and is currently at the certification stage at the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine. As for the FP-9, it is already a short-range missile, but with the ability to cover more than 800 km, this missile will be able to reach moscow.
Intercontinental missiles
Only a small number of countries in the world have the technological capabilities to develop and operate intercontinental ballistic missiles. This list includes nuclear-armed states, because ICBMs have become the primary carriers of nuclear weapons.
This class includes missiles with a range of more than 5,500 kilometers.
The U.S. military has land-based Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, with an average flight range of 13,000 kilometers depending on the payload, as well as Trident II missiles deployed on submarines, with a range of up to 12,000 km. Experts estimate the arsenals of both types at approximately 600 missiles.
russia’s ICBM stockpile is estimated at around 500 missiles, most of which are probably the relatively new, land-based Yars missiles, with a potential range of up to 12,000 km, as well as the sea-based Bulava and Sineva missiles. As for the Oreshnik, based on its range classification, it more likely belongs to the category of intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
China has the Dongfeng missile series—"East Wind." At least two of them—the DF-31 and DF-41—belong to the intercontinental class. According to various estimates, their range may be up to 15,000 kilometers.
France has ICBMs only on submarines. Thus, the French M51 missile has a potential range of up to 10,000 km.
Some countries, such as Israel, do not publicize the presence of ICBMs in their arsenals, but according to unofficial information, the Jericho IIІ missile is capable of covering more than 6,000 km. Information regarding India is also controversial—the Agni-V missile is estimated by various sources to have a range of between 5,000 and 8,000 km.
Information about North Korea is the most closely guarded, but it is assumed that the Hwasong missile family includes at least one missile of this class.
Who has shorter-range missiles
A somewhat larger number of countries have shorter-range ballistic missiles.
These include tactical ballistic missiles—with a range of up to 300 km; short-range ballistic missiles—with a range of 300 to 1,000 km; and intermediate-range ballistic missiles—with a range of 1,000 to 5,500 km.
We have already mentioned Chinese "Dongfeng" missiles – among them are systems that operate at tactical ranges, as well as medium-range missiles. Interestingly, China supplied ballistic missiles to Turkey. The Yıldırım systems were developed based on the Chinese B-611 missile, and later the Bora system also emerged through cooperation with China. Today, Turkey already has its own developments, such as the Tayfun Block-2, with a stated range of up to 800 km.
The US Army has ATACMS – 300 km (with upgrades extending the range to 450 km) – and PrSM (with a range of 500 km) in its arsenal.
Ukraine experiences the effects of Russian ballistic missiles almost every night. These include the Iskander-M, with a range of up to 500 km, as well as the already mentioned Yars and Bulava systems, capable of launching missiles of various ranges.
If we are talking about missiles with a range of up to 5,500 km, Iran, India, North Korea and Pakistan also have domestic production of such ballistic missiles.

Investigation into seizure of 18 hectares of Stolychny market land completed - NABU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:02:11 EEST
23:02:11 KST

The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) have completed the pre-trial investigation into the seizure and subsequent legalization of 18 hectares of state-owned land worth more than UAH 160 million at market value, NABU reported.
"In the spring of 2021, amid a corporate conflict between a former Party of Regions MP and a Kyiv-based developer for control of a wholesale agricultural produce market on the outskirts of Kyiv, the developer formed an intent to transfer the market’s assets to individuals and legal entities under her control," NABU said on its Telegram channel on Wednesday.
According to the bureau, in furtherance of the scheme, officials at the State Geocadastre’s Main Directorate in Kyiv region made unauthorized changes to the State Land Cadastre, allowing the directorate to dispose of the land tract on which the wholesale market, spanning more than 150 hectares, is located.
NABU said the land was then leased to a company controlled by the developer.
The head of that company subsequently waived part of the leased land in favor of nine predetermined individuals, who, based on an order signed by the acting head of the State Geocadastre’s Kyiv region directorate and in violation of land legislation, obtained ownership of nine land plots totaling 18 hectares, NABU said.
Those plots were later sold, through sham transactions, to three companies linked to the developer.
"In the course of settling the conflict, the developer and the former MP signed a memorandum (‘ponyatiyka’) on the joint use of the land tract, including for development. And in September 2021, a trusted associate of the former MP became a beneficiary of the companies owning the land plots," the statement said.

Portugal boosts maritime surveillance with Portuguese-made long-range drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:36 UTC
23:00:36 KST

The Portuguese Air Force will boost maritime surveillance using AR5 drones from Portuguese tech firm Tekever, which supplies autonomous systems to Ukraine. Delivery is due in early September.
Portuguese technology company Tekever is to supply AR5 drones to the Portuguese Air Force (FAP) for maritime surveillance missions. The autonomous platforms are scheduled for delivery in early September.
In a statement, the company, which has become an important player in the unmanned systems industry, especially when it comes to exporting drones to Ukraine, announced the signing of a contract with the FAP that also includes "operator training, as well as the supply of the Ground Control Station and the ATLAS mission system".
With a wingspan of almost 8 metres and weighing close to 200 kilos, purpose-built for maritime missions thanks to its robustness and ability to fly at higher altitudes, the AR5 will enable the FAP "to strengthen its operational autonomy on long-range missions".
These missions include "maritime surveillance, security and defence, monitoring of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and support for missions in the public interest", which in turn covers "the Special Rural Firefighting Device (DECIR), coastal security and environmental protection".
Portuguese-made drones
In the statement, Tekever explains that in the first phase, it will train Air Force personnel until September so they can operate the systems as soon as they are delivered. Then, from October, a "second phase of training" will take place to consolidate "full operational readiness and the development of new skills within the operating teams".
Tekever has not disclosed either the scope of the contract or the amount invested by the FAP. However, an order from the Ministry of Defence (source in Portuguese), dated November last year, authorised the Air Force to purchase an unmanned aerial system for maritime patrol with an overall maximum budget of just over 7.79 million euros, to be financed through the Military Programming Law.
Quoted in the statement, Lieutenant Colonel Luís Henriques, Operational Coordinator of the AR5 Working Group of the Portuguese Air Force, argues that "the integration of the AR5 system represents a significant improvement in the operational capabilities of the Portuguese Air Force."
"This platform meets current surveillance, security and defence requirements, offering greater range, endurance and operational flexibility," he says, stressing that its integration "will strengthen the nation's ability to monitor the Exclusive Economic Zone and support a wide range of missions in the public interest, contributing to an Air Force better prepared to respond to current and future challenges."
For his part, Pedro Petiz, Director of Strategic Development at Tekever, points out that this contract "puts an autonomous capability developed and produced in Portugal" to work protecting the country's airspace and maritime territory. "In addition to supplying the aircraft, we will work with the Portuguese Air Force to consolidate and develop its own operational capability, which will strengthen national autonomy, readiness and responsiveness," he adds.
'Information-gathering' missions
The company describes the AR5 as a "fixed-wing unmanned aerial system, medium-altitude and long-endurance, designed for information-gathering missions over large areas". With a flight endurance of up to 20 hours and able to carry up to 50 kg of payload, the system "incorporates satellite communications (SATCOM), enabling operations beyond radio line-of-sight (BRLOS)."
Tekever systems have been gaining prominence on the market, having logged thousands of flight hours on coastal patrols, persistent surveillance, border protection, detection of suspicious activities, environmental protection and search-and-rescue missions.
The company has been signing contracts with various national and international entities, including the United Kingdom Home Office and the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA). Tekever systems are also currently in operation in Ukraine, where they undertake surveillance and reconnaissance missions in an operational environment.
Recently, one of the company's drones made headlines after managing to catch Russian forces off guard in the border region of Bryansk. The Portuguese-made AR3 reconnaissance drone, operated by the Ukrainian army, was shot down by Russian forces, then recovered and transferred to a research institute, where its technical and engineering features are expected to be studied.

What time will the eclipse be visible in my city? Solar eclipse times for 12 August in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:27 UTC
23:00:27 KST

The total solar eclipse will cross Spain this Wednesday at sunset, peaking around 8.30 pm. See when it will be visible in each city, where it is total, and its peak in Madrid and Barcelona.
On Wednesday 12 August, Spain has a date with the sky. The total solar eclipse will sweep across much of the country in the final hours of the afternoon and millions of people will be able to witness one of the most eagerly awaited astronomical events of recent years.
But there is a key question before heading out to find a spot to watch it: what time will the eclipse be visible in my city?
There is no single answer for the whole of Spain. The Moon’s shadow will move from west to east and the moment of maximum darkness will vary slightly depending on the location. In general terms, the most eagerly awaited moment will come at around 20:30, although in some cities it will occur a few minutes earlier and in others a little later.
What is more, not all of Spain will see a total eclipse. The path of totality will cross parts of the north and east of the peninsula before reaching the Balearic Islands. Outside that path, the eclipse will be partial, although in many places the Sun will be almost completely covered.
What time will the eclipse be in each city?
These are the approximate times of the totality phase in the main Spanish provincial capitals that lie within the path of the lunar shadow:
- La Coruña: from 20:27 to 20:28. Totality will last for approximately 1 minute and 18 seconds.
- Oviedo: between 20:27 and 20:28, with close to 1 minute and 48 seconds of totality.
- Santander: between 20:26 and 20:28. Total darkness will last for around 1 minute and 2 seconds.
- Bilbao: at around 20:27, although totality will be much shorter, at about 27 seconds.
- Vitoria-Gasteiz: between 20:27 and 20:28, lasting for roughly 1 minute.
- Lugo: between 20:28 and 20:29, with 1 minute and 25 seconds of totality.
- León: between 20:28 and 20:30. Totality will last for around 1 minute and 45 seconds.
- Burgos: between 20:28 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 43 seconds.
- Logroño: between 20:28 and 20:29, with around 1 minute and 19 seconds of totality.
- Palencia: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 42 seconds.
- Soria: between 20:29 and 20:30, with 1 minute and 41 seconds of totality.
- Zaragoza: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 23 seconds.
- Lérida: at around 20:29, with a totality of barely 24 seconds.
- Tarragona: between 20:29 and 20:30, lasting for about 58 seconds.
- Zamora: between 20:30 and 20:31, with around 24 seconds of totality.
- Segovia: between 20:31 and 20:32. Totality will last for approximately one minute.
- Guadalajara: between 20:31 and 20:32, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 8 seconds.
- Teruel: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 35 seconds of totality.
- Castellón: between 20:31 and 20:32, lasting for approximately 1 minute and 34 seconds.
- Palma de Mallorca: between 20:31 and 20:32, with around 1 minute and 36 seconds of totality.
- Cuenca: between 20:32 and 20:33, lasting for about 57 seconds.
- Valencia: between 20:32 and 20:33, with approximately one minute of totality.
What time will the eclipse be in Madrid and Barcelona?
Two of Spain’s most populous cities will lie outside the main path of totality.
In Madrid, the eclipse will be partial and will reach its maximum at around 20:32. The situation is particularly unusual because the edge of the path of totality passes very close to the capital and reaches parts of the municipal area close to Barajas.
In Barcelona, totality will also not occur. The moment of maximum obscuration of the Sun will be at approximately 20:29.
That does not mean the phenomenon will go unnoticed. From both cities it will be possible to observe a very deep partial eclipse, although there will be no brief spell of darkness such as that experienced in towns and cities lying within the path of totality.
The shadow will cross Spain in just a few minutes
The time differences between cities are due to the path of the Moon’s shadow. The area of total darkness will enter from the west and cross Spain on its way towards the Balearic Islands.
That is why, while in places such as Santander, Oviedo or La Coruña the decisive moment will come at around 20:27, in locations further east such as Valencia, Castellón or Palma it will occur several minutes later.
All this will happen with the Sun very close to the horizon. The eclipse will coincide with sunset, a circumstance that will make it especially important to choose a place with a clear view to the west, without buildings, mountains or trees blocking the Sun in those crucial minutes.
An eclipse that will be visible across Spain
Those outside the path of totality will also be able to follow the event. The eclipse will be visible, at least partially, from all Spanish territory, including the Canary Islands.
The big difference will lie in those seconds when the Moon completely covers the solar disc. Within the path of totality, the sky will darken rapidly and it will be possible to observe the solar corona for a brief interval.
Outside that path, a small part of the Sun will remain visible even at maximum eclipse, so the sky will never take on the characteristic appearance of a total eclipse.
And one final warning will be essential, regardless of the city from which it is observed: you must not look directly at the Sun without certified protective equipment during the partial phases of the eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not suitable for observing the event safely.

The big difference will lie in those seconds when the Moon completely covers the solar disc. Within the path of totality, the sky will darken rapidly and it will be possible to observe the solar corona for a brief interval.
Outside that path, a small part of the Sun will remain visible even at maximum eclipse, so the sky will never take on the characteristic appearance of a total eclipse.
And one final warning will be essential, regardless of the city from which it is observed: you must not look directly at the Sun without certified protective equipment during the partial phases of the eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not suitable for observing the event safely.

How Africa is becoming a ‘strategic hub’ for Chinese industrial expansion
Countries including Zimbabwe and Guinea are ending the pit-to-ship model that saw them exporting raw minerals with limited local gains
Today, nations such as Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Ghana and Guinea are dismantling that system – by banning exports of raw materials and enforcing local processing rules.
These measures force international mining firms, including Chinese companies, to invest billions of dollars in domestic processing plants.
Now, instead of simply shipping out ore, Chinese firms are building local facilities to transform Zimbabwean lithium into its sulphate or carbonate forms, Guinean bauxite into alumina, and Mozambican graphite into battery materials.
According to Carlos Lopes, a professor at the University of Cape Town’s Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance, the shift runs far deeper than resource processing.

Nirim is thriving, but Oct. 7 still haunts its present – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Last week, I attended a vivid, moving photography exhibition, celebrating kibbutz and day-to-day Israeli life. I shouldn’t write about it because I’m not an objective observer, given that the photographer was my talented cousin, Adele Raemer.
But what made it exceptional, newsworthy, and inspiring yet heartbreaking was that her photographs capture life in Nirim, a Gaza border kibbutz, since 2020, meaning before it was invaded on October 7, and since.
Baseball fans love split-screen television. You watch the pitcher prepare to pitch, as the first-base runner prepares to bolt.
What a metaphor for life in Israel.
It’s the “great Israel disconnect.”
What’s true?
I wonder “what’s real in my amazing, enjoyable, reassuring, soul-expanding, day-to-day life?” 
Is it that life is full of wonderful, grounded, all-too-often heroic, self-sacrificing children, many weddings and births, fun coffee dates, scenic jogs around Jerusalem, and special relatives and friends?
Or, as many others fear, is “the real Israel” its toxic politics, the terrifying headlines, the threats from so many evil enemies?
The challenges are mind-boggling. And they’re exacerbated, I regret to say, by some American Jewish friends minimizing the threats, joining the pile-on demonizing of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while trying to bond with supposed allies who increasingly threaten them – and us.
Still, I live in the moment, and what a moment it was last Thursday. My cousin, Adele, a Bronx native who moved to the Negev decades ago, has long had a remarkable artistic flair.
In 2016, she joined the online network 52Frames to grow as a photographer. Since then, by 7 a.m. every Monday (midnight East Coast US time), she posts a photograph in response to the weekly challenge. It could be a self-portrait, a landscape, a group shot, or a photograph taken with a certain technique. She’s become Nirim’s unofficial photographer-in-chief, recording the community’s life, moment by moment.
So yes. After all these years, she deserved to be honored by her community for her eye, her composition, her technique. One woman thanked her for capturing so many of her family’s special moments as her kids grew.
The photographs were displayed in the old etching studio of the late Dov Heller, a Romanian-born artist who arrived at the nine-year-old Kibbutz Nirim in 1955.
His daughter, Galia Heller Kremer, offered Adele a converted dairy barn, which is now the community’s art gallery, and greeted the guests warmly. “We could have called it From New York to Nirim, but ultimately, Adele is from here. She’s one of us,” Kremer said.
It was more appropriate to call the exhibit Seeing Home, especially, she sighed, “after all we’ve been through.” Enough said.
To those who will never come home
The exhibit was dedicated “to all our friends who never got the opportunity to see home again, after October 7,” and especially commemorated Adele’s dear friend Judih Weinstein Haggai.
Weinstein Haggai was murdered by Hamas while walking in Kibbutz Nir Oz’s fields with her husband, Gadi Haggai, early on October 7. 
The snacks at the exhibit were vegan, honoring her passion. Recalling Weinstein Haggai’s warmth, patience, love, and goodness, Kremer observed, “She died so far from everything she lived.”
The split-screen nature of Nirim’s post-October 7 life hung over the delightful photos of kids in mid-jump at the pool, dads dressed in silly ways at a community Shavuot ceremony, and stunning landscapes of the surrounding fields.
Adele, who survived for 11 hours in her safe room, said that in the unnerving weeks following the massacre, “from week to week I didn’t know where I was going to sleep, but I knew that every Monday I would send in my photography assignment.” The power of ritual, of regularity, in defying catastrophe was quintessentially Israeli.
Beyond feeling how, for these survivors, the pall of October 7 infects everything, the juxtaposition of Nirim’s renaissance, with Weinstein Haggai’s beloved Nir Oz just 2.5 kilometers away, suspended in October 7, was sobering.
On the day of the massacre, Nirim lost five civilians and had five members kidnapped. Those devastating losses pale compared to the 47 souls Hamas murdered in Nir Oz, while kidnapping 76 people – 67 of whom were alive. Fifty-four eventually were freed.
What it costs to survive
Rehabilitating Nirim cost approximately 43 million shekels. Since last summer, it’s fully restored and functional – physically at least.
Most residents returned. It will cost over 10 times more to rebuild Nir Oz – and will take years. “Hamas didn’t just set out to murder us, kidnap us, abuse us,” Adele explained, “they wanted to destroy our communities, the societies we’ve built.”
Of more than 30 individual civilian communities assaulted that day, Hamas hit 22 kibbutzim. Intelligence documents and the terrorists’ boasts revealed that these terrorists delighted in ravaging the kibbutzim – all of which are within Israel’s original borders, the so-called Green Line.
But to Hamas and their enablers worldwide, every inch of Israel is “occupied territory.” Every Israeli is a “settler.” Even the most secular, left-wing, Peace Now kibbutz is an illegitimate “settlement,” reflecting the kind of Zionist success Hamas cannot tolerate and seeks to annihilate.
Apparently, it is quite easy for the world to forget that Hamas and other Gazans planned, intentional, unspeakable horrors. Yet the people of the Gaza border communities can’t forget – even the “lucky ones” back living their seemingly-normal lives.
Few Israelis forget either. That’s why we need our friends worldwide to understand how deep the trauma runs and how much we have learned about our many enemies’ non-negotiable evil.
Our friends should also take pride in Israel’s Zionist resilience. It’s remarkable that so many of those who were overrun on October 7 have returned, as Nirim’s members have, or are still vowing to return home.
Professor Gil Troy is a Distinguished Scholar of North American History at McGill University and a Senior Research Fellow at the JPPI, the Jewish People Policy Institute. He is the author of nine books on presidential history and nine on Zionism, including Theodor Herzl: Zionist Writings from the Library of the Jewish People, as well as his latest e-book, The Essential Guide to the US-Israel Partnership: the 250th Anniversary Edition.

‘Burn in hell’: Israeli settlers spread hate through graffiti, attacks

‘Burn in hell’: Israeli settlers spread hate through graffiti, attacks
Walls across occupied West Bank have been transformed into canvases for racist slogans, signaling a brazen drive for displacement of Palestinians.
Scrawled in black graffiti, the word “Revenge” stains the terracotta facade of a school in Jalud, a village in the occupied West Bank.
Other slogans carry a more direct threat: “Burn in hell,” reads one. “Get out of the village,” says another.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli government accused of complicity as settlers demolish Jericho homes
- list 2 of 3Israeli raids, arrests continue as UN warns West Bank at ‘breaking point’
- list 3 of 3Palestine weekly: Netanyahu hedges on Gaza roadmap
It is a familiar sight across this community, located 27km (17 miles) south of Nablus and home to some 1,000 Palestinians.
Under the cover of darkness or in broad daylight, Israeli settlers have been targeting Palestinian public institutions and homes with increased intensity, spraying slogans with racist and threatening messages, as well as invoking biblical passages to justify committing their crimes.
Residents and officials say the defacing of the buildings typically accompanies violent settler attacks. Jalud has been subjected to five major assaults since last January, the latest being on August 4 when settlers burned vehicles and sprayed racist slogans on a residential building.
‘Take revenge here’
Jalud resident Misbah al-Haj Mohammed said some of the slogans bear the names of settlers who carried out previous attacks, as if wanting to “challenge” people in the village and neighbouring areas.
He added that the messages written on school walls are aimed specifically at children to create a sense of fear in them about attending classes, while those threatening expulsion want to signify that “killing and displacement are inevitably coming”.
The head of the village council, Raed al-Haj Mohammed, described the slogans as “racist and liquidationist”, saying they are usually used by members of the Hilltop Youth group calling for the expulsion of Palestinians.
A decentralised network made up mostly of Jewish youths between the ages of 15 and 20, the Hilltop Youth is among the most prominent violent settler groups in the West Bank.
The group takes its name from a strategy of establishing settlement outposts on “hilltops”, a term referring not only to the land itself, but also to a settlement model based on creating new outposts outside existing illegal settlements and later imposing a fait accompli to pave the way for their legalisation.
“When a soldier is killed in Gaza, they take revenge here, and write the names of their dead on our walls,” Raed told Al Jazeera, adding that residents immediately move to remove the slogans.
‘Zero-Arab state’
Azzam Abu al-Adas, a researcher in Israeli affairs, said the settlers’ choice of writings was a “reflection of deep ideological concepts”.
He cited the slogan “Death to Arabs”, describing it as “an explicit call for genocide, within a replacement settlement vision seeking to reach a zero-Arab state in the region extending between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea”.
Abu al-Adas pointed out that the idea of genocide has become a “mainstream current” in Israeli society since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023, entrenching a conviction that solving the “Palestinian problem” could only happen through “annihilating Palestinians or expelling them permanently, and destroying the urban environment they inhabit to get rid of their presence completely”.
Referring to The Price Tag movement, a clandestine network of far-right settler groups that emerged in 2008, Abu al-Aldas said that from an ideological perspective, its members see Palestinians as the “occupier” of the land who must pay the price for their stay until they are “forced to leave and exit … permanently”.
He added that the scrawled slogans often include the names of killed settlers, meant to signal that the attack was a “retaliatory act for their memory” and pointed to an escalation in the use of religious texts employed to incite the killing of non-Jews, alongside slogans about “the promise of the Lord”.
Walid Habbas, a researcher in Israeli affairs, said the violent settler groups “want to punish the Palestinian existence itself because it obstructs the project of controlling the land and not only because it carried out resistance”.
Habbas said that burning crops, mosques and homes “is not a random choice” as it targets the elements of survival and connection to the place.
Habbas also noted that some of the messages, which are written in Hebrew, are not primarily directed at Palestinians, who may not read the language. Instead, they serve as an “ownership mark” addressing other settlers, as well as the Israeli state and public. Consequently, “the Palestinian wall turns into a banner declaring that the place has become, symbolically, a reclaimed land”, said Habbas.
He added that the writing of such slogans aims to strip Palestinians of their humanity and make harming them acceptable, as well as providing “holy cover” to perpetrators and entrenching the argument that the land “does not accommodate two peoples”.
Habbas cited an attack last month on the village of Qusra, where settlers set fire to a mosque and sprayed slogans and a Star of David on its walls. The targeting of the mosque “is not a revenge against an individual, but a strike at the unifying structure that produces collective identity and connection to the place”, he said.
The Star of David serves as a “sovereign signature”, saying that “this place is subject to us”, added Habbas.
He also highlighted what he believes is the attack’s most dangerous aspect: the writing is “crude, fast and unhidden”, drawn on a facade overlooking the public road so it is seen and photographed.
He described this deliberate act as “not recklessness”, but a “declaration of confidence that the perpetrator will not be held accountable”, and that “the public nature of the crime itself is a message about the balance of power and a structural complicity that makes this violence possible and recurrent”.

Solar energy plugs hydro-electric shortfall in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:57:37 UTC
22:57:37 KST

Solar energy plugs hydro-electric shortfall in Switzerland
Electricity production in Switzerland is declining because low water levels are reducing output from run-of-the-river hydropower plants. However, abundant solar power generation is helping to prevent supply bottlenecks.
Unlike just a few years ago, solar power is now making a substantial contribution to Switzerland’s electricity supply. This development is largely the result of the rapid expansion of photovoltaic installations since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine.
Small rivers are often reduced to mere trickles, while larger rivers like the Aare, Rhine, and Rhône are witnessing the lowest levels of water since records began. The ongoing drought, without any significant rainfall, has also had a major impact on electricity production. Power plants that use convert the flow of rivers into power are producing considerably less electricity compared to long-term averages.
More
I went solar in Switzerland – I now know why many people don’t
This is also evident when compared to other exceptionally dry years such as 2003 or 2022. The difference is particularly striking when electricity production is compared to a rainy year like 2016.
The lower electricity production also directly affects energy companies. Repower, the electricity supplier from the canton of Graubünden, writes in response to an inquiry: “In our hydroelectric power plants, electricity production in the months of May to July was around 25% below the long-term average due to the low water inflows.”
Less snow melt
The canton Valais energy company Forces Motrices Valaisannes (FMV) echoed a similar sentiment: “Due to the low amount of precipitation in winter, the snow cover at the end of winter was thin and below the long-term average. This led to less snowmelt and thus a decrease in electricity generation from run-of-river power plants between May and July.”
The same effects are evident outside the Alpine region as well. The Lausanne-based energy company Alpiq reports: “We are experiencing very low water inflows for our river power plants, particularly the facilities (…) along the Aare River.” Alpiq estimates the decline at these plants at around 15 percent compared to the long-term average.
More
Swiss Alpine solar farms show promise – and limits
Although the run-of-river power plants are currently supplying significantly less electricity than usual, and the two nuclear power plants Beznau I and II are also offline, there has been no electricity shortage in Switzerland so far.
This is mainly due to the many hours of sunshine. Because the sun shines daily from early morning until late at night, solar power plants produce a lot of electricity.
“Solar energy currently acts as a significant buffer against the unfavourable hydrological conditions in Switzerland. Without the strong expansion of photovoltaics in recent years, the electricity balance would currently be under more strain”, the Federal Electricity Commission Elcom told Swiss public broadcaster SRF.
Growth in photovoltaics
In recent years, the number of solar power systems (photovoltaics) in Switzerland has grown significantly. Consequently, the share of solar electricity has also increased considerably.
“Without this additional contribution, Switzerland would likely have to use more water from the reservoirs for electricity generation, import more electricity or export less, and could also face higher electricity prices,” stated Elcom, which oversees electricity supply in Switzerland.
Solar power plants help to conserve water in the pumped-storage reservoirs. This water is primarily used for electricity production before sunrise and after sunset, when the solar power plants are no longer generating electricity.

Russia Produces 3,000 Geran-4/5 Drones a Month, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:56:28 UTC
22:56:28 KST

Russia’s defense industry is producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones per month, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (DIU) told Militarnyi in an inquiry published Wednesday, Aug. 12.
According to the Militarnyi, the serial production of the drones has been established at a facility in Russia’s Yelabuga, within the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, while other Russian companies supply components for the production chain.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The growing use of the drones is linked to improvements in their flight characteristics, particularly their ability to overcome Ukrainian air defenses, according to the DIU.
Russia expands production in Tatarstan
Despite the current production rate, Russia’s Defense Ministry is seeking to further expand manufacturing capacity at Alabuga.
Large-scale construction of new facilities was observed at the special economic zone in July 2026, according to satellite imagery cited by Militarnyi. Construction reportedly began in May, although the exact purpose of the new buildings remains unclear.
The expansion comes as Russia prepares to increase its use of jet-powered attack drones.
In June, then-Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrsky said jet-powered drones could eventually account for 50% of Russia’s attack UAVs used in attacks against Ukraine.
The latest DIU information provided to Militarnyi supports the assessment that Russia is increasing production of jet-powered variants of the Geran drone family.
Ukraine Finds Nvidia AI Chip in New Russian Missile, HUR Says
At the same time, the intelligence agency said Russia has halted production of the Geran-3 jet-powered kamikaze drone.
Geran-4 is faster and has a longer range
The Geran-4 is based on the concept of the earlier Geran-3 but has a more powerful engine and an airframe optimized for higher speeds.
The drone has a wingspan of around 3 meters and is approximately 3.5 meters long. Its maximum takeoff weight has increased from 350 to 450 kilograms.
The Geran-4 uses a turbojet engine producing 160 kilogram-force of thrust, roughly twice the thrust of the Chinese Telefly JT80 used by its predecessor.
According to Militarnyi, this allows the drone to reach a cruise speed of 350–500 kilometers per hour, compared with 280–330 km/h for the previous version.
Its reported range has also increased from 600 to 850 kilometers.
The Geran-4 can operate at altitudes between 100 and 5,000 meters and remain airborne for around 2.5 hours. Its warhead weighs at least 50 kilograms.
Geran-5 resembles a missile
The Geran-5 has a substantially different design from earlier members of the Geran family.
Instead of the delta-wing configuration associated with Shahed-type drones, the aircraft has a fuselage shape more closely resembling a cruise missile.
Militarnyi therefore describes the Geran-5 as a “missile-drone,” a category also being developed by Ukrainian defense manufacturers.
The Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead and has a reported attack range of around 1,000 kilometers.
It can also reportedly carry R-73 (NATO: AA-11, “Archer”) air-to-air missiles equipped with infrared seekers.
According to the DIU, the Geran-5 can be launched from aircraft, including Su-25 attack aircraft.
The growing production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones suggests Russia is seeking to supplement its large-scale Shahed-type drone campaign with faster and more capable systems that are more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
On Aug. 12 Kyiv came under a second Russian drone attack, with air defenses engaging jet-powered drones approaching the capital from multiple directions. Kyiv Post team members across the city and surrounding villages reported hearing loud explosions as Russia continued its near-round-the-clock aerial attacks against Ukraine.
Earlier Russia targeted a shopping center in Zaporizhzhia overnight. The attack caused extensive damage to an Epicentr store, while overnight Russian attacks also killed two women in Kherson.

“Putin still hopes that attacks, cold and darkness will break the Ukrainians’ resistance. We will not let that happen. As a result of Russia’s continuing aggression, Ukrainians face yet another difficult winter of war. As the cold weather sets in, people across the country will have to contend with disruptions to electricity and heating and worry about how to keep their homes warm,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stressed.

That is why we are directing our assistance primarily to where it is needed most – to families trying to cope in their own homes, to people forced to flee their homes because of the war, and to rescue workers who come to their aid even in the most difficult circumstances,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna added.
Estonia is providing NGO Mondo with €160,000 to help accommodation centres for internally displaced people near the front line in Sumy, Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv oblasts prepare for winter. Thirteen centres will be supplied with heating equipment and materials, while two of them will also undergo repairs and improvements to their thermal insulation. With Estonia’s support, approximately 860 internally displaced people – primarily older people, people with disabilities, women and children – will have warm accommodation this coming winter.

The funding will help families keep their homes warm and cover the costs of keeping livestock through the winter, as livestock farming is an important source of livelihood for many. The project is co-funded by the European Commission’s Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO).
The Estonian Rescue Association will receive €20,000 to procure equipment for two mobile emergency points for rescuers from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SESU). The mobile emergency points will provide people in crisis areas with a place to keep warm, access electricity and, where necessary, receive psychological support. SESU will deploy the emergency points to areas where people are most in need of assistance due to hostilities, air attacks and damage to energy infrastructure.

Can US stop Netanyahu from derailing latest Gaza peace deal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:55:43 UTC
22:55:43 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s outright rejection of a key condition in the US-backed Gaza peace plan has thrown the whole initiative into uncertainty.
On Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet that Tel Aviv rejects the 15-point document, insisting the Israeli military will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.
Last month, Hamas dissolved its government in Gaza and formally handed over administration to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) under the US-backed ceasefire framework.
The dissolution of the Gaza government was followed by Hamas agreeing to a complete disarmament subject to Israeli withdrawal from Gaza.
The peace roadmap, part of the second phase of US President Donald Trump’s broader 20-point Gaza plan, originally presented in October 2025, links a phased Israeli withdrawal from Gaza to the demilitarisation of Hamas under a Palestinian technocratic administration backed by the Board of Peace.
Despite a ceasefire agreed in October 2025, Israel has continued to violate the fragile agreement by killing more than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza.
At the same time, Tel Aviv has kept expanding its control over the besieged territory by moving the demarcation line.
In other words, Israel’s unilaterally drawn boundary keeps moving further into the enclave, effectively making Gaza smaller by the month. Israel currently controls roughly two-thirds of Gaza.
Analysts are sceptical about whether Washington will be successful in preventing Netanyahu from sabotaging the US-backed Gaza peace plan.
Mustafa Yetim, professor of international relations at Eskisehir Osmangazi University, tells TRT World that the Trump administration appears willing to press the Israeli government to take steps consistent with the agreed Gaza peace plan.
But Israel continues to fiercely resist withdrawal, partly because of domestic reasons, such as the general elections scheduled for October.
“This position could seriously undermine the peace process, particularly because Hamas’s willingness to proceed with disarmament is closely linked to Israel’s full withdrawal from the territory,” he says.
According to Yetim, Trump appears to have sought greater alignment with key regional actors and broader international and domestic public opinion – all of which have placed increasing pressure on his administration to constrain Israel’s atrocities in Gaza.
“At the same time, radical Jewish-nationalist and Zionist elements within the Netanyahu government… remain committed to maintaining policies of military intervention and territorial control,” he notes.
This explains why the Israeli approach has increasingly come into conflict with the Trump administration’s broader regional vision, Yetim says.
“The unresolved issue of Israeli withdrawal could become a critical point of friction between Washington and Tel Aviv and potentially jeopardise the broader implementation of the Gaza peace framework,” he says.
Zahide Tuba Kor, a scholar of Middle Eastern studies, tells TRT World that she is highly sceptical that any US pressure on Israel will succeed.
She says she never expected Israel to abide by the ceasefire agreement. It was only a means for Israel to continue its genocide in Gaza without attracting the world’s attention and reaction, she notes.
The Trump administration may pressure Israel to reconsider its decision, but Kor does not believe it will work.
“Israeli politics and society cannot survive without war,” she says.
A powerful lobby supports reoccupation and settlement in Gaza, she says. No Israeli government can back down due to external pressures, especially in the run-up to the elections.
Kor recalls Netanyahu’s statement from his time in the US as deputy ambassador in the 1980s that remains relevant: “If the US government were to oppose Israeli policy, I know how to manipulate American public opinion against its own government”.
With US midterm elections in November and evangelicals in the Republican Party’s base being “more pro-Israel than Israel itself,” Kor says that no American president can afford to take such a risk.
Does US have leverage over Israel?
Yetim says Israel’s military power has long been enabled by comprehensive Western support, especially American, through advanced capabilities, political protection, economic aid, and diplomacy.
The US is the biggest backer of the Israeli military. According to the Costs of War Project at Brown University, the US spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel from October 2023 to September 2025.
“This dynamic could change significantly if the US were to reassess the broader costs that Israel’s regional policies impose on American economic, military, and diplomatic interests,” he says.
Washington possesses a relatively broad range of instruments, including adjustments to military assistance, diplomatic protection, arms transfers, and broader political and economic support, he says.
Yet, the effectiveness of these levers of influence ultimately depends on the willingness of the US administration to use them, he says.
The influence of pro-Israel constituencies and lobbying networks has also historically limited room for any US manoeuvre against Tel Aviv.
“As long as these political, economic, military, and discursive alignments remain largely intact, Washington’s leverage over Israel is likely to remain substantial in theory but considerably more limited in practice,” Yetim says.
Kor acknowledges the existence of the levers of US influence over Israel. But she casts doubt on whether the US will ever use those instruments of influence.
Cutting arms sales will leave Israel with “no choice but to submit”. That’s because neither Tel Aviv’s domestic production of arms nor that of its other allies can fully replace American weapons, she insists.
Washington can also remove diplomatic protection, allow international court proceedings, abandon Israeli propaganda framing in media coverage, or cut economic aid, she notes.
“Israel has survived on external support since its foundation. Israel will not back down unless that support is cut off. But the US will not use all its cards,” she says.
If the US does not force Israel to change its decision on the withdrawal question, the consequences for the peace process can be devastating, analysts say.
According to Yetim, a failure to convince Israel against a renewed military action and occupation is a “more plausible scenario” than the establishment of a stable political order in Gaza and the wider Palestinian territories.
The underlying Israeli security and political paradigm can pose a “persistent challenge to any regional arrangement” aimed at containing Israel’s interventionist and expansionist policies.
An even worse outcome would be the collapse of the plan and a broader cycle of confrontation involving other regional players, potentially drawing the US deeper into Middle East instability, he says.
“There is a relatively fragile boundary between containing regional instability and allowing it to escalate into a much wider conflict,” he adds.
Maintaining stability in Gaza is not merely a desirable outcome for Washington, he says.
“It is becoming a strategic necessity.”

Treasury Rolls Back Ownership Reporting Obligations for U.S. Companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

The U.S. Department of the Treasury has permanently eliminated beneficial ownership reporting requirements for domestic companies and individuals under the Corporate Transparency Act, gutting a major federal anti-money-laundering disclosure program for American small businesses.
The rule effectively exempts U.S. citizens operating domestic businesses from disclosing their beneficial ownership information as was mandated under the Corporate Transparency Act, a landmark anti-corruption law enacted in December 2020, aimed at combating money laundering and illicit finance.
Under the update, foreign companies must still report beneficial ownership information for foreign individuals to FinCEN. However, foreign companies are exempt from reporting ownership information regarding U.S. citizens, as well as details about Americans who assist them in registering to conduct business within the U.S.
FinCEN also announced that it will delete all previously collected information regarding U.S. business owners from its beneficial ownership database.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of Polish-Ukrainian relations has risen to 46%, the highest figure ever recorded by Polish state research agency CBOS. Only 12% think relations are good. By contrast, three years ago, in mid-2023, only 3% had a negative view and 64% a positive one.
Meanwhile, CBOS also found that belief among Poles that reconciliation between the two neighbours, who share a difficult history, is possible is at its lowest level on record, 53%, down from 78% three years ago.
The findings follow other polls showing worsening attitudes towards Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland in recent years, and come amid an ongoing diplomatic crisis triggered by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two.

Relations between Poland and Ukraine improved significantly in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, as Poland welcomed millions of Ukrainian refugees and provided Kyiv with extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support.
However, since 2023, those relations have been hit by a series of controversies over Ukrainian agricultural exports, border blockades by Polish farmers and truckers, and, above all, over the two nations’ difficult World War Two history.
Among Poles who now hold a negative view of relations, CBOS also asked them who was responsible for the situation. A large majority, 65%, primarily blamed Ukraine, while only 4% said it was Poland’s fault and 28% placed responsibility on both sides.
In its regular surveys since 1997, the agency has also asked Poles if they believe that reconciliation between Poles and Ukrainians is possible or not. In the early 2000s, that figure rose to a record level of 81%, and in 2023 it still stood at 78%. Now, however, it has dropped to an all-time low of 53%.
There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over their difficult, intertwined histories, in particular during the first half of the 20th century.
In World War Two, Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, in an ethnic-cleansing operation known as the Volhynia massacres.
Poland has officially recognised that episode as a genocide. However, Ukraine rejects that label and also points to the persecution of Ukrainians who lived in the interwar Polish state, as well as to massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during World War Two.

Those tensions recently boiled over after Zelensky, in May this year, approved a request to rename a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres but is remembered positively in Ukraine for its role in fighting Moscow-imposed Soviet rule.
Zelensky’s decision prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip the Ukrainian president of Poland’s highest honour. While tensions have since calmed somewhat, the dispute remains unresolved.
However, even before that diplomatic crisis broke out, polling showed increasingly negative attitudes in Poland towards both Ukraine and Ukrainians, who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group.
In its annual survey of attitudes towards various national and ethnic groups, published in February, CBOS found that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians had increased by five percentage points year-on-year, to 43%. Only 29% said they liked Ukrainians.

Retired Bundeswehr general says Nord Stream pipelines could have been legitimate target for Ukraine
Klaus Wittmann, a retired Bundeswehr brigadier general and lecturer in contemporary history at the University of Potsdam, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"I am prepared to go so far as to say that, from a military-strategic and moral perspective, this was a legitimate target," Wittmann said, commenting on whether Nord Stream could be considered a legitimate target if the German investigation's theory of Ukrainian involvement is confirmed.
At the same time, he stressed that he was not offering a legal assessment of the case and was not questioning the independence of the judiciary.
"I am not a lawyer and, of course, I do not want to question the independence of the judiciary. But if you look at the background, I was among those who strongly opposed Nord Stream 2," the retired general said.
According to him, the decision to build Nord Stream 2 was made after Russia had already occupied Crimea, despite warnings from Ukraine and Central and Eastern European countries.
"The decision on Nord Stream 2 was made when Crimea had already been occupied for a long time. Despite this, people continued to believe that Russia could be relied upon as a reliable supplier of cheap gas and called it a purely economic project. At the same time, they turned a blind eye to what the Baltic states, Poland and, of course, the Ukrainians had repeatedly told us: from Russia's perspective, it was a geopolitical project," Wittmann said.
He also recalled the position of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
"Here I would like to quote Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who said that the problem was the construction of Nord Stream 2, not its destruction," Wittmann said.
At the same time, he acknowledged the seriousness of destroying someone else's property but urged that the case also be viewed in the broader political context of Russia's war.
"Of course, destroying someone else's property is a serious matter. But we also need to look at it from a political and psychological perspective and ask whether it is in Germany's interests for the first conviction for a 'war crime' in the war in Ukraine to be handed down against a Ukrainian – and in Germany, of all places?" Wittmann said.
He noted that he did not know how much room for maneuver Germany's Federal Prosecutor General's Office had in the case or "whether it was obliged to seek extradition."
"But given the scale and horror of Russia's war crimes, I do not consider it acceptable for the German justice system to focus primarily on a 'Ukrainian war crime,'" Wittmann said.
On September 26, 2022, explosions damaged three of the four pipelines of Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 in the Baltic Sea. In June 2026, Germany's Federal Prosecutor General's Office charged a Ukrainian citizen, identified as Serhii K., a former Ukrainian serviceman, with, among other offenses, aiding and abetting a war crime through an attack on a civilian object. According to the prosecution, the group acted on the orders of Ukrainian state bodies, with the aim of halting Russian gas supplies and depriving Russia of revenues that could be used to finance the war. The arrested Ukrainian has denied involvement.
In July 2026, Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said that its investigation had found no evidence of involvement by Ukrainian state bodies or officials in organizing the explosions.

Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:53:02 UTC
22:53:02 KST

Lebanon passes a controversial general amnesty law
BEIRUT (AP) — Lebanon’s parliament Wednesday passed a controversial general amnesty law, a day after a majority of legislators voted to formally abolish the death penalty.
Lawmakers who backed the bill call it a beginning to correcting past overreach by the judiciary and security agencies and help reduce prison overcrowding, but critics say it is skewed and largely benefits Sunni Islamist prisoners.
The initial proposal, debated since 2019, has exposed sectarian tensions among the country’s multitude of Islamic and Christian sects.
A sweeping law that has exceptions
The last time Lebanon approved a similar amnesty was in 1991, when the majority of the country’s combatants and militia leadership were absolved of any atrocities and possible war crimes following the country’s devastating 1975-90 civil war that killed about 150,000 people and left 17,000 missing.
The new law replaces death sentences with long prison terms, reduces life sentences, and frees some convicted militants and drug dealers. It excludes rape, trafficking, corruption, terror funding, and premeditated murder, but reduces sentences for killing Lebanese troops. Some detainees will be released immediately.
Repeated drug offenders and Lebanese who have been convicted of collaborating with Israel were excluded from the amnesty.
It also remains unknown if the amnesty applies to Lebanese families who took refuge in Israel after occupying Israeli forces withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000 but who were not involved in military operations against Lebanon.
Released foreign prisoners, mainly Syrian Islamist militant prisoners, would be transferred to Lebanon’s General Security intelligence agency that is responsible for enforcing immigration laws. It wasn’t immediately known if they would be deported.
Concerns rise over the fate of extremist Islamist prisoners
While the law was debated in parliament, lawmakers from various sects made different demands.
Sunnis wanted the release of Islamist militants while Shiites demanded drug dealers, mostly from Lebanon’s eastern Baalbek region where cannabis is planted, to be freed. Christians required amnesty for hundreds of Lebanese who fled to Israel after the Israeli withdrawal. Many have links to the Israeli-backed South Lebanon Army militia, which collapsed following the withdrawal.
However, the most controversial point in the yearslong debate was the fate of extremist Islamist prisoners, including firebrand cleric Ahmad al-Assir.
Al-Assir gained support in southern Lebanon for his vocal criticism of the powerful Shiite militant Hezbollah group’s involvement in Syria’s uprising that turned into civil war. In 2013, clashes between his supporters and opponents killed 18 Lebanese soldiers. He was sentenced to death in 2017.
His fate remains unclear, but Lebanese lawmaker Waddah Sadek, a Sunni Muslim and supporter of the law, told The Associated Press al-Assir could be released “between a year and a half and two years.”
Some celebrate while others feel wronged
Sunni legislators largely celebrated the law passing.
Bilal Abdullah, who represents the Druze-led Progressive Socialist Party, said the amnesty law is not intended to benefit just one sect.
“We are turning a political page where (Sunnis were) targeted, justly and unjustly,” Abdullah told reporters in parliament. “Targeted by a regime, security agencies, and unfortunately the military tribunal with some of its unjust convictions.”
Supporters of detained Islamists claim their sentencings came at a time when the Shiite Muslim Hezbollah militant group had greater political power in the country and larger sway over its security institutions and judicial system, directly targeting the country’s Sunni Muslims.
They also said the detainees weren’t allowed a fair trial and some were held for too long in pretrial detention due to Lebanon’s swamped courts.
Videos circulating on social media showed Islamist prisoners in the notorious Roumieh prison chanting “God is great” in celebration once the law was approved.
The families of the killed Lebanese soldiers have called the law a grave injustice, saying that the perpetrators behind the death of their loved ones should remain behind bars or even be sentenced to death.
Civil society and reformists have largely been critical of the move.
Activist and lawyer Nizar Saghieh, who co-founded the watchdog group Legal Agenda, said justice “comes through accountability and building institutions, not a general amnesty.”
Saghieh criticized lawmakers who called the amnesty a form of justice due to what they said were unfair trials in military and civil courts. However, they haven’t made any real structural reforms, he said.
“They talk about injustice in military courts, but they are still functioning as before.”
