Ex-Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, who drove economic reforms and led China into the WTO, dies at 97
BEIJING (AP) — Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji, the impatient, sharp-tongued reformer who helped ignite China’s explosive economic boom by forcing wrenching change on state industry in the 1990s and leading the country into the World Trade Organization, has died of illness, state media reported Wednesday. He was 97.
Zhu died in Beijing at around 11 a.m. on Wednesday, the official news agency Xinhua reported.
Once sent into rural exile to do manual labor for praising reforms in other communist countries, Zhu pushed through a dizzying array of changes as premier, China’s top economic post, from 1998 to 2003 under former President Jiang Zemin.
Zhu clashed with Communist Party conservatives and state industry bosses as he pushed state-owned companies to become efficient and profitable. That cost millions of layoffs, but helped propel China to overtake Japan as the second-largest economy behind the United States in 2010.
Building on former leader Deng Xiaoping’s 1979 reforms, Zhu is credited with supplying the resourcefulness and tenacity to push through history-making changes such as China’s WTO membership, which helped to transform China into the world’s biggest exporter.
Those changes helped to keep economic growth above 8% a year from 2000 to 2010, peaking at 14.2% in 2007.
A spiky personality who fought corruption and conservatives
Named premier in 1998 at age 69, Zhu became a popular figure by criticizing official bungling and graft and accepting blame when the government fell short. His demanding style earned him the nicknames Boss and Zhu Fengzi, or Madman Zhu.
“I have prepared 100 coffins here — 99 for corrupt officials and one for myself,” Zhu said in 1998, according to the party newspaper People’s Daily.
Zhu ranked No. 3 in the party hierarchy behind Jiang and Li Peng, chairman of the ceremonial legislature, the National People’s Congress. But he was a technician without his own power base. Zhu complained that allowed officials to ignore his orders.
Zhu made his name as a deputy premier in the 1990s by crushing inflation. He enforced price controls and cut off loans to money-losing state companies, rebuffing resistance by local leaders — a pattern Zhu would repeat as he fought conservatives over the pace of reform.
Zhu led efforts to secure WTO membership following marathon negotiations that began in the 1980s. That status would enshrine free trade as a national commitment, giving Zhu a tool to force local officials to stop protecting favored companies.
Zhu’s campaign was nearly derailed when he went to Washington in 1999 with market-opening concessions to win U.S. endorsement of the WTO bid. The Clinton administration rejected the offer as inadequate, while his political enemies at home accused him of offering too much, but Zhu survived and China went on to join the body in December 2001.
Zhu launched China’s home ownership boom in 1998 with an initiative to sell apartments owned by state companies. Families rushed to buy, and within a decade the majority of urban housing was privately owned.
Still, Zhu was less an advocate of free enterprise than a skilled bureaucrat who carried out party orders to whip state industry into shape.
Zhu showed no interest in privatizing the economy. He played a key role in drafting plans in the 1990s to turn banks, airlines, oil companies and other enterprises into profit-oriented corporations but to retain government ownership.
Zhu stood out for admitting official failings
Born Oct. 23, 1928, in Mao Zedong’s home province of Hunan, Zhu paid an early price for his willingness to take risks and speak out.
After a start as an economic planner, his career went into a 22-year eclipse when he was labelled a “rightist” in 1957 for praising reforms in Hungary and Yugoslavia. He was banished to the countryside during the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution to do manual labor.
Rehabilitated in 1979, Zhu rose swiftly, becoming deputy Shanghai party secretary in 1987 and mayor the next year.
As mayor in 1989, Zhu gained a reputation for moderation when he placated protesters and pledged not to call in the military.
“He managed to defuse, with considerable subtlety, a tense political situation that could have developed into localized violence or worse if the military had felt it necessary to intervene,” wrote Australian diplomat Shelley Warner in the 1991 book “The Pro-Democracy Protests in China: Reports from the Provinces.”
Zhu’s boss, Jiang, would soon be called to Beijing by Deng and made party leader. Zhu was named deputy premier in 1991 and joined the party’s ruling Standing Committee in 1993.
Zhu broke with the leadership’s stance of infallibility by admitting and taking blame for official failings.
In 1998, after summer floods killed 4,150 people and officials were accused of embezzling money meant for anti-flood dikes, Zhu complained some barriers were no stronger than bean curd.
Three years later, he apologized on national television for his Cabinet’s failure to protect the public after an explosion in a schoolhouse in southern China killed at least 42 people, most of them children.
Zhu enlivened the party’s bland image by cracking jokes in public, sometimes at his own expense. Laughter erupted at a 1999 news conference when he said a recent photo “made me look like a dead man.”
One of Zhu’s proudest triumphs as deputy premier was to craft a tax system that required local officials to hand more revenue to Beijing. He said in 1996 that he deserved a Nobel Prize in economics for that.
Zhu rarely appeared in public after leaving office as premier.
Zhu was married to Lao An, a fellow Hunan native. Their son, Yunlai, also known as Levin Zhu, is a former CEO of China International Capital Corp., a government-owned investment bank.
Their daughter, Yanlai, led a charity organization supporting schoolchildren that was backed by Zhu Rongji.
___
A previous version of this report incorrectly stated that Zhu died at 98. He was 97 years old.
___
Leung reported from Hong Kong. McDonald, a longtime Associated Press journalist who retired in 2023, was the main author of this obituary.

Israel says Gaza drone strike targeted a Hamas commander, and other developments in the Mideast
The Israeli military said it struck a Hamas commander Wednesday in northern Gaza using a targeted drone strike despite pressure to halt such attacks from officials overseeing peace efforts.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Israel says it struck a Hamas commander, but unclear if he was killed
An Israeli drone strike hit a man in the city of Beit Lahiya who was described by Israel’s military as a Hamas commander. It was the first targeted strike Israel has announced since Aug. 3.
Targeted strikes have come under closer scrutiny since U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal aimed at advancing peace efforts in Gaza that would include halting such strikes.
Though Hamas accepted the plan to decommission its weapons, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected it earlier this week, saying Hamas must fully disarm before Israel accepts the terms. Board of Peace officials have urged Israel to stop the strikes as a way of moving the deal forward.
The Israeli military did not provide details about the man targeted or say whether he was killed. Officials at Shifa and Nasser hospitals said four injured people were brought in Wednesday.
The Health Ministry in Gaza has reported 45 people killed since Aug. 1.
Three Pakistanis among the dead in Houthi attack on ship
Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday condemned an attack by Houthi rebels on a ship in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, saying three Pakistanis were killed and another wounded. The attack Tuesday killed six people total.
With the Strait of Hormuz effectively shut down by Iran and a U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, there has been a renewed focus on the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb strait at Yemen’s southern tip, which is an alternate route for Saudi Arabia to ship its oil.
The attack came as part of a growing number of Houthi strikes against government forces in Yemen and oil facilities in neighboring Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, and the kingdom’s shipping in the Red Sea.
Trump insists blockade gives US control of Strait of Hormuz
Claiming the U.S. has “total control” of the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump said Wednesday: “I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!”
Trump’s social media post referred to the U.S. blockade of Iran’s ports. A vital route for one-fifth of the world’s traded oil before the war, the strait has been largely closed to other traffic since the start of the war because of Iran’s attacks on shipping.
Those attacks have continued despite the blockade and U.S. strikes.
Iran has said the strait will only reopen if the U.S. meets a list of demands, including lifting the blockade.
Pakistan presses to defuse tensions between US and Iran
Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Iranian Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam in Islamabad on Wednesday as Pakistan seeks to resume peace negotiations between Iran and the U.S.
Their meeting came a day after Pakistan sent Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi to Tehran for talks with Iran’s top leaders.
An interim deal to end the fighting reached in mid-June is set to expire Monday. The ceasefire collapsed last month as the U.S. and Iran exchanged strikes over more than two weeks before pausing.
Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi told reporters Wednesday the June deal remains valid and the deadline could be extended.
“We are not closing the chapter,” Andrabi said.
Turkey condemns Colombia’s recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights
Turkey condemned the decision by Colombia’s new government to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, calling it a move to “legitimize Israel’s occupation” of the territory.
Colombia, shortly after the swearing-in of conservative Abelardo de la Espriella as president on Friday, became just the second country to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the territory, which Israel captured during the 1967 Middle East war and annexed in 1981.
The United States was the first during Trump’s first term, reversing a longstanding U.S. policy.
The United Nations recognizes the territory as part of Syria.
Kuwaiti authorities thwart plot against unnamed facility
Kuwait’s Interior Ministry said a “terrorist plot” against an unspecified facility was thwarted Wednesday when a Kuwaiti citizen affiliated with the Islamic State group was detained shortly before carrying out his plan.
The ministry said the man had received training on making explosives and activating drones to be used in the planned attack.
The ministry said a vital facility had been targeted but gave no further details.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,260 Troops and 60 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russian forces lost an estimated 1,260 troops and 60 artillery systems over the past 24 hours, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 12.
The latest figures bring Russia’s total estimated personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,461,660.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Russian forces also lost seven armored combat vehicles, two multiple launch rocket systems, one air defense system, 13 UGVs, and 1,767 operational-tactical UAVs over the past day.
Ukraine additionally reported the destruction of 388 vehicles and fuel tankers and two pieces of special equipment. No Russian tanks, aircraft, helicopters, or cruise missiles were recorded as destroyed during the reporting period.
Russia’s cumulative equipment losses are estimated at 12,259 tanks, 25,127 armored combat vehicles, 47,773 artillery systems, 2,022 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,561 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,203 UGVs, 456,339 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,007 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 132,931 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,516 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine’s General Staff recorded 237 combat engagements across the front over the past 24 hours.
The heaviest fighting was reported in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka sectors, which remained the most active areas of the battlefield during the reporting period.
Earlier, British Ambassador to Ukraine Neil Crompton said Russian forces are suffering heavy losses in eastern Ukraine while making only limited battlefield gains, describing their advance as slower than a snail.

Germany Sends Ukraine Firefighting Robots Built for Operations in Dangerous Environments

Germany Sends Ukraine Firefighting Robots Built for Operations in Dangerous Environments
On August 11, Germany provided Ukraine's State Emergency Service with a package of equipment that includes robotic systems for firefighting and operations in hazardous conditions.
The German Embassy in Ukraine announced the transfer in comments to European Pravda on the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The embassy detailed that the robotic complexes include the Alpha Robotics Wolf R1, the LUF 60, the LUF-CRV, and the Magirus AirCore TAF60.
Each is built to fight fires and operate in dangerous conditions. Berlin also handed over fire tanker trucks, a heavy evacuation tractor, and trucks fitted with crane manipulators.
The delivery also included buses and minibusses to transport personnel, portable fire pumps, booster pumps, and personal protective equipment for rescuers.
The package forms part of the broader support Germany has extended to the State Emergency Service since 2015. The transfer took place under the project "Support for State and Municipal Emergency Management in Ukraine," implemented by the German Society for International Cooperation (GIZ) on behalf of the German government.
Germany's chargé d'affaires, Katrin Buchholz, underscored the strain the war has placed on Ukrainian rescuers and the durability of the two countries' cooperation.
"In conditions of Russia's brutal war, the challenges for Ukraine's State Emergency Service have become even more complex. Ukrainian rescuers demonstrate extraordinary dedication to duty and heroism… Our partnership has lasted more than 10 years and goes far beyond the transfer of equipment: we strengthen institutions, exchange experience, and develop joint capabilities," she stated.
The robotic systems are meant to spare rescuers exposure in the most hazardous conditions, a danger that has proven lethal throughout the war. Russian attacks have killed at least 111 Ukrainian emergency responders and injured more than 550 since the 2022 full-scale war.
They have also destroyed hundreds of units of firefighting equipment and numerous fire stations, with the heaviest toll in frontline regions.

Russia Ramps Up Geran-4/5 Drone Production to 3,000 Per Month, Ukraine’s Intelligence Says
Russia’s defense industry produces approximately 3,000 Geran-4/5 strike drones each month, Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) told Militarnyi on August 12.
The use of these drone variants has become increasingly widespread as Russia improves their flight and technical characteristics, including capabilities intended to help them penetrate Ukrainian air defenses.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Serial production of the Geran-4/5 drones has been established at a facility in Yelabuga, within the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan.
Other Russian enterprises are also involved in the production process, supplying individual components and forming a broader manufacturing chain for the drones, according to Militarnyi.
The increased production of these variants comes as Russia’s military-industrial complex targets an overall output of 11,000 strike drones in August.
Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy chief of HUR, told RBC-Ukraine that the monthly production plan includes Geran-1, Geran-2, Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 drones, as well as Harpy, Gerbera, Gerbera Strike, and Gerbera Seeker variants.
Skibitskyi noted that Russia reduced both drone production and the intensity of its attacks in July while restructuring its manufacturing capacity. The changes are aimed at increasing production of the turbojet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.
Alongside the expansion of its drone arsenal, Russia is also redirecting resources within its ballistic missile production. Deputy chief added that Russia has increased ballistic missile output largely by suspending production of Kh-47 Kinzhal missiles, with rocket fuel previously allocated to the Kinzhal program now being redirected to other ballistic missile systems.

Lok Sabha inquiry panel indicts ex-HC judge Yashwant Varma in cash-at-home case
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 12, 2026, 16:39 IST
Comments

The panel found Justice Varma’s explanation over the discovery of unaccounted cash at his official residence "evasive" and "unsatisfactory".
NEW DELHI: A Lok Sabha inquiry committee on Wednesday indicted former Allahabad High Court judge Yashwant Varma in the cash-at-home case.The panel found Justice Varma’s explanation for the discovery of unaccounted cash at his official residence "evasive" and "unsatisfactory". Its report, tabled in both Houses of Parliament, said all three charges against Varma were proved.The committee said the charges are threefold - firstly, discovery and possession of unexplained Indian currency notes within official premises; secondly, failure to preserve and causing interference with material evidence; and thirdly, furnishing evasive and misleading explanations.
The committee examined documentary and electronic material and recorded evidence from witnesses. It also noted that Varma was given an opportunity to respond to the charges and present his defence."The statement of grounds accompanying the charges records the occurrence of fire, discovery of cash, location of the storeroom within the Government-allotted residence, the alleged conduct after the fire, and the explanation offered by the Judge," the inquiry report said."Article I is proved. Substantial unexplained Rs 500 denomination currency notes were found in the storeroom situated within the official residential premises at 30, Tughlaq Crescent, New Delhi.
The Judge failed to furnish a satisfactory explanation regarding the presence, source or ownership thereof," it said.On the third charge, the committee said Varma’s explanation, including his March 22, 2025 response and subsequent statements, did not demonstrate the "candour, transparency and institutional responsibility" expected in the circumstances. It remained evasive and unsatisfactory when tested against evidence from independent officials and other corroborative material.
A large amount of unaccounted, partially burnt cash was discovered in the outhouse of Varma’s official residence following a fire in March 2025. The discovery triggered allegations of judicial corruption, which Varma denied.Following an in-house inquiry ordered by the then Chief Justice of India, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla constituted a three-member panel headed by Supreme Court judge Aravind Kumar under the Judges (Inquiry) Act. The motion for the inquiry was backed by MPs from different political parties.Varma resigned during the inquiry. It remains unclear whether Parliament will proceed with the committee’s findings, as some legal experts have argued that the Judges (Inquiry) Act can be invoked only against a serving judge.

Ukraine Hits 2,200 Km Deep Into Russia—and Knocks Out Plant Producing 40% of Its LPG
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:21:08 UTC
19:21:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits 2,200 Km Deep Into Russia—and Knocks Out Plant Producing 40% of Its LPG
Russia’s largest producer of liquefied petroleum gas has halted operations indefinitely after a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ZapSibNeftekhim petrochemical complex in Tobolsk, more than 2,200 kilometers—roughly 1,370 miles—from the front line, Reuters reported on August 11.
The strike, carried out by Ukrainian Armed Forces on August 10, appears to have disrupted one of the most important links in Russia’s petrochemical production chain.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One industry source said the plant had been shut down indefinitely “while the extent of the damage and its consequences are being assessed.”
The impact was already visible on Russia’s commodity market the following day. No liquefied petroleum gas volumes scheduled for shipment from the Tobolsk loading point were offered on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange.
Earlier this year, around 4,000 metric tons of technical propane-butane mixture were sold through the Tobolsk loading point every day.
ZapSibNeftekhim is owned by Russian petrochemical giant Sibur and sits deep inside Russia’s Tyumen region, more than 2,200 kilometers from the line of contact.
That distance makes the attack another demonstration of Ukraine’s rapidly expanding ability to strike major Russian energy and industrial facilities far beyond the battlefield.
According to an OSINT analysis by Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, the drones struck the plant’s Central Gas Fractionation Unit.
The unit is particularly important because it sits at the beginning of the Tobolsk complex’s production chain. It processes broad fractions of light hydrocarbons obtained from associated petroleum gas and gas condensate before the resulting materials move into further petrochemical production.
Disrupting that stage can therefore affect operations beyond the individual unit that was physically hit.
ZapSibNeftekhim produces around six million metric tons of LPG per year—roughly 40% of Russia’s total production, making the indefinite shutdown potentially significant for the country’s domestic petrochemical industry.
Around half of the LPG produced at the facility is used directly as feedstock for petrochemical manufacturing at Sibur’s wider Tobolsk complex.
Earlier, the Omsk oil refinery, Russia’s largest, had halted processing after a Ukrainian drone strike.
The plant processed 22 million tons of oil in 2024, or around 440,000 barrels a day, according to source-based figures cited by Reuters. That output included 5 million tons of gasoline and 8 million tons of diesel—volumes now at risk while the two main units stay offline.

Turkey to keep Black Sea closed to military vessels - expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:19:40 UTC
19:19:40 KST

ISTANBUL, August 12. /TASS/. Turkey will not make concessions regarding the Montreux Convention and will not allow military ships into the Black Sea amid the Ukraine conflict, Turkish expert on international relations Canan Tercan told TASS.
Omer Celik, spokesperson for the ruling Justice and Development Party, earlier reported that several NATO allies had approached Ankara seeking possible waivers to the convention. However, he added that Turkey remains firmly committed to complying with the treaty.
"Despite increasing international pressure, it is unrealistic to expect Turkey to make concessions regarding the Montreux Convention and open the Black Sea for military vessels. For Turkey, the convention is not just a regulation of maritime traffic through the [Bosporus and Dardanelles] straits, but an essential framework for maintaining security and strategic balance in the region," the expert heading the IAU Politics Academy at Istanbul’s Aydin University said. She recalled that the Turkish Foreign Ministry has repeatedly and clearly stated its position on adhering to the convention. "Reviewing the principle of regional responsibility and the Montreux Convention is out of the question," Tercan emphasized, while commenting on today’s situation.
She said that withdrawing from the convention is legally possible, but quite unlikely. "The convention provides a firm mechanism for making amendments to it or denunciating it. But in practice, it is highly unlikely, as it requires negotiations between the sides and international consensus. This decision cannot be taken unilaterally, as the convention, being an international agreement, is binding for all its signatories. Even Articles 20 and 21 of the document, which provide for Turkey’s exclusive rights to control the passage of military vessels through the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits if it is at war or feels directly threatened by a war, do not give the country the right to change or withdraw from the convention unilaterally at its discretion," the expert said.
The Montreux Convention was signed in 1936 in Switzerland by representatives of ten states (Australia, Bulgaria, Great Britain, Greece, Romania, the Soviet Union, Turkey, France, Yugoslavia, Japan). It guarantees freedom of commercial shipping in the straits in peacetime. Article 19 stipulates that if Turkey does not participate in a war, the straits are closed for warships of parties to the conflict or landlocked countries. Turkey has enforced this article since the start of the special military operation in Ukraine.
According to the convention, all of the signatories may propose amendments to the document. A unanimous approval of all signatories is needed for amending key military articles, while a three-quarters majority, including Turkey, is required for less significant articles. However, analysts note that changing the convention would primarily be detrimental to Turkey itself, as under the Montreux Convention, it controls navigation in the straits.

Flight of 'ancient' Assad-era aircraft raises concerns in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:19:32 UTC
19:19:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel ‘concerned’ with reconstitution of Syrian Air Force after flight of ‘ancient’ Assad-era aircraft
Israel has privately conveyed its concerns over the reconstitution of Syria's air force to the US, though analysts who spoke to The New Arab expressed scepticism that the "ancient" Syrian aircraft pose any direct threat.
Israeli media reported on the communications between Washington and Tel Aviv after video emerged on Monday of what appeared to be two Syrian Sukhoi SU-22 aircraft conducting a flight in the northwestern province of Idlib.
The aircraft, which are remnants of the airforce of Syria's deposed Baathist government, were designed in the Soviet Union during the 1960s.
Israel's public broadcaster Kan, quoting a senior official, said Israel's concerns were being shared with the US.
It added that alongside the establishment of a new Syrian air force, Israel was also concerned about the movement of Turkish air defence systems into the country.
Nanar Hawach, Senior Analyst for Syria at the International Crisis Group, told The New Arab that "Israel can probably live with a Syrian air force of two ageing jets, few pilots and no spare parts", though is probably more alarmed by Ankara's involvement.
"What concerns it is the Turkish military presence taking shape around that force," he said, noting that Turkish training and defence agreements, as well as reports of basing plans, give their presence cover.
In late July, Syria's air force held a graduation ceremony for 1,000 cadets which saw the flight of a 1960s Czech-built L-39 trainer aircraft.
"It raises the question whether Turkish air defences and radars will follow, which would constrain Israeli operations over Syria in a way no salvaged Sukhoi can," Hawach said.
Aron Lund, a fellow at Century International and senior analyst at the Swedish Defence Research Agency, agreed that the "ancient" Sukhoi aircraft pose little danger to Israel, and are likely more useful for monitoring, suppressing internal threats, acting as symbols of prestige for the military, and providing training for pilots.
"It's not a realistic threat to Israel, which has a world-class, very modern air force with F-35 stealth fighters," he told The New Arab. "In so far as Israel protests this, it's hardly out of a sense of danger."
Rather, there are three other reasons why Israel might complain about the ongoing reconstitution of the Syrian Air Force, one of which is Israel's future use of Syrian airspace to bomb Iran, which a new air force would prevent.
"They [Israel] don't want Syria to have fighter jets or air defences and radars, at all. They might as well try to nip any reconstruction effort in the bud"
The second is on Israel's ongoing negotiations over Syria, which is largely focused on Israel's occupation of southern Syria following the toppling of the Assad regime in December 2024.
"Israel may want to raise the issue with the United States to extract whatever favours and benefits it can, since they're already negotiating over other things related to Syria."
Lund also pointed to Israel's desire to keep Syria "weak and dependent".
"Even an old, small air force could make the Syrian military better positioned to overpower the Israel-backed Druze groups in Suwayda. Israel does not want that."

A total of 4,769 young Palestinian men and women are being held in Israeli prisons, the head of the Palestinian Commission of Detainees' Affairs said on Wednesday.
Raed Abu al Hummus made the remarks on International Youth Day, observed annually on August 12 to highlight youth issues and their role in building societies.
“The number of young male detainees in Israeli prisons between the ages of 18 and 40 stands at 4,713, while the number of young female detainees is 56,” Abu al Hummus said.
He said 41 of the 91 Palestinian prisoners killed in Israeli prisons since October 2023 were young people.
“The bodies of 40 of them remain held by Israeli authorities, along with dozens of bodies of prisoners from different age groups,” he added.
Israel has escalated violations against Palestinian prisoners since launching its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

“Palestinian youth are the backbone of the Palestinian people’s struggle and the true fighters for liberation from occupation, injustice and oppression,” Abu al Hummus said.
“They will remain so until their hopes and dreams of freedom and independence are realised, and until they attain a normal life in security and stability,” he added.
He called on international institutions, particularly youth-focused organisations, to reject the targeting of Palestinian youth and raise their voices for their right to live free from the restrictions imposed by the Israeli occupation.
More than 9,400 Palestinian prisoners are held in Israeli jails, including 92 women and more than 370 children, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups. They face torture, starvation and medical neglect, which have led to the deaths of dozens of detainees.
In 1948, Israel was established on land occupied by armed Zionist gangs that carried out massacres and displaced at least 750,000 Palestinians, before Tel Aviv occupied the rest of the Palestinian territories and refused to withdraw from them or allow the establishment of a Palestinian state under UN resolutions.

Moscow mocks Romanian ‘evidence’ linking downed drones to Russia
Romanian officials have presented pieces of foam plastic as supposed evidence that drones recently shot down over the country were Russian, Moscow’s embassy in Bucharest has said.
Speaking to the Izvestia newspaper on Wednesday, the mission responded to Romania’s accusations that Russian UAVs have on numerous occasions strayed onto its territory during attacks on Ukrainian military-related sites.
During a meeting at Romania’s Foreign Ministry on the matter, Russian diplomats were shown “pieces of foam plastic” and were asked to regard them as evidence of the drones’ supposed Russian origin. “Naturally, we were provided with no facts linking these drones to our country,” the embassy said.
The mission suggested that the incidents amounted to a “prearranged performance” involving shooting at training targets, intended to justify Romania’s military buildup and higher defense spending. “The local political establishment has long pursued this goal and is actively implementing it in practice,” the embassy said, adding that Bucharest is purchasing expensive Western-made weapons with taxpayers’ money, justifying it by the alleged “threat from the East.”
Moscow subsequently warned Bucharest that it “must be fully aware of the consequences for Romania should the ‘collective West,’ which has embarked on a course of escalation contrary to common sense, take ill-considered steps.”
The dispute comes after the Romanian Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador Vladimir Lipayev in late July when Romanian F-16s shot down three drones that entered national airspace on three consecutive days. Officials in Bucharest blamed Russia, while Moscow said no evidence or technical flight data was provided to prove its involvement.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones aimed at Russian infrastructure have on numerous occasions fallen on NATO territory over the past several months, with Kiev acknowledging Ukrainian ownership in most cases but blaming Russian electronic warfare for diverting them. NATO nations have mostly refrained from criticizing Kiev.
In most cases, Romania continued to attribute its own incidents to Russia, including in May when a drone hit an apartment building in Galati, injuring two people. Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the time that the UAV’s origin could not be established without examining the wreckage, while recalling previous incidents with stray Ukrainian drones.
Pointing to earlier incidents in the Baltics, Putin noted that “the initial reaction was exactly the same as it is now in Romania: ‘Alarm! The Russians are coming!.. Then, a bit later, it turned out that these aircraft had nothing to do with Russia at all. They were Ukrainian drones that had gone off course.”

Mecca Agreement vision extends beyond Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan: President Erdogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:16:43 UTC
19:16:43 KST

The vision in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement "is not limited" to only Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday, expressing his desire to bring regional countries under the deal.
"Indeed, our vision is not limited to three countries. We want it to expand further and, if possible, one day bring all countries in the region under this framework. This would be one of the most important steps toward achieving lasting regional stability," Erdogan said in an interview with Asharq Al-Awsat, one of the leading Arabic newspapers.
While US-Iran tensions are important to regional developments, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement should not be viewed merely as a response to them, Erdogan said, adding: "Such an interpretation would fail to properly understand the policies and intentions of our countries."
Noting that the agreement does not pose a threat to any country, the president said the deal is open to participation by "all brotherly countries that seek peace, prosperity, and stability in our region."
There is a history behind the deal, Erdogan said, pointing to discussions with the other signatories and other regional countries that have been ongoing "for a very long period."
Noting his remarks on remaining in regular consultation with regional countries in order to strengthen peace, stability and security in the region, Erdogan said Ankara has acted "accordingly" in this regard.
"We know the kinds of disasters that externally imposed prescriptions have caused in attempts to resolve the region’s problems. For this reason, Türkiye has always pursued a policy aimed at making the will and collective wisdom of regional countries decisive," he said.
The deal is a representation of "a strategic determination" in response to changing regional circumstances, he said, adding that the trilateral mechanism is not a reaction to "day-to-day developments."
"Türkiye has always favored diplomacy over tension, dialogue over conflict, and stronger regional cooperation over division. As a country capable of speaking with all parties and assuming responsibility on difficult issues when necessary, we will continue to do our part to establish lasting peace and stability in our region," he further added.
The agreement is "the result of the new circumstances" and a shared sense of responsibility, Erdogan said.
"We have always favored regional countries taking ownership of regional issues and resolving them themselves," he added.
"The problems of the region should be resolved by the region’s own actors, and we can say that we have now taken the first step in that direction," he stressed.
Recent developments have highlighted the necessity of solidarity among friendly and brotherly nations, whereas long-term peace necessitates not only an end to conflict but also mutual trust, political will and a shared vision for the future, he noted.
The agreement represents more than cooperation among Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Erdogan said, adding that it is intended as a broader framework for regional stability and remains open to other countries seeking peace and security.
Ankara views the deal as the beginning of a new era of regional cooperation and solidarity, with the possibility of expanding participation in the future, he said.
Erdogan said the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement is built on the principle of collective deterrence and aims to deepen security and defense cooperation among its members while contributing to regional stability.
The agreement will pave the way for joint defense industry projects and strengthen cooperation in the fight against terrorism, he explained, stressing that it does not target any country.
Under the deal, a threat to one member’s security will be treated as a common security concern by the other parties, he said.
He added that the agreement should not be viewed solely as a military arrangement, saying its broader purpose is to reinforce deterrence, strengthen mutual security through solidarity and preserve peace and stability in the region.
Erdogan also said the signatories are sending a message that they will not pose a threat to one another but will instead work to guarantee each other’s security.
“The security of one of us is the security of all of us,” he said, adding that an inclusive application of this approach can help establish lasting peace, stability and prosperity across the region.
Erdogan said regional countries must take greater responsibility for their own security, stability and future, arguing that the region’s challenges are best addressed by its own countries and peoples.
Stronger regional ownership, solidarity and coordination will not only bolster stability in the Middle East but also contribute to global stability, the president said.
He stressed the importance of establishing stronger and more permanent mechanisms among regional countries, including institutionalized cooperation aimed at safeguarding both security and economic stability.
“The future of the region cannot be shaped independently of the will of the countries of the region,” Erdogan said.
He added that Türkiye does not seek exclusionary blocs, but rather a regional cooperation framework based on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, mutual trust and shared interests.
Türkiye, he said, will continue to assume responsibility when necessary and pursue diplomatic initiatives to strengthen regional peace, security and stability.
Erdogan said he believed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will help enhance security in the Gulf region, adding that it aims to promote the region’s prosperity, peace and security.
He underscored the importance of security in the Gulf region for the global economy and international trade.
The security of the Gulf region is of great importance not only to the countries of the region but also to the global economy and international trade.
"Many issues, from energy supply security and the safety of maritime routes to the continuity of trade and global economic stability, are directly connected to peace and stability in this region," he further said.
"This is not merely a theoretical statement; developments over the past few months have demonstrated it clearly," he added.
Erdogan said every step to strengthen security and stability in the Gulf would benefit not only the region but also global peace and prosperity.
He said the agreement could deepen regional security cooperation and solidarity, stressing that security and economic development are closely linked.
Pointing to Europe’s postwar experience, Erdogan said political stability can pave the way for economic integration and prosperity, adding that trade and investment cannot be sustained without peace.
He also described Gulf stability as strategically important for economic links connecting Asia, Europe and Africa, saying Türkiye views peace and stability in the Gulf as closely tied to its own security and to broader regional peace.
He expressed Türkiye's determination to assume "every responsibility that falls upon us and continue our constructive diplomatic efforts."
Erdogan said the Strait of Hormuz is of global strategic importance because of its role in energy supplies and international trade, warning that tensions there can have worldwide economic consequences.
He said Türkiye hopes the current tensions will ease and that the waterway will return to operating safely, stably and without disruption, stressing that this depends on restraint and keeping diplomatic channels open.
The president reiterated that Türkiye favors dialogue and negotiation over escalation, saying lasting solutions in Hormuz, Ukraine and Palestine can only be achieved through diplomacy.
He added that regional countries bear significant responsibility for the security of the Strait and said stronger regional cooperation and a shared security approach could help ensure its long-term stability.
"Our hope and expectation is that the current tensions will end as soon as possible and that the Strait of Hormuz will once again serve international trade safely, stably, and without interruption.
“Achieving this depends on the parties acting with common sense and keeping diplomatic channels open," he added.
Erdogan described Türkiye’s ties with Saudi Arabia as "a strategic relationship rooted in shared history, close bonds and mutual interests," saying cooperation between the two countries has gained momentum in recent years.
“We regard our relations with Saudi Arabia as a strategic relationship shaped by our shared history, bonds of brotherhood and mutual interests,” the president said.
He said Ankara and Riyadh are strengthening political dialogue while expanding cooperation in trade, investment, defense industries, energy and tourism.
“At a time when our region is undergoing very serious challenges, close consultation and cooperation between Türkiye and Saudi Arabia have become even more important,” he stressed.
Erdogan added that the agreement can further deepen bilateral ties, particularly in defense cooperation.
“We believe the Mecca Agreement will help further strengthen our relations in many areas, particularly defense cooperation,” he said.
He also stressed the wider regional impact of instability, saying even a limited crisis could affect neighboring countries through migration and terrorism.
“I believe that in the period ahead, we will take steps that will raise relations between our two countries to much higher levels.”
Erdogan said Lebanon’s security and stability are vital to regional peace, stressing the need to protect the country’s sovereignty, political unity and territorial integrity.
“Lebanon’s peace, security and stability are of great importance to the stability of our entire region,” he said, adding that Türkiye opposes foreign interference and efforts to turn Lebanon into “an arena of rivalry among external powers.”
He said the people of Lebanon should make decisions regarding their own future.
The president also called for an immediate end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon, saying: “Israel’s attacks against Lebanon must be brought to an immediate end.”
He welcomed ongoing efforts to secure a ceasefire, adding that Lebanon’s security “cannot be considered separately from regional peace.”
“The fate of the Middle East should not continually be written through conflict, destruction and suffering. This region also deserves peace, tranquility and prosperity,” he said.
Erdogan said Türkiye wants Lebanon to regain stability, strengthen its institutions and enable its people to look to the future with confidence.
He added that Ankara is ready to provide technical support and deepen cooperation, noting that this commitment was recently conveyed to Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam.
Erdogan described the developments in Syria as a “historic turning point,” saying the process should enable Syrians to determine their own future while preserving the country’s territorial integrity, political unity and sovereignty.
“We regard the process of change taking place in Syria as a historic turning point in terms of the Syrian people’s ability to determine their own future,” he said.
He added that Türkiye hopes the new period will lead to lasting peace, stability and reconstruction after years of war, terrorism and instability that have imposed high costs on the region.
Erdogan also stressed that Ankara will not tolerate any structure in Syria that threatens Türkiye’s national security.
“We will also not permit structures in northern Syria, or in any other part of the country, that threaten Türkiye’s security,” he said, adding that Syria’s territorial integrity and Türkiye’s national security are equally important.
He said Syria has made "great progress" since December 2024 in improving security conditions, setting the groundwork for economic development and achieving social reconciliation, with regional support for the Syrian government playing a crucial role.
Erdogan added that Syria’s normalization has become strategically important for the wider region, saying the country is increasingly being associated with connectivity and development projects rather than instability.
“Now that a new page has been opened in Syria, that page must be written not with new suffering, but with peace, brotherhood, sovereignty and a shared vision for the future,” he said.
The president vowed that Türkiye will continue supporting Syria’s stability and recovery in cooperation with regional and international partners.

How Chinese culture links 4 cardinal directions to life’s natural cycle – and why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:14:51 UTC
19:14:51 KST

How Chinese culture links 4 cardinal directions to life’s natural cycle – and why
In a primarily agricultural society, sunset signifies the end of the day, leading to the metaphor ‘going west’ to represent death
In traditional Chinese culture, the cardinal directions – east, west, south, and north – represent more than mere points on a compass; they reveal how ancient societies comprehended life, death, and human nature.
The Shuowen Jiezi, the earliest surviving dictionary of China compiled during the Eastern Han dynasty (25–220), explains the four cardinal directions in relation to the movement of the sun.
The east, or dong in Chinese, the direction of the sunrise, signifies spring, hope, and prestige. The Book of Rites delineates a ritual order where hosts occupy the east and guests the west, a practice mirrored in the households of ancient elites.
This association persists in modern Chinese: a landlord is literally referred to as “house east,” a shareholder as “stock east,” and the term zuo dong – to host a meal – means “to act as the east.”
In contrast, the west, or xi, symbolises endings and demise.

Head of US travel association sounds alarm on potential expansion of visa bond program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:14:47 UTC

Head of US travel association sounds alarm on potential expansion of visa bond program
NEW YORK, Aug 12 - The U.S. Travel Association said it is concerned the Trump administration's visa bond program could be broadened beyond the dozens of countries currently covered, a move it says would have a detrimental impact on the travel industry and economy.
The U.S. Department of State this month made permanent a visa bond program first launched as a pilot in August 2025, allowing consular officers to require certain tourist and business visa applicants from 50 countries to post refundable bonds of up to $20,000.
"There are already rumblings of expanding this program to additional countries where visas are required, perhaps all countries where visas are required," U.S. Travel Association President Geoff Freeman told Reuters. "That would have an extraordinarily detrimental effect on the U.S. economy, on the travel industry."
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The administration said visa issuances in the pilot countries fell 83% during the program's first 10 months, while overstays from those countries dropped from 45,488 in fiscal 2024 to fewer than 50 during the pilot period.
The 50 countries covered by the program are predominantly in Africa, with a smaller number in Asia, the Caribbean, Central Asia and Latin America. The administration said the program is aimed at reducing visa overstays from nationals of countries with high overstay rates or deficiencies in information-sharing, vetting and document security. New countries can be added to the list with 15 days' notice, the State Department said.
Under the rule, the bond can be forfeited if a traveler overstays or violates other conditions of their status.
Freeman said that while the countries currently covered by the program account for less than 2% of visitors to the United States, the U.S. travel industry is already nursing a 25% decline in travel from Canada, while travel from Asia is 50% of what it was in 2019.
Total overseas travel to the U.S. declined 4.3% year-to-date as of June, according to preliminary data from the National Travel and Tourism Office, including a 1.8% fall in June during the soccer World Cup.
Freeman said the industry had hoped policymakers would use lessons from the World Cup to encourage international visitation rather than adopt policies that discourage travel.
"If we can't have year-over-year increases in travelers during the World Cup, which we didn't, what the heck are we going to do in an average September?" REUTERS

Therefore, a certain part of the Polish economy depends on war refugees from Ukraine. In general, these are Ukrainians living in Poland, and we need to repeat this more and more often, because if we had a situation where one day all Ukrainians colluded and didn’t go to work, the Polish economy would come to a standstill," he said.

When asked whether refugees will start returning to Ukraine after the end of the war, Duszczyk replied that "this is a process that we have observed in other countries, and it is very easy to predict."
"It happens that those who claim ‘I am staying’ leave because something happens. And those who say, ‘I will leave as soon as the war ends’ stay. Of course, these trends change with every month as the roots they put down in the host society, in this case Polish society, become deeper and deeper. If someone has enrolled their children in school, they are learning the Polish language, if a person is working in the labor market, then the probability that they will return to Ukraine without a strong incentive to return is practically very low," he noted.

A record 4.41 million Ukrainians are under EU protection—and few are going home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:13:55 UTC
19:13:55 KST

The number of Ukrainian citizens holding temporary protection status in EU countries reached 4.41 million as of 30 June 2026, the highest since the mechanism was activated in March 2022, according to data published by Eurostat on 11 August. The total rose by 24,380 (+0.6%) from the previous month.
The displacement is one dimension of the broader demographic damage that Russia's war is inflicting on Ukraine. The country's population has contracted from over 41 million before the full-scale invasion to roughly 31 million, driven by displacement, war casualties, and a fertility rate that has collapsed to among the lowest in the world. Only 23% of Ukrainian women refugees with children say they plan to return, even if the war ends.
The figure has been edging upward since mid-2023. It crossed 4 million in September 2023, reached 4.2 million by October 2024, and has now hit a new high. New decisions granting protection are now falling: EU countries issued 155,640 in the first quarter of 2026, down 17% from the previous quarter, and 2025's annual total was 14% below 2024's — even as the overall number of people already holding the status keeps rising.
The numbers suggest an accumulation effect: fewer people are leaving the system than are entering it. Cumulatively, EU countries have issued 7.1 million temporary protection decisions since March 2022, meaning roughly 2.7 million of those decisions are no longer active — as people returned to Ukraine, moved on, switched to other residence statuses, or were deregistered.
- Germany hosted the most beneficiaries at about 1.29 million (29.2% of the EU total), followed by Poland with roughly 961,000 (21.8%) and Czechia with about 391,000 (8.9%).
- Relative to population, the ranking shifts. Czechia recorded 35.8 beneficiaries per thousand residents, followed by Slovakia (27.2) and Cyprus (26.8), against an EU average of 9.8 per thousand.
- Protection numbers rose in 24 of 27 EU countries. Italy posted the largest absolute increase (+4,115, or +8.8%), followed by Czechia (+3,835) and Germany (+2,960). Poland was the only country with a significant decrease (-6,335, or -0.7%). Belgium and Ireland posted negligible declines.
The EU just extended shelter for Ukrainians to 2028—with a new catch for military-age men
Ukrainian citizens accounted for over 98.5% of all beneficiaries. Adult women made up 43.4%, adult men 27%, and minors nearly a third (29.6%). The share of adult men has risen from 23% in October 2024, around the time Czech Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar's government pushed for the new military-compliance condition adopted by the Council in August.
The EU's temporary protection mechanism, activated in March 2022, has been renewed annually since. The most recent extension, a Council decision that took effect on 5 August, prolonged the framework to March 2028 while adding a new condition: Ukrainian men of military age applying for the first time must now prove they have met their mobilization obligations, including through Ukraine's Reserve+ app. The June data predates that rule, making it a baseline for measuring its impact.

Afghanistan will ensure safe rail route from Russia to India – Taliban spokesman

The full interview will be aired soon.
The Russia-India rail route was mooted by Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, who said last week that Moscow wants a rail link to the Indian Ocean to reduce risks from maritime disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. 
Khusnullin had said any options providing access to India would be acceptable, and suggested that routes could be explored through Turkmenistan, Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. 
Afghanistan is a resource-rich but landlocked country with no direct sea access. A rail link to the Indian Ocean, and India itself, would help Kabul increase its trade revenues.
The Taliban has largely brought peace to Afghanistan since taking power in Kabul following the withdrawal of US forces in 2021 after 20 years of war. 
Moscow and the Taliban government signed a military cooperation pact in May, aimed at strengthening Russia’s influence in Central Asia.
India is the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil, which has to transit the Bab-el-Mandeb chokepoint on the Red Sea and pass through the conflict zone around the Strait of Hormuz and Oman.
New Delhi and Moscow are also traditional friends, who share a robust defense relationship. Both nations have set a $100 billion goal for their bilateral trade by 2030.

Why Chris Philp wrong to say Burnham has had more small boat arrivals during his first 3 weeks than any other PM
In an interview with Times Radio, Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, claimed that Andy Burnham has had more small boat arrivals in his first three weeks in office than any other prime minister. Philp said:
Three thousand have entered our country in the first 22 days of Andy Burnham’s premiership, that is more … than any other prime minister has seen in their first 22 days.
The Press Association’s QuickCheck team have been looking at this – and they say Philp is wrong.
PA says:
Burnham’s first 22 days saw considerably fewer migrants cross the English Channel than the first 22 days of the premierships of Rishi Sunak and Liz Truss.
Government data shows 3,003 people crossed on small boats between July 20 when Burnham became prime minister and August 10, 22 days later.
In the first 22 days of Keir Starmer’s premiership, 2,258 people crossed the English Channel on small boats. In Sunak’s first 22 days, 4,105 people crossed, and the figure for the first 22 days of Liz Truss’s premiership was 4,739.
During Boris Johnson’s first 22 days in office, 138 people were recorded crossing the Channel.
Data collection on small boat crossings started in January 2018 so the figures do not include any other prime minister’s first 22 days.
Boat crossings are very seasonal, meaning prime ministers who enter the role in peak season are likely to see higher crossings in their first few weeks.
Between 2018 and 2025, the months that saw the most crossings were September (28,734 people), August (26,591), July (20,672), and October (20,324).
Starmer, Burnham and Johnson all became prime minister during July. Sunak became prime minister in late October and Truss took the role in early September.

Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, according to a report by Verdant, a Green thinktank.
The report is here, and here is Heather Stewart’s write-up.
The report says:
Successive heatwaves from May to the end of July 2026 have an estimated economic cost of at least £4.4bn. Previous estimates by Verdant placed the cost of the June 2026 heatwave alone at £2.36bn; this figure now includes all three heatwaves this year, from May to the end of July. May’s relatively minor event cost around £500m; July’s larger hit was £1.5bn, over two distinct peaks.
These losses are the result of reduced productivity due to the well-documented effect of all work becoming harder at higher temperatures, and that infrastructure and equipment overheat and fail. For each one degree Celsius temperature increase above 30 degrees in Europe, a 3% reduction in average output per hour has been observed. In a prolonged heatwave, these impacts add up to become significant economic losses. This is only the direct economic cost from productivity losses, and excludes things like losses from wildfires, or higher costs of energy for businesses and households.
Commenting on the report, Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said it showed why the government needed to “set out an emergency response to the danger facing us now, and the damage coming fast down the tracks as heatwaves and flooding get more extreme”.

Neglect, nature, and war are burying Sudan's Meroe pyramids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:11:18 UTC
19:11:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Neglect, nature and war are burying Sudan's Meroe pyramids
Two hundred kilometres north of Sudan's capital, Khartoum, sand accumulates inside the pyramids of the ancient city of Meroe. Regular maintenance of the site has been disrupted since April 2023 by the war in Sudan.
Amid these conditions, archaeologists have warned of possible collapses at the site, which contains royal tombs of rulers of the Kingdom of Kush and more than 200 pyramids built between the eighth century BC and the fourth century AD.
Signs of deterioration, according to Associated Press in a recent report, include structural cracks affecting several pyramids, the growth of weeds at the archaeological site, and the crystallisation of salts inside the sandstone, threatening ancient inscriptions and sculptures with erosion.
With the antiquities authority's limited ability to carry out regular maintenance, climate fluctuations throughout the year, such as seasonal floods and winds, have become significant threats to archaeological landmarks.
The damage caused by the war has affected Sudanese antiquities both at open-air sites and in museums, such as the National Museum and the Ethnographic Museum in Khartoum and the Khalifa House in [Omdurman], according to a UNESCO report in April.
The report recorded damage to more than 100 cultural and archaeological sites and the looting or destruction of 22 museums.
In addition to the direct damage caused to antiquities by the war and the suspension of archaeological teams, the lack of security at archaeological sites has led to the growth of illegal excavations.
Sudanese teams and international partners have made limited attempts to save archaeological sites, including removing sand, improving water drainage and restoring damaged sections.
These efforts have also included documentation work ultimately aimed at recovering looted artefacts, according to another UNESCO report issued last July.
Meroe Island, which has been on the World Heritage List since 2011, includes three archaeological groups: the royal city, the Meroe cemeteries and the Naqa site.
These groups contain pyramids, temples, palaces and water facilities that document the history of the Kingdom of Kush.
Meroitic architectural styles combine Mediterranean and Egyptian influences, as the rule of Kushite kings extended north to Egypt, while caravan routes crossing the Nile intersected there.
Because of its location, it also linked the African interior with Egypt and the Red Sea and served as a gateway for many peoples to the Mediterranean world through a network of commercial and cultural interactions.
The city, like the Nile Valley, witnessed developments in the history of ideas and religions.
Over more than 700 kilometres north of Khartoum, sites documenting successive eras are scattered across the region, according to a study by researchers Habbab Idris Ahmed and Geoff Emberling.
The study, titled "Archaeology and Cultural Heritage in Wartime: Sudan 2023–2025", was published in the British archaeology journal Antiquity in its October 2025 issue.
Sites documented by the study include the Kerma archaeological site, one of the oldest urban centres in Africa and the centre of the first phase of the Kingdom of Kush.
They also include Jebel Barkal, Napata, the cemeteries of El-Kurru and Nuri, and Christian Nubian kingdom cities such as Old Dongola.
The study also documents many sites dating to Islamic history, such as Suakin and Soba, among others.

Myanmar steps up civilian attacks with drones and paragliders, UN says
The attacks rose ahead of elections held in December and January, according to a team of UN investigators
The military increasingly relies on motorised paragliders, gyrocopters and drones for low-altitude strikes using unguided explosives, including mortar shells, according to the report. In several incidents in Sagaing region, paraglider pilots cut their engines as they approached targets and glided silently, giving civilians less warning and time to seek shelter.
Investigators also said casualties were exacerbated by so-called “double-tap” aerial attacks, in which the military strikes a target and then attacks again shortly afterwards, apparently targeting first responders, people helping the wounded and those trying to flee.
The mechanism said its investigations showed the frequency and intensity of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by Myanmar’s military and various armed groups continued to escalate over the past year. It also collected “extensive evidence” of arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence in military-run facilities, including cases linked to a 2025 law criminalising criticism of the elections.

New research from travel booking platform Klook reveals just how thankless the role of travel planning can be and has launched a global search for five planners keen on a chance to swap the spreadsheets for a Swiss getaway.
With great travel planning power comes great responsibility, but not always a vote of thanks…
Despite taking on the arduous role of mapping out spreadsheets, pinpointing a date that suits everyone’s calendar and creating a detailed itinerary, travel planners rarely get any credit for their efforts.
Now, new research from booking platform Klook, which surveyed 2,725 travellers across 10 countries, has found that travel planning ranks among the least thanked tasks people do for others.
The survey also found that for eight in 10 respondents, travel planning can take upwards of over 10 hours to organise a single trip.
And even handing over the reins doesn’t necessarily mean switching off, with 42% saying that even when someone else takes over planning, they continue quietly and anxiously monitoring the planning from the sidelines – ready to step in again at a moment’s notice.
That’s why Klook is looking to reward those long-suffering planners with the launch of its global search for five traveller planners at their wit’s end from being unappreciated.
For those looking to be promoted to “pampered passengers,” Klook is offering a treat of a seven-day hosted trip to Switzerland.
"We built Klook to make travel planning simpler, so travellers can spend less time on admin and more time on experiences," said Marcus Yong, VP of Global Marketing at Klook. "Now we're taking that promise one step further with a fully-planned getaway for five travel planners who always get travel right for their friends and families.
"It's their turn to take a vacation from planning vacations," he added.

This August, the search is on for travel planners that have tracked everything from bookings, backup plans and that one friend who hasn’t paid up yet, and are ready to travel planning-free so they can truly relax.
Five spaces are up for grabs on the seven-day VIP treatment to Switzerland this December, with round trip flights, premium accommodation and curated activities included – all preplanned and covered by Klook. Winners get to have a plus one accompany them, too.

President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would retaliate in kind if European countries carried out plans to seize Russian commercial vessels, describing the proposed measures as “piracy and robbery.”
“We see the authorities of certain countries attempting, in violation of international maritime law, to restrict the movement of vessels operated by our businesses,” Putin said during a meeting with Pacific Fleet personnel aboard the missile cruiser Varyag on Wednesday.
“And recently, they went so far as to consider seizing our vessels and selling the property they have plundered from us. This is, of course, nothing other than piracy and robbery.”
The warning follows the European Union’s adoption in July of a mechanism allowing member states to confiscate and sell Russian oil carried aboard shadow fleet vessels attempting to evade the bloc’s sanctions. The measure, introduced as part of the EU’s 21st sanctions package, also covers grain cargoes.
Putin said Russia would take similar action if European countries put the measures into practice, adding that Moscow’s response would not necessarily be confined to the same waters where Russian ships were seized.
“We will not necessarily act in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are being planned, but wherever we ourselves consider it necessary and appropriate. Anywhere, including in the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility,” he said.
Putin said the Defense Ministry had already received instructions to prepare a response.
Pacific Fleet Commander Viktor Liina then told Putin that the Russian military had conducted a “detailed analysis” of maritime traffic in the Asia-Pacific region.
“We know the routes, what they are carrying and whose ships they are,” Liina said.
He said 1,001 vessels had passed through Russia’s exclusive economic zone along the Kuril Islands between April 24 and Aug. 6, including 379 sailing under the flags of countries that Moscow officially classifies as “unfriendly.”
Those vessels included 273 dry bulk carriers and 71 tankers, Liina said. Twenty-six were British and nine were French.
EU countries and Britain have detained five tankers carrying Russian oil since the start of the year.
The MV South Star was stopped on July 20 in an operation involving EU countries. France intercepted the tankers Grinch, Deyna and Tagor before later releasing them, while Britain has held the Smyrtos, carrying 100,000 metric tons of oil, since June 14.
Sweden in March detained the dry cargo ship Caffa, which Kyiv said had been transporting grain from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory. Sweden’s Supreme Court ruled in August that the ship should be handed over to Ukraine.

The attacks, in the Gulf of Oman leading to the strait and at the entrance to the Red Sea – both chokepoints for global oil supplies – come as the war shows no signs of ending despite repeated assertions from US President Donald Trump of a deal being imminent.
Oil prices gained, and global shares retreated amid renewed pessimism about a quick end to the conflict. Brent crude futures climbed 1.4 per cent to settle at US$88.91 (S$113.75) per barrel, and US crude rose 1.3 per cent to US$83.20.
At the southern end of the Red Sea, four crew members were killed in a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Aug 11, Yemen’s Transport Ministry said. Two Yemeni rescuers from an anti-Houthi military group were also killed, Yemen’s Coast Guard said.
The fatalities aboard the Egyptian-owned Tihamah, if confirmed, would be the first deaths on shipping attributed to the Houthis since the Iran war began.
The Houthi-run news agency Saba reported that the group, which said in July it would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, attacked a Saudi ship it said was carrying military equipment in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It did not name the ship, and there was no immediate Saudi response to the report.
The US military, meanwhile, said a US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles to disable the steering gear of a Panama-flagged cargo ship.
The ship ignored repeated warnings to stop violating a naval blockade on Iranian ports, the US Central Command said. Maritime sources said the ship was hit off Pakistan while sailing into the Gulf of Oman.
‘Sort of negotiating’
Both Iran and the US have stepped up rhetoric in the past two days.
Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said on Aug 11 that the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping route will remain closed unless the US accepts Iran’s conditions to end the war: the release of Iran’s frozen assets and an end to conflicts throughout the region, including in Lebanon and Gaza.
That followed a new demand from Trump on Aug 10 that Iran should pay compensation for people killed in 50 years of wars, attacks and protests.
Throughout the conflict, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.
In an interview released late on Aug 10, he suggested the uncertainty could last for a while, saying he might just “bop along” and let Tehran fail economically, or hit them “really, really hard”.
“I am sort of negotiating,” Trump told Real America’s Voice. “They are very devious negotiators.”
Speaking to reporters after a visit to Ohio on Aug 11, Trump said: “Iran is going fine, going just absolutely fine.
“We totally control the Strait of Hormuz; nobody else, only us.”
He said of Iran: “At some point, maybe they will do something, and then they get blown away. But right now, we are in a very good position. We have a country that has been the bully of the Middle East for 50 years, really 51 if you think about it, and they are no longer the bully of the Middle East.”
Asked about an incident in which he switched planes in Turkey in July because of worries over reports of a potential Iranian assassination threat, Trump suggested the alternative aircraft may have faced greater risk.
“That would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he told reporters after The Washington Post broke the story about him secretly taking a military flight instead of Air Force One in an operation involving him being moved between aircraft in a catering truck.
“Any consequential president has a lot of threats,” Trump added. “I don’t worry about anything.”
The comments from Rezaei, appointed on Aug 9 as second-in-command of the body that coordinates Iran’s security and foreign policy, were the strongest indication the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen to shipping anytime soon. The waterway handled a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flow before the war.
“As long as America does not change its behaviour and does not accept Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened,” Rezaei said, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Thousands of people have been killed in the conflict since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb 28.
Iran has struck US assets and infrastructure in Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
Raising the prospect of further escalation, Mohammad Reza Naqdi, an adviser to the commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, said on Iranian state TV on Aug 11 that the corps was developing the ability to carry out operations “on enemy soil”.
“We need to be able to move the operations to the enemy’s soil, whenever this is needed and ordered,” he said. “This is the characteristic of the offensive doctrine that has to be attained.” REUTERS

Turkey's PKK peace law brings hope to mothers, anguish to veterans

Turkey's PKK peace law brings hope to mothers, anguish to veterans
DIYARBAKIR, Turkey/ANKARA, Aug 12 - Longing to be reunited with her son, Ayten Elhaman was glued to the television all day as Turkey’s parliament debated and passed a law this week enabling Kurdish militants to return home under a peace process to end their decades-old insurgency.
She recalled how Bayram had left his job in a bakery one morning nine years ago to join the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) in a conflict with NATO-member Turkey that has killed tens of thousands.
“My son, if you can hear me, come home. There is peace now. What is this war for anymore? Let no more children die,” she said at a vigil that has been running for seven years in the mainly Kurdish city of Diyarbakir, where mothers of PKK recruits are waiting in hope.
“That hope became the joy of all of Turkey. It became the joy of all mothers. In the end, it was mothers who suffered.”
The legislation passed late on Monday establishes a framework for the PKK’s disbandment. It paves the way for the return and reintegration of militants from hideouts in northern Iraq and the suspension of some prison sentences.
The move is a major step towards ending one of the world's longest-running insurgencies, which has killed 40,000 people, fuelled social division and, according to President Tayyip Erdogan, cost more than $2 trillion. If successful, it could become a legacy achievement of his 23 years in power.
WHY DID WE GO TO THE MOUNTAINS?
But military veterans and families of security personnel killed fighting the PKK voiced anger at the prospect of reintegrating into society people who have been viewed as terrorists for years.
Ibrahim Colakoglu, a veteran who showed the scars from a leg wound suffered in clashes with the group, said the prospect of former militants reentering society left him questioning the sacrifices made by Turkish soldiers who had battled the PKK in the mountainous southeast.
“If they were going to pass that law, why did I go to the mountains? Why did they send us there?” he told Reuters at a protest in Ankara seeking improved rights for military veterans.
The PKK, designated as a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the United States and European Union, took up arms against the state in 1984. Last year, jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disband and it agreed three months later.
At the Ankara protest, the head of an association for military veterans and the families of security force members killed in the conflict slammed the parliamentary move as “pardoning” the PKK.
“This is a great disgrace for the Republic of Turkey. As families of martyrs and veterans, we will never accept this," said association head Erdem Cercioglu. “These are baby killers, cruel people who have no understanding of humanity."
The PKK campaign initially sought an independent Kurdish state in southeast Turkey, but later refocused on seeking autonomy and Kurdish political rights.
HARD FOR SOCIETY TO DIGEST
Aydin Erdem, general manager of Istanbul-based KONDA Research and Consultancy, said that for all parties involved it was a difficult process to convince society that peace was coming.
"It is hard for society to digest because all of those PKK members have been called baby killers for the last three decades,” he told Reuters.
"On the other side, it's hard for Kurdish society to digest because they don't trust (Erdogan's) AKP and the state itself anymore."
Hatice Yasar, whose two sons joined the PKK and never returned, welcomed the prospect of peace, but was distrustful.
"We want peace this minute, but it must be an honourable peace," she said. "We trust the guerrillas, but we don't trust the state because for more than 100 years they have deceived us."
The new law does not deal with broader Kurdish demands for expanded political and cultural rights, changes to anti-terrorism legislation or the status of Ocalan, who has been imprisoned on Imrali island, in the Sea of Marmara south of Istanbul, since 1999.
Ahmet Buyukburc, whose younger brother was a Turkish soldier killed in the conflict, said in Diyarbakir he was not opposed to the reintegration of PKK militants, as long as they showed remorse.
“If people genuinely realise their mistakes and work for the good of society and the country, reintegration can succeed. If there is no sincerity, it will fail.” REUTERS

'Not a Marriott:' Tate brothers held in solitary confinement in Miami jail
